37469.q: Where does “Doctors Without Borders” get most of its money from?
37469.e: Most of the money comes from donations by private individuals. That way the organisation stays independent.
37469.m: Doctors Without Borders lives mainly on donations.

37470.q: What is “Doctors Without Borders” called in French?
37470.e: In French, the organisation is called “Médecins Sans Frontières”. That is why it is abbreviated to MSF.
37470.m: Doctors Without Borders is called Médecins Sans Frontières in French.

37471.q: What colour is the “Doctors Without Borders” logo?
37471.e: The logo shows a running figure in red. You can see it, for example, on the organisation's vehicles and tents.
37471.m: The Doctors Without Borders logo is red.

37472.e: “Doctors Without Borders” helps all people in need. Origin, religion or opinion make no difference.
37472.m: Doctors Without Borders helps all people in need.

37473.q: In which city is the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) based?
37473.e: The ITU is based in Geneva. Experts from almost every country meet there.
37473.m: The ITU is based in Geneva.

37474.q: What does the International Telecommunication Union deal with?
37474.e: The ITU makes sure that telephone, radio, television and internet work between countries. To do this, it makes common rules.
37474.m: The ITU deals with telephone, radio and internet.

37475.q: What special position does the ITU have in the UN?
a: It is the oldest specialised agency
It is the youngest specialised agency
37475.e: The ITU is the oldest specialised agency of the United Nations. It is even much older than the UN itself.
37475.m: The ITU is the oldest specialised agency of the UN.

37476.q: In which year was the International Telecommunication Union founded?
37476.e: The ITU was founded on 17 May 1865. So it is over 150 years old.

37477.q: How were messages sent when the ITU was founded?
37477.e: The ITU began as a telegraph union. With the telegraph, messages were sent along wires as short and long signals.
37477.m: In the past, messages were sent by telegraph.

37478.q: What does the ITU allocate to countries so that radios do not interfere with each other?
37478.e: The ITU shares out radio frequencies among countries. That way radio, mobile phones and satellites do not interfere with each other.

37479.q: What is Switzerland's international dialling code?
37479.e: Switzerland has the country code +41. The ITU sets such codes for all countries.

37480.q: What does the ITU also allocate for satellites?
37480.e: The ITU allocates orbits for satellites. That way satellites from different countries do not get in each other's way.
37480.m: The ITU assigns satellites their places in space.

37481.q: What do you call a form of government in which one person or a small group rules without any checks?
37481.e: In a dictatorship one person or a small group has all the power. Nobody can really keep them in check.
37481.m: In a dictatorship a few people rule without checks.

37482.q: May people in a dictatorship freely criticise the government?
a: Yes, but only on the radio
37482.e: In a dictatorship criticism of the government is often forbidden. Anyone who criticises it anyway can be punished.
37482.m: In a dictatorship you usually may not criticise the government freely.

37483.q: What often happens to newspapers in a dictatorship?
a: They always belong to the readers
They are checked by the people
37483.e: In dictatorships the state often decides what goes in the newspapers. So people only find out what the rulers want.
37483.m: In a dictatorship newspapers are often controlled by the state.

37484.q: What does a dictatorship often do with the internet?
a: It makes it free for everyone
37484.e: Many dictatorships block websites so that people cannot read free information. This is called censorship.

37485.q: What can happen in a dictatorship to people who protest against the government?
37485.e: In dictatorships people who protest are often locked up. The rulers want no resistance.
37485.m: Anyone who protests in a dictatorship often risks prison.

37486.q: What do you call a police force that secretly watches people in a dictatorship?
37486.e: A secret police secretly watches what people say and do. Many dictatorships have such a police force.
37486.m: Dictatorships often watch their people with a secret police.

37487.q: Why do some people flee from a dictatorship?
a: Because they are not free there
Because there are too many bikes there
Because the holidays there are too long
Because all schools there are free
37487.e: In a dictatorship many freedoms are missing, and some people are persecuted. That is why they seek protection in another country.
37487.m: Many people flee a dictatorship because they cannot live freely there.

37488.q: What do you call a ruler who decides alone and without any checks?
37488.e: A dictator has all the power in a country. Nobody may contradict him.
37488.m: A dictator rules alone and without checks.

37489.q: Which language does the word “dictator” come from?
37489.e: The word “dictator” comes from Latin. It is linked to “dictare”, which means to say aloud or to prescribe.
37489.m: The word dictator comes from Latin.

37490.q: Where did the office of dictator already exist over 2000 years ago?
37490.e: In ancient Rome a dictator could be appointed in an emergency. He then had all the power for a short time.
37490.m: Ancient Rome already had a dictator for emergencies.

37491.q: For how long was a dictator normally appointed in ancient Rome?
37491.e: A Roman dictator was usually appointed only for a short time, about six months at most. As soon as his task was done, he was supposed to give up power again.
37491.m: A Roman dictator normally ruled only for a short time.

37492.q: Which Roman had himself made dictator for life in 44 BC?
37492.e: Julius Caesar became dictator for life in 44 BC. He was murdered in the same year.
37492.m: Julius Caesar wanted to be dictator of Rome for ever.

37493.q: What was the name of the man who ruled Italy from 1922 and turned it into a dictatorship?
37493.e: Benito Mussolini came to power in Italy in 1922. After that he abolished freedoms step by step.
37493.m: Benito Mussolini was a dictator in Italy.

37494.q: What often hangs everywhere in schools and streets in dictatorships?
37494.e: Many dictators have their picture hung up everywhere. Everyone is supposed to see and worship them.
37494.m: Dictators often show their picture all over the country.

37495.q: How long does a dictator often stay in power?
37495.e: A dictator usually does not give up power voluntarily. He wants to rule as long as possible.
37495.m: A dictator usually wants to rule as long as possible.

37496.q: What do you do when you “dictate” something to someone?
a: You say it aloud for them to write down
37496.e: Dictating means saying aloud what someone else has to write down. A dictator tells everyone what they must do.
37496.m: When you dictate, you tell others what to write.

37497.q: What do you call it when a single person decides for a whole country?
37497.e: In an autocracy only one person has power. Everyone else has to obey.
37497.m: In an autocracy one person decides everything.

37498.q: Whom does an autocrat have to ask before making a decision?
37498.e: An autocrat does not have to ask anyone for permission. He decides everything himself.
37498.m: An autocrat doesn’t have to ask anyone.

37499.q: In a class, one child alone decides which game everyone plays. What do you call this way of deciding?
37499.e: If only one child decides and the others have no say, that child rules alone. In a vote everyone would be able to help decide.
37499.m: When one person decides for everyone, that is sole rule.

37500.q: What is a disadvantage when one person decides alone?
a: Everyone has to discuss for a long time
37500.e: When one person decides alone, the wishes of others are ignored. Mistakes are then often not corrected.
37500.m: When one person decides alone, other people’s opinions don’t count.

37501.q: What do you call a ruler who rules over people alone and cruelly?
37501.e: A tyrant is a ruler who uses his power cruelly. The word comes from Greek.
37501.m: A tyrant rules alone and cruelly.

37502.q: In an autocracy, who decides on war and peace?
a: The people at the ballot box
37502.e: In an autocracy the ruler also decides on war. The people are not asked.
37502.m: In an autocracy one person alone decides on war and peace.

37503.q: Why can the people hardly remove an autocrat?
a: Because he controls the army and police and there are no free elections
Because the people re-elect him every year
Because he must resign every four years
37503.e: An autocrat cannot be voted out. He often keeps the army and police on his side.
37503.m: It is very hard to get rid of an autocrat.

37504.q: What is usually missing in a dictatorship?
37504.e: In a dictatorship the people cannot vote freely. That is why they cannot replace the rulers.
37504.m: In a dictatorship there are usually no free elections.

a: Nobody sees whom you vote for
The election is held in the cellar
37505.e: In a secret ballot everyone fills in their ballot paper alone. That way nobody can put pressure on them.
37505.m: In a secret ballot nobody sees whom you vote for.

37506.q: What is often the case with elections in a dictatorship?
37506.e: In dictatorships there is often only one party or one candidate to vote for. The result is decided in advance.
37506.m: In a dictatorship voters often have no real choice.

37507.q: What does it mean when an election is rigged?
37507.e: In a rigged election votes are miscounted or made up. So whoever cheats wins.
37507.m: In a rigged election the result is deliberately changed.

37508.q: From what age can you vote in federal elections in Switzerland?
37508.e: For nationwide elections in Switzerland you must be 18 years old. This rule applies to Swiss citizens.
37508.m: In Switzerland you can vote nationally from 18.

37509.q: What is the container called that you put your ballot paper into in Switzerland?
37509.e: You put your ballot paper into a ballot box. Many people today also vote by post.
37509.m: Ballot papers go into a ballot box.

37510.q: How often is the National Council elected in Switzerland?
37510.e: The National Council is elected every four years. The last election was in autumn 2023.
37510.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

37511.q: Since which year have women in Switzerland been able to vote nationally?
37511.e: Swiss men voted in favour of women’s suffrage in 1971. Since then women have been able to vote in national elections and referendums.
37511.m: Since 1971 women in Switzerland have been able to vote nationally.

37512.q: Whom can you vote for in a free election?
37512.e: In a free election several parties and people are on offer. You may decide freely.
37512.m: In free elections you can choose between different parties.

37513.q: Who has to obey the laws in a democracy?
37513.e: In a democracy the laws apply to everyone. Even those who govern are not above the law.
37513.m: In a democracy the laws also apply to the government.

37514.q: In which city was there an early democracy around 2500 years ago?
37514.e: In ancient Athens free men could help decide in an assembly. But women and slaves were not allowed to take part.
37514.m: There was an early democracy in ancient Athens.

37515.q: Is Switzerland a democracy or a dictatorship?
37515.e: In Switzerland the people elect their parliament and vote often. That is why it is a democracy.

37516.q: What do you call it when the people vote on issues themselves, as in Switzerland?
37516.e: In a direct democracy the people vote on laws themselves. Switzerland is famous for it.
37516.m: In a direct democracy the people vote on issues themselves.

37517.q: About how many voting dates for federal proposals are there in Switzerland each year?
37517.e: Each year the Federal Council sets up to four voting dates. Several proposals can be voted on at one date.
37517.m: In Switzerland there are national votes about four times a year.

37518.q: In which canton do people still vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde?
37518.e: In the canton of Glarus the voters gather in a square every year and vote by raising their hands. Appenzell Innerrhoden also still has the Landsgemeinde.
37518.m: In Glarus people vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde.

37519.q: How many signatures does a popular initiative need in Switzerland?
37519.e: A popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures within 18 months. Then the people vote on it.

37520.q: Why is power in a country shared among several people?
a: So that nobody becomes too powerful
So that there are more posters
So that nobody has to work
37520.e: When several people share power, nobody can decide everything alone. This makes abuse harder.
37520.m: Shared power stops anyone becoming too powerful.

37521.q: How does the Swiss Federal Council make decisions?
37521.e: The Federal Council decides together as a body. Afterwards all members stand by the decision in public.

37522.q: How many cantons does Switzerland have?
37522.e: Switzerland has 26 cantons. They have many rights of their own and share power with the Confederation.

37523.q: What do you call a country in which cantons or states have many rights of their own?
37523.e: In a federal state the federal government and the member states share power. Switzerland and Germany are federal states.
37523.m: In a federal state the Confederation and the cantons share power.

37524.q: What is the government of a Swiss municipality often called?
37524.e: In many municipalities the government is called the municipal council. In towns it is often called the town council.
37524.m: A municipality is often run by a municipal council.

37525.q: What is the government called in many Swiss cantons?
37525.e: In most German-speaking cantons the government is called the Regierungsrat. In French-speaking Switzerland it is often called the Council of State.
37525.m: Many cantons are run by a Regierungsrat.

37526.q: How many parties are represented in the Swiss Federal Council (as of 2025)?
37526.e: The Federal Council has members from the SVP, SP, FDP and The Centre. In this way the big parties share the government.
37526.m: Four parties share power in the Federal Council.

37527.q: Into how many branches is state power divided under the separation of powers?
37527.e: State power is divided into three parts: making laws, governing and judging. Each part has its own people.
37527.m: Under the separation of powers there are three branches.

37528.q: Who makes the laws at federal level in Switzerland?
37528.e: Parliament is called the Federal Assembly and passes the laws. The people can often still have a say.

37529.q: Who forms the government of Switzerland?
37529.e: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It makes sure that the laws are carried out.
37529.m: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland.

37530.q: Who judges when someone has broken a law?
37530.e: Courts decide whether someone has broken a law. They are independent of the government.
37530.m: Courts decide what is right and wrong under the law.

37531.q: In which city is the Swiss Federal Supreme Court based?
37531.e: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland. It is in Lausanne.
37531.m: The Federal Supreme Court is in Lausanne.

37532.q: What is the building in Bern where the Swiss parliament meets called?
37532.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace in Bern. The Federal Council also works there.
37532.m: Parliament meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.

37533.q: How many members does the Swiss National Council have?
37533.e: The National Council has 200 members. Big cantons have more seats than small ones.

37534.q: What about the separation of powers in a dictatorship?
a: It is elected by the people
37534.e: In a dictatorship the ruler often holds all three branches of power. That is why nobody checks him.
37534.m: In a dictatorship the separation of powers is usually missing.

37535.q: In Switzerland, what do you call the people as the highest power in the state?
37535.e: In Switzerland people say that the people are the sovereign. They have the last word in votes.
37535.m: In Switzerland the people are the sovereign.

37536.q: Does a dictator ask the people for permission before taking power?
37536.e: A dictator usually takes power without the people’s consent. Violence often helps him do so.
37536.m: A dictator does not ask the people for permission.

37537.q: In a democracy, from whom does power in the state come?
37537.e: In a democracy the people have the highest power. This is called popular sovereignty.
37537.m: In a democracy power comes from the people.

37538.q: How many signatures does a referendum against a federal law need in Switzerland?
37538.e: With 50,000 signatures within 100 days you can demand a popular vote on a new law. Then the people decide.

37539.q: Who must agree in Switzerland when the Federal Constitution is changed?
37539.e: A change to the Federal Constitution needs a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons. It cannot happen without the people.
37539.m: A new constitutional rule needs the people and the cantons.

37540.q: What do you call a state headed by a king or queen?
37540.e: In a monarchy a king, a queen or a prince is the head of state. Switzerland, on the other hand, has no king.
37540.m: A state with a king or queen is called a monarchy.

37541.q: What does “mono” mean in the word monarchy?
37541.e: “Monos” is Greek and means alone. So monarchy means rule by one person.
37541.m: Monarchy means rule by one person.

37542.q: Which of Switzerland’s neighbours is a principality?
37542.e: Liechtenstein is a principality with a prince at its head. It lies between Switzerland and Austria.

37543.q: Who was King of the United Kingdom in 2025?
37543.e: Charles III became king in 2022 after his mother Elizabeth II died. The United Kingdom is a monarchy.
37543.m: Charles III is King of the United Kingdom.

37544.q: Does the King of the United Kingdom decide alone about his country today?
a: Yes, he makes all the laws
37544.e: In the United Kingdom the elected parliament makes the laws. The king mainly has ceremonial duties.
37544.m: The British king does not rule alone.

37545.q: What do you call a monarchy in which the king rules completely alone and without limits?
37545.e: In an absolute monarchy the king has all the power. That is very similar to a dictatorship.
37545.m: In an absolute monarchy the king rules without limits.

37546.q: Which French king is said to have said: “I am the state”?
37546.e: Louis XIV ruled France as an absolute king. The famous sentence is attributed to him, but it is uncertain whether he really said it.
37546.m: Louis XIV is seen as an example of an absolute king.

37547.q: Who governs under a military government?
37547.e: Under a military government officers and generals take power. The people then have no say.
37547.m: Under a military government the army rules.

37548.q: What do you call a group of officers who govern a country?
37548.e: A military junta is a group of officers in power. It governs without elections.
37548.m: A junta is a group of officers in power.

37549.q: Which language does the word “junta” come from?
37549.e: “Junta” is Spanish and means assembly or council. The word became known through military governments in Spain and South America.
37549.m: The word junta comes from Spanish.

37550.q: In which country did General Pinochet take power with the army in 1973?
37550.e: On 11 September 1973 the army in Chile overthrew the elected government. General Augusto Pinochet then ruled until 1990.
37550.m: General Pinochet led a military government in Chile from 1973 to 1990.

37551.q: When does Switzerland elect a general?
a: Only in war or great danger
37551.e: In normal times Switzerland has no general. One is elected only when there is a major threat.
37551.m: Switzerland only has a general in war or great danger.

37552.q: Who elects the general in Switzerland in an emergency?
a: The President of the Confederation alone
37552.e: The general is elected by the United Federal Assembly. This keeps the army under political control.
37552.m: In Switzerland parliament elects the general.

37553.q: What was the name of the Swiss general in the Second World War?
37553.e: Henri Guisan was elected general in 1939. He led the Swiss army during the Second World War.
37553.m: Henri Guisan was the Swiss general in the Second World War.

37554.q: What does a military government often impose so that nobody may go out at night?
37554.e: Under a curfew people may not go outside at certain times. The military government wants to prevent protests this way.
37554.m: A curfew forbids going outside at certain times.

37555.q: In a democracy, who is above the army?
37555.e: In a democracy elected politicians decide about the army. Under a military government it is the other way round.
37555.m: In a democracy the elected government commands the army.

37556.q: What do you call it when a group suddenly overthrows the government by force?
37556.e: In a coup a small group seizes power. It happens suddenly and against the law.
37556.m: A coup is a sudden overthrow of the government by force.

37557.q: Which language does the word “putsch” come from?
37557.e: The word “putsch” comes from Switzerland. From there it spread all over the world.
37557.m: The word putsch comes from Swiss German.

37558.q: What did the dialect word “Putsch” originally mean?
37558.e: Originally “Putsch” meant a push or a clash. Later the word was used for an uprising.
37558.m: Putsch used to mean a push.

37559.q: Which overthrow in 1839 made the word “putsch” well known?
37559.e: In 1839 the government in Zurich was overthrown. Newspapers reported on it, and so the word became known throughout the German-speaking world.
37559.m: The Züriputsch of 1839 made the word putsch well known.

37560.q: Who carries out a military coup?
37560.e: In a military coup soldiers and officers overthrow the government. Afterwards generals often rule.
37560.m: In a military coup the army overthrows the government.

37561.q: What do coup plotters often take over first?
37561.e: Whoever controls the stations can announce news to the whole country. That is why coup plotters often take them over first.
37561.m: Coup plotters often take over radio and TV first.

37562.q: Which term means almost the same as “putsch”?
37562.e: A coup d’état is a violent overthrow of the government. It is also called a putsch.
37562.m: A coup d’état is the same as a putsch.

37563.q: In which city did Adolf Hitler attempt a putsch in 1923?
37563.e: In November 1923 Hitler wanted to seize power in Munich. The putsch failed, and he went to prison.
37563.m: Hitler’s putsch in Munich in 1923 failed.

37564.q: Is a coup a permitted way of changing the government?
a: No, it goes against the constitution
Yes, if the people are unhappy
Yes, if the president is ill
37564.e: A coup gets round the rules of the constitution. That is why it is not lawful.
37564.m: A coup is not a lawful change of power.

37565.q: How does the government normally change in a democracy?
37565.e: In a democracy the people decide at the ballot box who governs. This way power can change hands peacefully.
37565.m: In a democracy power changes through elections.

37566.q: How long does someone remain President of the Swiss Confederation?
37566.e: The office passes to a different member of the Federal Council every year. That way nobody gets too much power.
37566.m: In Switzerland the presidency changes every year.

37567.q: What does a government in a democracy do if it loses an election?
37567.e: In a democracy the loser of an election gives up power. This is called a peaceful transfer of power.
37567.m: In a democracy the loser of an election hands over power peacefully.

37568.q: What do you call it when the people overthrow a government through mass protests?
37568.e: In a revolution a large part of the people rises up. In a coup only a small group acts.
37568.m: In a revolution the people overthrow the government.

37569.q: Which wall fell in 1989 after peaceful protests?
37569.e: On 9 November 1989 East Germany opened the Berlin Wall. Before that many people had demonstrated peacefully.

37570.q: In which country did a famous revolution against the king begin in 1789?
37570.e: The French Revolution began in 1789. The king later lost his power and his life.

37571.q: What do you call the person who will be the next king or queen?
37571.e: The heir to the throne takes the crown when the king dies or abdicates. It is usually the eldest child.
37571.m: The heir to the throne becomes the next king.

37572.q: Who elects the members of the Federal Council in Switzerland?
37572.e: The National Council and the Council of States elect the Federal Councillors together. The people do not elect them directly.
37572.m: The Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.

37573.q: Which statue in New York is a symbol of freedom?
37573.e: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York harbour. It is a well-known symbol of freedom.
37573.m: The Statue of Liberty in New York stands for freedom.

37574.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the USA?
37574.e: France gave the statue to the USA. It was unveiled in 1886.
37574.m: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France.

37575.q: What does the Statue of Liberty hold in her raised hand?
37575.e: The Statue of Liberty holds a torch up high. The light is meant to show the way to freedom.
37575.m: The Statue of Liberty holds a shining torch.

37576.q: Which hero from a Swiss legend is seen as a symbol of freedom?
37576.e: In the legend William Tell fights against the wicked bailiff Gessler. He stands for the freedom of the Swiss.
37576.m: William Tell is a Swiss freedom hero from legend.

a: At eight o’clock in the evening
37577.e: I may do a lot, but I must not harm others. That is why my freedom has limits too.
37577.m: My freedom ends where I would harm others.

37578.q: What do you call people who in the past belonged to other people and were not free?
37578.e: Slaves were not free and had to work for their owners. Today slavery is banned everywhere.

37579.q: What does a bird get when you open its cage and it flies away?
37579.e: Without a cage the bird can decide for itself where to fly. That is freedom.
37579.m: You are free when you can decide for yourself where to go.

37580.q: What is the important UN document from 1948 that promises freedom to all people called?
37580.e: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights says: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
37580.m: All human beings are born free and equal in rights.

37581.q: According to human rights, who has a right to freedom?
37581.e: Human rights apply to all people in the world. Nobody is excluded.
37581.m: Human rights apply to all people.

37582.q: Which law states that you may speak your mind freely in Switzerland?
37582.e: Freedom of expression is in Article 16 of the Federal Constitution. It is a fundamental right.
37582.m: Freedom of expression is protected in the Federal Constitution.

37583.q: In Switzerland, may you say that you think a law is bad?
37583.e: Thanks to freedom of expression you may criticise laws and politicians. But you must respect others when you do.
37583.m: Criticising laws is allowed in Switzerland.

37584.q: Does freedom of expression allow you to insult other people?
37584.e: Freedom of expression has limits too. Anyone who abuses and belittles others can be punished.
37584.m: Freedom of expression does not allow insults.

37585.q: Do children also have the right to say what they think?
37585.e: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child gives children the right to express their views freely.
37585.m: Children may also say what they think.

37586.q: What should you do if someone has a different opinion from you?
37586.e: Freedom of expression applies to everyone. That is why you listen respectfully to other opinions too.

37587.q: In which council can pupils give their opinions in many schools?
37587.e: In the school council children discuss wishes and ideas for the school. That way they practise saying what they think.
37587.m: In the school council children give their views on the school.

37588.q: What do you call a newspaper article in which journalists write their own opinion?
37588.e: A commentary shows the writer’s opinion. A news report, on the other hand, should only report facts.
37588.m: A commentary shows an opinion; a news report shows facts.

37589.q: What is the difference between an opinion and a fact?
a: An opinion is your own view
37589.e: “Pizza tastes best” is an opinion. “Bern is the federal city” is a fact.
37589.m: An opinion is a view; a fact can be checked.

37590.q: What is press freedom called in the Swiss Federal Constitution?
37590.e: Article 17 of the Federal Constitution is called “Freedom of the media”. It protects newspapers, radio, TV and other media.
37590.m: In the Federal Constitution press freedom is called media freedom.

37591.q: What do you call people who write reports for newspapers?
37591.e: Journalists gather information and write reports. Press freedom protects their work.

37592.q: On which day is World Press Freedom Day?
37592.e: The UN declared 3 May World Press Freedom Day. On this day people remember persecuted journalists.
37592.m: World Press Freedom Day is on 3 May.

37593.q: What is a well-known organisation that stands up for journalists called?
37593.e: Reporters Without Borders helps persecuted journalists. Every year it publishes a press freedom ranking.
37593.m: Reporters Without Borders stands up for journalists.

37594.q: Which country was ranked first in the press freedom index in 2026?
37594.e: According to Reporters Without Borders, Norway was first in 2026, as in previous years. Journalists there can work very freely.
37594.m: Norway had the greatest press freedom in the world in 2026.

37595.q: What is press freedom like in Switzerland?
a: Only the Federal Council may write
37595.e: Switzerland has been near the top of the Reporters Without Borders ranking for years. Journalists can work freely here.
37595.m: Switzerland is one of the countries with good press freedom.

37596.q: Which invention by Gutenberg made it easier to produce many newspapers and books?
37596.e: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type. This meant texts could be copied quickly.

37597.q: Must a journalist always reveal who told them a secret?
37597.e: Journalists may protect their sources. The Swiss Federal Constitution guarantees editorial confidentiality for this.
37597.m: Journalists may keep their informants secret.

a: So that everyone is well informed
So that there are more adverts
37598.e: Free newspapers also report on the mistakes of powerful people. That way everyone can form their own opinion.
37598.m: A free press helps everyone to be well informed.

37599.q: What does freedom of assembly mean?
a: You must go to church every day
37599.e: Freedom of assembly means people may meet peacefully to discuss something or show something together.

37600.q: What is the meeting called at which all members of a club meet once a year?
37600.e: At the general meeting the members of a club come together. For example, they elect the committee and decide things together.
37600.m: At the general meeting club members decide together.

37601.q: At the Landsgemeinde, how do you show that you agree?
37601.e: At the Landsgemeinde you raise your hand or your voting card. That shows how many people are in favour.
37601.m: At the Landsgemeinde people vote with a raised hand.

37602.q: What may people set up thanks to freedom of association?
37602.e: In Switzerland you may set up clubs, for example a football club or a choir. This is freedom of association.
37602.m: In Switzerland you may freely set up clubs.

37603.q: What is the meeting called at which voters in many Swiss villages vote?
37603.e: At the municipal assembly voters decide, for example, on a new school building.
37603.m: At the municipal assembly the people of the village have a say.

37604.q: In Switzerland, may you hold a gathering to protest against something?
37604.e: The Federal Constitution protects peaceful gatherings. You may also use them to show that you are against something.
37604.m: Peaceful protests are allowed in Switzerland.

37605.q: In a dictatorship, who is often not allowed to hold meetings?
37605.e: Dictatorships often ban meetings of critics. They are afraid that people will join together against them.
37605.m: Dictatorships often ban meetings of critics.

37606.q: What does freedom of religion mean?
37606.e: With freedom of religion everyone may decide for themselves what they believe. Nobody may be forced.
37606.m: Everyone may decide for themselves what they believe.

37607.q: In Switzerland, may you also belong to no religion at all?
37607.e: Freedom of religion also allows you to belong to no religion. Nobody has to join a church.
37607.m: You may also live without a religion.

37608.q: What is the Christian place of worship called?
37608.e: Christians pray in church. In Switzerland there is a church in almost every village.

37609.q: What is the Muslim place of worship called?
37609.e: Muslims pray in a mosque. There are mosques in Switzerland too.

37610.q: What is the Jewish place of worship called?
37610.e: Jewish people pray in the synagogue. There is a large synagogue in Basel, for example.

37611.q: With freedom of religion, what is important towards people of another faith?
37611.e: Freedom of religion applies to everyone. That is why you also respect people who believe differently.
37611.m: People of other faiths deserve respect.

37612.q: In Switzerland, does a child have to attend the church’s religious education lessons?
37612.e: Because of freedom of belief nobody may be forced to attend religious education. Parents have a say.
37612.m: Nobody has to attend religious education against their will.

37613.e: A censor checks texts, films or pictures. Anything the government doesn’t like, he bans or cuts.
37613.m: A censor cuts things the government does not want.

37614.q: Does the Swiss Federal Constitution say that censorship is forbidden?
37614.e: Article 17 of the Federal Constitution says clearly: censorship is prohibited.

37615.q: How is it often made visible in a text that something has been censored?
37615.e: Censored passages are often painted over with black bars. That way they can no longer be read.
37615.m: Black bars often cover censored passages.

37616.q: Under censorship, what often happens to a banned book?
37616.e: Banned books may not be printed or sold. Sometimes they are even collected up.
37616.m: Censored books often cannot be bought.

37617.q: Who usually carries out censorship in dictatorships?
37617.e: In dictatorships the government decides what may be published. Criticism is often banned.
37617.m: In dictatorships the government decides what people may read.

37618.q: Why may some films only be watched from a certain age?
37618.e: Age limits protect children from content that could frighten them. That is child protection, not censorship.
37618.m: Age limits on films protect children.

a: You say nothing out of fear
37619.e: In self-censorship you choose to stay silent because you are afraid of punishment. This often happens in dictatorships.
37619.m: If you stay silent out of fear, you are censoring yourself.

37620.q: In a country with strict censorship, what do people often not get to hear?
37620.e: Censorship is mainly meant to prevent criticism. People then don’t find out what the government is doing wrong.
37620.m: Censorship often hides criticism of the government.

37621.q: What is important in free elections?
a: You must vote for the king
37621.e: In free elections there are several options. Everyone votes for whoever they want, without being forced.
37621.m: In free elections everyone decides for themselves.

37622.q: How can you vote in Switzerland without going to the polling station?
37622.e: In Switzerland most people vote by post. They send the envelope through the post.
37622.m: In Switzerland you can vote by post.

37623.q: What is the paper you write the names on in an election called?
37623.e: On the ballot paper you write the names of the people you want to vote for.
37623.m: You write the names on the ballot paper.

37624.q: How many votes does each voter have in a vote?
37624.e: Every vote counts equally. This is called equal suffrage.

37625.q: What do you call groups like the SP, the SVP or the FDP?
37625.e: Parties are groups of people with similar political ideas. You can vote for them in elections.
37625.m: Parties are what you choose between in elections.

37626.q: Which election will next take place in Switzerland in 2027?
37626.e: The National Council was elected in 2023. The next National Council election is in 2027.
37626.m: The next National Council election is in 2027.

37627.q: How is a class representative often chosen in a class?
37627.e: Many classes elect their representatives with slips of paper. That way the children practise how an election works.
37627.m: You can vote freely in class too.

37628.q: Who counts the votes after an election in Switzerland?
37628.e: At the electoral office helpers count the votes carefully.
37628.m: The electoral office counts the votes.

37629.q: In a free election, may anyone order you whom to vote for?
37629.e: In free elections nobody may put pressure on you. Everyone votes according to their own opinion.
37629.m: Nobody may tell you whom to vote for.

37630.q: What do people do at a demonstration?
a: They show their opinion in public
37630.e: At a demonstration people go out onto the streets together. This is how they show what matters to them.
37630.m: At a demonstration people show their opinion.

37631.q: What do people often carry at a demonstration?
37631.e: Placards and banners show demands. That way everyone can see what it is about.
37631.m: People often carry placards at demonstrations.

37632.q: What do you need in many Swiss towns to hold a demonstration in the street?
37632.e: The town issues a permit. That way it can divert traffic and make sure everything is safe.

37633.q: What is the short form of demonstration?
37633.e: Instead of demonstration people often just say “demo”.
37633.m: A demonstration is also called a demo.

37634.q: What did many pupils demonstrate for in 2019, including in Switzerland?
37634.e: During the climate strike many young people took to the streets. They demanded more protection for the climate.
37634.m: In the climate strike young people demonstrated for the climate.

37635.q: What did many women in Switzerland demonstrate for on 14 June 1991?
37635.e: In the women’s strike of 1991 many women demanded equal rights and equal pay with men.
37635.m: In 1991 women in Switzerland went on strike for equal rights.

37636.q: Who led a big demonstration in Washington in 1963 and said “I have a dream”?
37636.e: Martin Luther King fought peacefully for equal rights for black people in the USA.
37636.m: Martin Luther King demonstrated peacefully for equal rights.

37637.q: Who led the peaceful Salt March in India in 1930?
37637.e: With the Salt March Gandhi protested against British rule. He always relied on non-violence.

37638.q: What is forbidden at a demonstration?
37638.e: Demonstrations are only allowed if they are peaceful. Anyone who uses violence or damages things is punished.

37639.q: What is a letter to the editor?
37639.e: In a letter to the editor readers write their opinion to the newspaper. Some are printed.
37639.m: With a letter to the editor you tell the newspaper your opinion.

37640.q: Who decides whether a letter to the editor appears in the newspaper?
37640.e: The editorial team chooses which letters are printed. It may also shorten long letters.
37640.m: The editorial team chooses the letters.

37641.q: What do you usually have to give in a letter to the editor?
37641.e: Newspapers usually only print letters with the writer’s name and town. Completely anonymous letters are rarely printed.
37641.m: A letter to the editor usually carries the writer’s name.

37642.q: What should a good letter to the editor be like?
37642.e: Short, polite letters are more likely to be printed. No newspaper prints insults.
37642.m: A good letter to the editor is short and polite.

37643.q: What do you usually write about in a letter to the editor?
37643.e: A letter to the editor often replies to an article. You say whether you agree or not.
37643.m: Letters to the editor often reply to an article.

37644.q: Which right are you using when you write a letter to the editor?
37644.e: When you write a letter to the editor you express your opinion in public. This is protected by freedom of expression.
37644.m: A letter to the editor is freedom of expression in action.

37645.q: How does a letter to the editor often begin?
37645.e: A letter to the editor is addressed to the newspaper’s editorial team. That is why it often begins with “Dear Editor”.
37645.m: A letter to the editor is addressed to the editorial team.

37646.q: May children write a letter to the editor too?
37646.e: Children may also say what they think. Children’s magazines like to print letters from children.
37646.m: Children may write letters to the editor too.

37647.q: Who is a children’s magazine made for?
37647.e: Children’s magazines explain news and knowledge in a way that children understand well.
37647.m: Children’s magazines are made for children.

37648.q: What is a well-known Swiss magazine for children called?
37648.e: “Spick” is a Swiss magazine for children. The others are newspapers and magazines for adults.
37648.m: Spick is a Swiss children’s magazine.

37649.q: Why is news for children important?
a: So that parents get some peace
37649.e: Children’s news explains what is happening in the world. That way children can join in and form an opinion.
37649.m: Children’s news explains the world to children.

37650.q: What is a well-known news programme for children on German television called?
37650.e: “logo!” is a news programme for children on ZDF. It explains the news simply.
37650.m: logo! explains the news to children.

37651.q: How often does a monthly magazine come out?
37651.e: A monthly magazine comes out once a month. A daily newspaper comes out every day.
37651.m: A monthly magazine comes out every month.

37652.q: What can children do for a school newspaper?
37652.e: For a school newspaper children write their own reports and interviews. That way they learn how journalists work.
37652.m: Children write the school newspaper themselves.

37653.q: What do you call a conversation in which a reporter asks someone questions?
37653.e: In an interview you ask questions and write down the answers. Children’s magazines often have them.
37653.m: In an interview you ask questions.

37654.q: What should a good newspaper for children do?
37654.e: Children’s magazines should tell the truth too. They explain difficult things in simple language.
37654.m: Good children’s news is true and easy to understand.

a: You may use the internet freely
The internet is free of charge
37655.e: With internet freedom the state does not block websites just because they contain criticism.
37655.m: Internet freedom means the state does not block critical websites.

37657.q: In which country are almost no people allowed on the global internet?
37657.e: In North Korea only very few people have access to the global internet. The government controls everything.
37657.m: In North Korea the internet is almost completely blocked.

37658.q: What should you do before you believe a piece of news on the internet?
37658.e: There is also false news on the internet. That is why you check whether the source can be trusted.
37658.m: Check news on the internet before you believe it.

37659.q: What do you call deliberately false news on the internet?
37659.e: Fake news is made-up news. It is meant to deceive people.

37660.q: May you spread nasty lies about other people on the internet?
37660.e: Laws apply on the internet too. Insults and lies about others are forbidden.
37660.m: Lies about others are forbidden on the internet too.

37661.q: What do you call it when someone is repeatedly picked on on the internet?
37661.e: In cyberbullying someone is insulted or shown up on the internet. That is not part of freedom of expression.
37661.m: Cyberbullying is hurtful and not allowed.

37662.q: What do some governments do so that people cannot open certain websites?
37662.e: Blocked websites can no longer be opened in the country. Governments want to hide criticism this way.

37663.q: In Switzerland, do parents have to pay for school books at state primary and lower secondary school?
37663.e: The Federal Constitution promises free basic schooling. That is why teaching materials at state schools are free.
37663.m: School books at state schools in Switzerland are free.

37664.q: What are school books and other teaching materials often called in Switzerland?
37664.e: In Switzerland school books are often called “Lehrmittel”, teaching materials. This also includes workbooks.
37664.m: In Switzerland school books are often called teaching materials.

37665.q: What should good school books show in a democracy?
37665.e: In a democracy school books should inform in a factual way. Children should learn to think for themselves.
37665.m: Good school books show the truth.

37666.q: What is often written in school books in dictatorships?
37666.e: Dictatorships change school books so that the ruler looks good. That is a form of propaganda.
37666.m: In dictatorships school books often praise the ruler.

37667.q: Where can you borrow books for free in Switzerland?
37667.e: At libraries you can borrow books for free or very cheaply. That way everyone has access to knowledge.
37667.m: You can borrow books at the library.

37668.q: What do children learn when they read different books?
37668.e: Anyone who reads many books gets to know different opinions. That way you can form your own picture.
37668.m: Many books show different points of view.

37669.q: What often comes with a school book for you to write in?
37669.e: In the workbook children do exercises that go with the school book. It is often part of the same set of teaching materials.
37669.m: You do exercises in the workbook.

37670.q: In Switzerland, who decides which teaching materials are used in state schools?
37670.e: State schools are the responsibility of the cantons. They decide which teaching materials are used.
37670.m: The cantons decide on the teaching materials.

37671.q: Which of these countries has a one-party system today?
37671.e: In North Korea only one party decides. People cannot choose between different parties.
37671.m: North Korea has a one-party system.

37672.q: In a one-party system, what usually happens to other parties?
37672.e: The ruling party wants no competition. That is why it bans other parties or only lets them exist for show.
37672.m: In a one-party system other parties are usually banned.

37673.q: Which party was the only one allowed in Germany from 1933?
37673.e: In July 1933 a law banned the founding of new parties. Adolf Hitler’s NSDAP was now the only permitted party.
37673.m: Under Hitler only the NSDAP was allowed.

37674.q: In which country was there a one-party system until 1989?
37674.e: In East Germany, the eastern part of Germany, a single party had all the power. It was called the SED.
37674.m: In East Germany only one party had power.

37675.q: Which party ruled the Soviet Union alone?
37675.e: In the Soviet Union the Communist Party was the only permitted party for decades.
37675.m: The Soviet Union was ruled by the Communist Party.

37676.q: Which party rules China alone today (as of 2026)?
37676.e: In China the Communist Party has all the power. There are no free elections between different parties.
37676.m: China is ruled by the Communist Party.

37677.q: In a one-party system, can you vote the government out?
37677.e: If only one party may stand, there is no real election. That is why the people cannot vote the government out.
37677.m: In a one-party system you cannot vote the government out.

37678.q: In a one-party system, what often happens to someone who starts a new party?
37678.e: A new party would be competition for those in power. That is why founders are often persecuted or locked up.
37678.m: Anyone who starts a party in a one-party system is often punished.

37679.q: What is there in a multi-party system?
37679.e: In a multi-party system several parties compete against each other in elections. The people can choose between them.
37679.m: In a multi-party system you can choose between many parties.

37680.q: What do you call the parties that are not in government and criticise it?
37680.e: The opposition scrutinises and criticises the government. In a democracy this is allowed and important.
37680.m: The opposition keeps a check on the government.

37681.q: What do you call it when several parties govern together?
37681.e: If no party has enough seats on its own, several parties join forces. This cooperation is called a coalition.
37681.m: A coalition is an alliance of several parties.

37682.q: Which party won the most votes in the 2023 National Council elections?
37682.e: In the 2023 National Council elections the SVP became the strongest party with around 28 percent of the vote.
37682.m: The SVP was the strongest party in the National Council in 2023.

37683.q: Which of these parties had members in the Swiss Federal Council in 2026?
37683.e: In 2026 the SVP, SP, FDP and The Centre sit on the Federal Council. The Greens, the GLP and the EVP have no seat.
37683.m: The SP is one of the parties in the Federal Council.

37684.q: In Switzerland, what do you call the way the Federal Council seats are shared among the big parties?
37684.e: Since 1959 the big parties have shared the seven Federal Council seats according to an unwritten rule. This rule is called the magic formula.
37684.m: The magic formula shares out the Federal Council seats among the parties.

37685.q: May you start a new party in Switzerland?
37685.e: Freedom of association applies in Switzerland. Anyone who wants to may start a new party with others.
37685.m: In Switzerland anyone may start a party.

37686.q: What do you call it when a ruler is excessively worshipped like a hero?
37686.e: In a personality cult a ruler is praised and celebrated everywhere. He is shown almost as a superhuman.
37686.m: A personality cult is the excessive worship of a ruler.

37687.q: In a personality cult, what does propaganda often say about the ruler?
37687.e: In a personality cult the ruler is shown as perfect. Mistakes or weaknesses are kept quiet.
37687.m: In a personality cult the ruler is seen as flawless.

37688.q: Which city in Russia used to be named after the dictator Stalin?
37688.e: The city on the Volga was called Stalingrad from 1925 to 1961. Many places were named after Stalin at that time.

37689.q: Whose large picture hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing?
37689.e: A huge portrait of Mao Zedong hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace. He founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949.
37689.m: A huge picture of Mao hangs in Beijing.

37690.q: In which country are there huge statues of the ruling Kim family?
37690.e: In North Korea’s capital Pyongyang there are large statues of Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il. People have to worship them.
37690.m: In North Korea the Kim family is worshipped with statues.

37691.q: What do visitors in North Korea do in front of the Kim statues?
37691.e: In front of the large statues in Pyongyang people bow and lay flowers. This is part of the personality cult.
37691.m: In North Korea people bow in front of the Kim statues.

37692.q: In which city does the embalmed body of the Russian revolutionary leader Lenin lie?
37692.e: Lenin died in 1924. His body still lies today in a mausoleum on Red Square in Moscow.

37693.q: What did the ruler Niyazov in Turkmenistan have named after himself and his mother?
37693.e: In 2002 Saparmurat Niyazov renamed the months. January was named after him and April after his mother.
37693.m: A ruler in Turkmenistan named months after himself.

37694.q: What do you call it when a government influences people with one-sided messages?
37694.e: Propaganda aims to steer people in a particular direction. It only shows the side that helps those in power.
37694.m: Propaganda influences people with one-sided messages.

37695.q: Which language does the word “propaganda” come from?
37695.e: The word comes from the Latin “propagare”. That means “to spread”.
37695.m: Propaganda comes from the Latin word for spreading.

37696.e: Propaganda leaves out awkward things. It shows the government as good and its opponents as bad.

37697.q: Where is propaganda often shown very large in dictatorships?
37697.e: Dictatorships put up big posters with slogans and pictures. That way everyone sees the messages every day.
37697.m: Dictatorships often spread propaganda on posters.

37698.q: Which cheap radio did the Nazis have built so that many people could hear their speeches?
37698.e: From 1933 the Volksempfänger was sold cheaply. That way many families could hear the speeches and broadcasts of the Nazis.

37699.q: What was the name of the minister in charge of propaganda under Hitler?
37699.e: Joseph Goebbels was propaganda minister from 1933. He controlled newspapers, radio and films.

37700.q: How does propaganda often show the government’s opponents?
37700.e: Propaganda turns opponents into a picture of the enemy. People are supposed to be afraid of them.

37701.q: What do you call a report that is deliberately false?
37701.e: A false report deliberately spreads something that is not true. Propaganda often uses them.
37701.m: A false report is deliberately untrue.

37702.q: What was the secret police of East Germany called?
37702.e: The Stasi was the secret police of East Germany. It spied on many people in its own country.
37702.m: The secret police of East Germany was called the Stasi.

37703.q: What does the abbreviation “Stasi” stand for?
37703.e: Stasi is short for the Ministry for State Security of East Germany.

37705.q: What was the well-known secret service of the Soviet Union called?
37705.e: The KGB was the secret service of the Soviet Union from 1954 to 1991. It also spied on its own citizens.
37705.m: The secret service of the Soviet Union was called the KGB.

37706.q: What were people called who secretly spied on their neighbours for the Stasi?
37706.e: The Stasi had many secret informers. They were called unofficial collaborators, or IM for short.
37706.m: Stasi informers were called unofficial collaborators.

37707.q: What did the Stasi collect about many people?
37707.e: The Stasi wrote down in files what people said and did. Today the files fill huge archives.
37707.m: The Stasi collected files on many people.

37708.q: May former East German citizens read their own Stasi file today?
37708.e: After the end of East Germany the files were opened. Anyone who wants to can apply and read their own file.
37708.m: Today you can read your Stasi file.

37709.q: What do secret police officers often wear at work?
37709.e: Secret police officers do not want to be recognised. That is why they often wear completely ordinary clothes.
37709.m: Secret police officers often wear no uniform.

37710.q: Why is a political prisoner in prison?
37710.e: A political prisoner is locked up because they criticised the government or stood up for freedom.
37710.m: Political prisoners are in prison because of their opinions.

37711.q: Which organisation campaigns worldwide for political prisoners?
37711.e: Amnesty International was founded in 1961. It fights for the release of people imprisoned for their opinions.

37712.q: What does Amnesty International call people imprisoned only for their opinions who have not used violence?
37712.e: Amnesty calls them prisoners of conscience. They have harmed nobody but only spoken their minds.
37712.m: Prisoners of conscience are locked up only for their opinions.

37713.q: What can children also do for political prisoners?
37713.e: In letter-writing campaigns many people write to governments or to prisoners. This shows that the world is watching.

37714.q: What were the prison camps in the Soviet Union called, where many political prisoners were sent?
37714.e: The Gulag was the system of labour camps in the Soviet Union. Millions of people had to work there in harsh conditions.
37714.m: The Soviet Union had the prison camps of the Gulag.

37715.q: What do political prisoners in dictatorships often lack?
37715.e: In dictatorships the courts are not independent. Often the verdict is decided in advance.
37715.m: Political prisoners often get no fair trial.

37716.q: When are political prisoners often released?
37716.e: When a dictatorship collapses, the prisons often open. Then many political prisoners are freed.
37716.m: At the end of a dictatorship political prisoners are often freed.

37717.q: What do you call it when someone has to live abroad because of persecution?
37717.e: Exile means having to leave your home country because you are persecuted there. You then live in a foreign country.
37717.m: Someone who is persecuted and lives abroad is in exile.

37718.q: What does the Latin word “exilium” mean?
37718.e: The word exile comes from the Latin “exilium”. It means banishment.

37719.q: In which country has the Dalai Lama lived in exile since 1959?
37719.e: The Dalai Lama fled from Tibet in 1959. Since then he has lived in India, in the town of Dharamsala.
37719.m: The Dalai Lama lives in exile in India.

37720.q: In which Swiss city did the Russian revolutionary Lenin live in exile before returning to Russia in 1917?
37720.e: In 1916 and 1917 Lenin lived on Spiegelgasse in Zurich. In April 1917 he travelled back to Russia by train.
37720.m: Lenin lived in exile in Zurich.

37721.q: To which country did Albert Einstein go in 1933 because he was persecuted in Germany?
37721.e: Einstein was Jewish and was attacked by the Nazis. From autumn 1933 he lived in the USA and never returned to Germany.
37721.m: Einstein went to the USA in 1933.

37722.q: To which island was the French emperor Napoleon finally banished?
37722.e: After his defeat at Waterloo in 1815 Napoleon was banished to the island of St Helena in the Atlantic. He died there in 1821.
37722.m: Napoleon died in exile on St Helena.

37723.q: What do many people in exile miss most?
37723.e: People in exile have to leave family, friends and their homeland behind. Many are very homesick.
37723.m: Many people in exile miss their homeland.

37724.q: What do you call a person who lives in exile?
37724.e: An exile lives abroad because they are persecuted at home. They did not leave voluntarily.
37724.m: An exile is forced to live abroad.

37725.q: What do you call people who flee their country because of war or persecution?
37725.e: Refugees leave their homeland because they are in danger there. They look for protection in another country.
37725.m: Refugees look for protection from danger.

37726.q: In which Swiss city does the UN Refugee Agency have its headquarters?
37726.e: The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, has its headquarters in Geneva. It helps refugees all over the world.
37726.m: The UN Refugee Agency is based in Geneva.

37727.q: What do you call the protection a country gives to persecuted people?
37727.e: Anyone who is persecuted can ask for asylum in another country. Asylum means protection from persecution.
37727.m: Asylum is protection for persecuted people.

37728.q: In which city was an important agreement to protect refugees adopted in 1951?
37728.e: The agreement is called the Geneva Refugee Convention. It sets out who is a refugee and what rights they have.
37728.m: The Refugee Convention was adopted in Geneva in 1951.

37729.q: From which country did many refugees come to Switzerland in 1956?
37729.e: In 1956 the Soviet Union crushed an uprising in Hungary. Many Hungarians fled and were taken in by Switzerland.
37729.m: In 1956 many people fled from Hungary to Switzerland.

37730.q: How did two families escape across the East German border in 1979?
37730.e: Two families secretly sewed a huge hot-air balloon. In September 1979 they flew in it to Bavaria.
37730.m: In 1979 two families escaped from East Germany in a balloon.

37731.q: What do you call people who secretly help others to escape?
37731.e: Escape helpers dug tunnels under the Berlin Wall, for example. That way people could escape from East Germany.
37731.m: Escape helpers help people to flee.

37732.q: Why did East Germany build walls and fences on its border?
37732.e: Many people wanted to leave East Germany. The government wanted to stop them escaping with walls and fences.
37732.m: East Germany built fences so its citizens could not escape.

37733.q: What was the border called that divided Europe into East and West after the Second World War?
37733.e: The Iron Curtain separated the countries under Soviet influence from the West. Many borders were secured with fences.
37733.m: The Iron Curtain divided Europe into East and West.

37734.q: Which city was divided by a wall for almost 30 years?
37734.e: From 1961 to 1989 a wall separated East Berlin and West Berlin. Families and friends were torn apart.
37734.m: Berlin was divided by a wall.

37735.q: What was the guarded strip behind the Berlin Wall called?
37735.e: Behind the Wall there was a guarded strip with watchtowers and obstacles. Border soldiers shot at people trying to escape there.
37735.m: Behind the Berlin Wall was the death strip.

37736.q: Between which countries was the border fence ceremonially cut in June 1989?
37736.e: On 27 June 1989 the foreign ministers of Hungary and Austria cut through a piece of border fence together. It became a symbol of the end of the Iron Curtain.
37736.m: In 1989 the fence between Hungary and Austria was cut.

37737.q: Which country is still divided into North and South by a heavily guarded border today?
37737.e: Since the Korean War a heavily guarded border has separated North Korea and South Korea. You cannot simply cross it.
37737.m: Korea is divided into North and South.

37738.q: Who stood on the watchtowers on the East German border?
37738.e: Armed border soldiers stood on the watchtowers. They were supposed to stop anyone escaping across the border.
37738.m: Border soldiers guarded the East German border.

37739.q: In which year did the Nazis publicly burn books in many cities?
37739.e: On 10 May 1933 books were burned in Berlin and many other cities. They were books by authors the Nazis rejected.
37739.m: Books were burned in Germany in 1933.

37740.q: Which children’s author watched his own books being burned in 1933?
37740.e: In 1933 Erich Kästner stood in the crowd in Berlin and watched his books being thrown into the fire.
37740.m: Erich Kästner saw his books being burned.

37741.q: Why do dictatorships ban certain books?
37741.e: Banned books often contain ideas that those in power don’t like. People are not supposed to read them.
37741.m: Dictatorships ban books with unwanted ideas.

37742.q: How did people in the Soviet Union spread banned texts?
a: They copied them and passed them on secretly
They sold them openly at kiosks
They read them on state radio
They put them up on billboards
37742.e: People typed out banned texts and passed them on secretly. This was called samizdat, “self-publishing”.
37742.m: Banned texts were secretly copied and passed on.

37743.q: What on Bebelplatz in Berlin commemorates the book burning?
37743.e: Under a glass panel in the ground you can see empty bookshelves. They would have room for around 20,000 burned books.
37743.m: Empty shelves in Berlin commemorate the book burning.

37744.q: Which book about a surveillance state was banned for a long time in the Soviet Union?
37744.e: The novel “1984” by George Orwell describes a state that watches everyone. It was banned in the Soviet Union until the late 1980s.
37744.m: The book “1984” was banned in the Soviet Union.

37745.q: In dictatorships, what often happened to people who owned banned books?
37745.e: Anyone who had banned books could be arrested. That is why many people hid such books well.

37746.q: What were the Nazis’ lists of books that were to disappear called?
37746.e: The Nazis drew up blacklists of unwanted authors. These books were removed from libraries.

37747.q: In a dictatorship, who decides what is shown on state television?
37747.e: In a dictatorship the government controls television. It decides which news is broadcast.
37747.m: In a dictatorship the government decides the TV programmes.

37748.q: Who decided what was on the news on East German television?
37748.e: The main news programme in East Germany was called “Aktuelle Kamera”. It reported things the way the SED wanted.
37748.m: In East Germany the SED decided the TV news.

37749.q: What was the news programme on East German television called?
37749.e: “Aktuelle Kamera” was the main news programme of East Germany. It reported things the way the SED wanted.
37749.m: The East German news was called Aktuelle Kamera.

37750.q: Which television did many people in East Germany watch secretly?
37750.e: Many East German citizens received channels from West Germany. That way they learned things their own television kept quiet.
37750.m: In East Germany many people secretly watched West German TV.

37751.q: What did the East German TV programme “Der schwarze Kanal” (The Black Channel) show?
a: Clips from West German TV that were run down
37751.e: “Der schwarze Kanal” ran from 1960 to 1989. It showed clips from West German television and ran them down.
37751.m: The Black Channel ran down West German TV.

37752.q: How are radios and TVs set in North Korea?
a: Only state channels can be received
37752.e: In North Korea devices are fixed to the state channels. That way people only hear the government’s messages.
37752.m: In North Korea you can only receive state channels.

37753.q: May the Federal Council tell Swiss television what to show on the news?
37753.e: The Federal Constitution protects the independence of radio and television. The government may not decide on the news.
37753.m: In Switzerland television is independent of the government.

37754.q: Which way did many East German citizens point their TV aerials?
37754.e: To receive West German television many people turned their aerials towards West Germany. This was frowned upon.
37754.m: Many East German aerials pointed west.

37755.q: What do you call a state that constantly watches its citizens?
37755.e: In a surveillance state the government watches what people do and say. There is hardly any privacy.
37755.m: A surveillance state constantly watches its citizens.

37756.q: What do you call a tiny hidden microphone used for listening in?
37756.e: A bug is a small hidden microphone. Secret services hid them in flats to listen in on conversations.
37756.m: A bug is a hidden microphone.

37757.q: What do you call it when someone secretly listens in on phone calls?
37757.e: In phone tapping conversations are secretly listened to. The Stasi tapped many phones in East Germany.
37757.m: Secretly listening in on calls is called phone tapping.

37758.q: What did the Stasi secretly open to find out more about people?
37758.e: Every day the Stasi opened many letters and parcels. Afterwards it stuck them shut again.
37758.m: The Stasi secretly read other people’s letters.

37759.q: What is the figure in the novel “1984” who watches everyone called?
37759.e: In George Orwell’s novel “1984” there are pictures of Big Brother everywhere. Underneath it says that he is watching you.
37759.m: In the novel 1984 Big Brother watches everyone.

37760.q: Which technology do some states use today to recognise people in the street automatically?
37760.e: Cameras with facial recognition can pick out people in a crowd. Some states use this to find opponents.
37760.m: Facial recognition can identify people automatically.

37761.q: What do many people do when they know they are constantly being watched?
a: They stop saying what they think
37761.e: People who fear surveillance become careful. Many then no longer dare to speak openly.
37761.m: Surveillance makes people quiet and careful.

37762.q: What is the 1989 scandal called, when it came out that the Swiss federal police had secretly kept index cards on many people?
37762.e: In 1989 it came out that the federal police had kept index cards, known as “Fichen”, on many people for decades. After that the rules became stricter.
37762.m: The Secret Files Scandal showed that there was secret surveillance in Switzerland too.

37763.q: What do you call protecting your personal details from access by others?
37763.e: Data protection makes sure that nobody collects personal data without permission. In Switzerland a special law covers this.

37764.q: In a one-party system, how many candidates are often on the ballot paper for each seat?
37764.e: In one-party systems like North Korea there is only one candidate on the ballot paper for each seat. So you cannot really choose.
37764.m: In a one-party system there is often only one candidate per seat.

37765.q: What do you call it when propaganda stirs people up against a group?
37765.e: Incitement portrays a group as guilty or dangerous. Other people are supposed to reject or hate them.
37765.m: Incitement stirs people up against a group.

37766.q: In which country did Nelson Mandela fight for freedom?
37766.e: Nelson Mandela was born in South Africa in 1918. There he fought for equal rights all his life.
37766.m: Nelson Mandela is South Africa’s best-known freedom fighter.

37767.q: What did Nelson Mandela fight against?
37767.e: South Africa had apartheid: black and white people were kept apart and black people had fewer rights. Mandela wanted equal rights for all.
37767.m: Mandela wanted all people to be treated equally, whatever their skin colour.

37768.q: How long was Nelson Mandela in prison?
37768.e: Mandela was arrested in 1962 and was held prisoner for about 27 years in total. Even so, he never gave up his fight for freedom.
37768.m: Nelson Mandela spent almost three decades in prison.

37769.q: What did Nelson Mandela become in 1994?
37769.e: In 1994 everyone in South Africa was allowed to vote for the first time. Afterwards Mandela became the country’s first black president.
37769.m: Nelson Mandela was South Africa’s first black president.

37770.q: What affectionate nickname did many people use for Nelson Mandela?
37770.e: “Madiba” is the name of Mandela’s family clan. Many people in South Africa call him that out of respect and affection.
37770.m: Many South Africans affectionately call Nelson Mandela Madiba.

37771.q: Which famous prize did Nelson Mandela receive in 1993?
37771.e: Mandela received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 together with Frederik Willem de Klerk. Both had peacefully paved the way to a fairer South Africa.
37771.m: Nelson Mandela was honoured with the Nobel Peace Prize for his peaceful path.

37772.q: On which day is the international Nelson Mandela Day each year?
37772.e: 18 July is Mandela’s birthday. The UN declared this day Nelson Mandela Day, a day for helping other people.
37772.m: On 18 July the world remembers Nelson Mandela.

37773.q: In which year was Nelson Mandela released from prison?
37773.e: On 11 February 1990 Mandela was freed. Millions of people all over the world watched it on television.
37773.m: Nelson Mandela was finally freed in 1990.

37774.q: Which country did Mahatma Gandhi come from?
37774.e: Gandhi was born in India in 1869. He fought for India to become a free country.
37774.m: Mahatma Gandhi is one of the most important people in India’s history.

37775.e: “Mahatma” is an honorary title and means “great soul”. His real first name was Mohandas.
37775.m: Mahatma is an honorary title meaning great soul.

37776.q: How did Gandhi fight for his country’s freedom?
37776.e: Gandhi rejected violence. He protested with marches, strikes and boycotts.
37776.m: Gandhi showed that you can achieve a lot without violence.

37777.q: From which country did Gandhi want to free India?
37777.e: India was a British colony for a long time. Gandhi wanted Indians to decide about their country themselves.
37777.m: India used to be a colony of Britain.

37778.q: On the famous march to the sea in 1930, what did Gandhi want to make himself?
37778.e: The British banned Indians from making their own salt. Gandhi walked several hundred kilometres to the sea with many people and made salt there.
37778.m: With the Salt March Gandhi protested against an unfair law.

37779.q: Which device is often seen with Gandhi in pictures, because he used it to make his own yarn?
37779.e: Gandhi wanted Indians to make their own clothes and not buy cloth from abroad. So the spinning wheel became a symbol of freedom.
37779.m: The spinning wheel is a symbol of Gandhi’s fight for independence.

37780.q: Which international day is celebrated on Gandhi’s birthday, 2 October?
37780.e: The UN declared Gandhi’s birthday the International Day of Non-Violence. In this way people remember his peaceful struggle.
37780.m: On 2 October the world thinks of Gandhi and of peace without violence.

37781.q: Which country does Malala Yousafzai come from?
37781.e: Malala was born in 1997 in the Swat Valley in Pakistan. Her father ran a school there.

37782.q: What does Malala Yousafzai campaign for?
37782.e: In her home region the Taliban wanted to ban girls from going to school. Malala said loudly that all children should be allowed to learn.
37782.m: Malala fights for every girl to be allowed to go to school.

37783.q: What did Malala already write for an English broadcaster at the age of 11?
37783.e: Under a different name, Malala wrote an online diary for the BBC. In it she described how hard life was for schoolgirls.
37783.m: Even as a child Malala told the world about her daily life.

37784.q: Who attacked Malala in 2012 because she campaigned for girls’ schools?
37784.e: The Taliban are a radical group. They attacked Malala on her school bus and badly injured her, but she survived.
37784.m: Malala would not be silenced, even after an attack.

37785.q: In which country was Malala treated after the attack, and where has she lived since?
37785.e: Malala was taken to a hospital in Birmingham in England. Afterwards she stayed in the UK with her family and went to school there.
37785.m: Malala found a new home in the United Kingdom.

37786.q: How old was Malala when she received the Nobel Peace Prize?
37786.e: Malala received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 at the age of 17. That makes her the youngest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.
37786.m: Malala is the youngest Nobel Prize winner of all time.

37787.q: Where did Malala give a famous speech on her 16th birthday?
a: At the UN in New York
At the Federal Palace in Bern
37787.e: In 2013 Malala spoke at the UN about education for all children. She said one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world.
37787.m: Malala spoke at the UN for every child’s right to education.

37788.q: At which famous university did Malala study?
37788.e: Malala studied at the University of Oxford in England. She finished her degree in 2020.
37788.m: Malala studied at the University of Oxford.

37789.q: What does the UN remember on “Malala Day”?
37789.e: Malala Day is on 12 July, Malala’s birthday. It is a reminder that all children should be allowed to go to school.
37789.m: Malala Day is a reminder of the right to education.

37790.q: With which famous words does the best-known sentence of King’s 1963 speech begin?
37790.e: King dreamed that his children would not be judged by the colour of their skin.
37790.m: In his speech Martin Luther King spoke of his dream of a fair world.

37791.q: What did Martin Luther King fight for?
37791.e: At that time black people in the USA were treated unfairly on buses, in schools and in restaurants. King wanted equal rights for black and white people.
37791.m: King campaigned for black and white people to have equal rights.

37792.q: Which prize did Martin Luther King receive in 1964?
37792.e: King received the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 35. He was honoured for his non-violent struggle.
37792.m: Martin Luther King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

37793.q: What happened to Martin Luther King in 1968?
37793.e: Martin Luther King was shot dead in Memphis in 1968. Many people all over the world mourned him.
37793.m: Martin Luther King died in 1968, but his ideas live on.

37794.q: In which month is the US public holiday for Martin Luther King?
37794.e: Martin Luther King Day is always on the third Monday in January. King’s birthday is 15 January.
37794.m: In the USA a public holiday in January remembers Martin Luther King.

37795.q: In which city did King give his famous speech to around 250,000 people in 1963?
37795.e: The speech was given at the great March on Washington. King spoke in front of the Lincoln Memorial in the US capital.
37795.m: King gave his most famous speech in the capital, Washington.

37796.q: From whom did Martin Luther King learn the idea of protesting without violence?
37796.e: King admired Gandhi’s ideas of peaceful protest. In 1959 he even travelled to India to learn more about them.
37796.m: Martin Luther King was a great admirer of Gandhi.

37797.q: What did Rosa Parks refuse to do in 1955?
a: Give up her seat on the bus
37797.e: At that time black people on some buses had to give up their seats for white people. Rosa Parks simply stayed seated.
37797.m: Rosa Parks stayed in her seat on the bus and became famous.

37798.q: In which US city did Rosa Parks stay seated on the bus?
37798.e: Montgomery is in the state of Alabama in the south of the USA. Strict rules there put black people at a disadvantage.
37798.m: Rosa Parks became a heroine in Montgomery.

37799.q: What happened to Rosa Parks after she stayed in her seat?
37799.e: The police arrested Rosa Parks because she had broken the rules on the bus. She had to pay a fine.
37799.m: Rosa Parks even accepted being arrested to protest against injustice.

37800.q: What did many black people in Montgomery do after Rosa Parks was arrested?
37800.e: Many walked or shared cars. This bus boycott left the bus company short of money.
37800.m: With the bus boycott many people protested together.

37801.q: How long did the Montgomery bus boycott last?
37801.e: The boycott lasted over 380 days. It only ended when a court had banned segregation on the buses.
37801.m: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted more than a year.

37802.q: What honorary title was Rosa Parks later given?
a: Mother of the civil rights movement
37802.e: Her brave act inspired many people to fight for their rights. That is why she is called this.
37802.m: Rosa Parks is seen as the mother of the civil rights movement.

37803.q: Who became famous as the leader of the Montgomery bus boycott?
37803.e: Martin Luther King led the boycott. After that he was known all over the USA.
37803.m: The bus boycott made Martin Luther King famous.

37804.q: Which country did Václav Havel come from?
37804.e: Havel was born in 1936. His home country was then called Czechoslovakia; today it is the Czech Republic.
