37805.q: What was Václav Havel’s job before he became a politician?
37805.e: Havel mainly wrote plays. In them he made fun of the government, which is why they were banned.
37805.m: Václav Havel was a playwright before he became president.

37806.q: Why did Václav Havel have to go to prison several times?
37806.e: The communist government tolerated no criticism. So Havel spent almost five years in prison in total.
37806.m: Havel was a political prisoner because he spoke his mind.

37807.q: What is the group called that Havel co-founded in 1977 to demand human rights?
37807.e: Charter 77 was a text signed by many brave people. They demanded that the government respect human rights.
37807.m: With Charter 77 brave people demanded their rights.

37808.q: In which year did the Velvet Revolution take place in Czechoslovakia?
37808.e: In November 1989 huge numbers of people took to the streets of the capital. After a few weeks the communist government gave up.
37808.m: The Velvet Revolution brought freedom in 1989.

37809.q: Why is the revolution in Czechoslovakia called the “Velvet” Revolution?
a: Because it happened almost without violence
Because it lasted a very long time
37809.e: Velvet is a soft fabric. The name shows that the change to democracy happened gently and without bloodshed.
37809.m: The Velvet Revolution is called that because it was gentle and peaceful.

37810.q: Which office did Václav Havel take up at the end of 1989?
37810.e: At the end of 1989 Havel became President of Czechoslovakia. From 1993 to 2003 he was the first President of the Czech Republic.
37810.m: Václav Havel went from prisoner to president.

37811.q: Which airport is named after Václav Havel today?
37811.e: Since 2012 Prague airport has been called “Letiště Václava Havla”. This is how the Czech Republic honours its famous president.
37811.m: Prague airport is named after Václav Havel.

37812.q: Which country does Lech Wałęsa come from?
37812.e: Lech Wałęsa was born in Poland in 1943. He became one of the most important fighters for his country’s freedom.
37812.m: Lech Wałęsa is a famous freedom fighter from Poland.

37813.q: Where did Lech Wałęsa work when he became famous?
37813.e: Wałęsa worked at the big shipyard in Gdańsk. Ships are built there.
37813.m: Lech Wałęsa worked at the Gdańsk shipyard.

37814.q: What trade had Lech Wałęsa learned?
37814.e: Wałęsa was an electrician. At the shipyard he looked after the cables and power.
37814.m: Lech Wałęsa was an electrician by trade.

37815.q: How did the workers in Gdańsk put pressure on the government in 1980?
37815.e: The workers stopped work and demanded more rights. The government had to negotiate with them.
37815.m: A strike can put pressure on a government without violence.

37816.q: What is the trade union that Lech Wałęsa led in 1980 called?
37816.e: “Solidarność” is Polish and means “solidarity”. The union soon had around ten million members.
37816.m: The trade union Solidarność fought for freedom in Poland.

37817.q: Which prize did Lech Wałęsa receive in 1983?
37817.e: Wałęsa did not collect the prize himself, because he feared he would not be allowed back into Poland afterwards. His wife accepted it in Oslo.
37817.m: Lech Wałęsa was honoured with the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983.

37818.q: Which office did Lech Wałęsa hold from 1990 to 1995?
37818.e: After the end of communism the Poles elected Wałęsa president. He was Poland’s first president freely elected by the people.
37818.m: Lech Wałęsa went from electrician to President of Poland.

37819.q: In which country did the Carnation Revolution take place?
37819.e: The Carnation Revolution happened in Portugal. It ended a long dictatorship there.
37819.m: The Carnation Revolution brought democracy to Portugal.

37820.q: In which year did the Carnation Revolution take place?
37820.e: The revolution began in spring 1974. The old government was overthrown on the very same day.
37820.m: The Carnation Revolution took place in 1974.

37821.q: What did people put into the soldiers’ rifles?
37821.e: A woman handed out carnations to the soldiers, and many put them into the barrels of their rifles. That is how the revolution got its name.
37821.m: The carnations in the rifles are a symbol of a peaceful revolution.

37822.e: Young officers wanted to end the dictatorship and the wars in the colonies. Many people on the streets supported them.
37822.m: The Carnation Revolution was started by soldiers who wanted peace.

37823.q: What was the secret signal to start the Carnation Revolution?
37823.e: Shortly after midnight a radio station played the song “Grândola, Vila Morena”. For the officers that was the signal to go.
37823.m: A song on the radio gave the signal to start the Carnation Revolution.

37824.q: What ended with the Carnation Revolution in Portugal?
37824.e: Portugal had been a dictatorship since the 1920s and 1930s. Afterwards the country became a democracy with free elections.
37824.m: After the Carnation Revolution Portugal became a democracy.

37825.q: In which city did the Carnation Revolution mainly take place?
37825.e: The soldiers occupied important places in the capital Lisbon. Thousands of people cheered them there.
37825.m: The Carnation Revolution took place mainly in Lisbon.

37826.q: Which day is a public holiday in Portugal today in memory of the Carnation Revolution?
37826.e: In Portugal 25 April is called “Freedom Day”. On this day many people wear a red carnation.
37826.m: On 25 April Portugal celebrates Freedom Day.

37827.q: Which countries in Africa became independent in 1975 after the Carnation Revolution?
37827.e: Angola and Mozambique were Portuguese colonies. The new government in Portugal ended the colonial wars and let them go.
37827.m: After the Carnation Revolution Portugal’s colonies also became free.

37828.q: In which country did the Peaceful Revolution take place in 1989?
37828.e: East Germany was the eastern part of Germany and a dictatorship. In 1989 huge numbers of people there took to the streets peacefully.
37828.m: The Peaceful Revolution of 1989 brought freedom to East Germany.

37829.q: In which city did the famous Monday demonstrations take place?
37829.e: In Leipzig people met every Monday after a peace prayer. Afterwards they marched through the city together.
37829.m: The Monday demonstrations in Leipzig became world-famous.

37830.q: In which church in Leipzig were the peace prayers held?
37830.e: People met for prayers in St Nicholas Church every Monday. The demonstrations started from there.
37830.m: St Nicholas Church in Leipzig was a place of peaceful protest.

37831.q: What did people chant at the demonstrations in East Germany?
37831.e: With this sentence people showed that the people, not the government, should decide. It became the best-known chant of the revolution.
37831.m: With the chant “We are the people” people demanded democracy.

37832.q: Which chant showed that the demonstrators wanted to stay peaceful?
37832.e: The demonstrators did not want to give the police any reason to attack. That is why they chanted this sentence again and again.
37832.m: People in East Germany deliberately protested without violence.

37833.q: How many people demonstrated in Leipzig on 9 October 1989?
37833.e: Despite great fear, about 70,000 people came. The police and the army did not intervene, because there were so many.
37833.m: On 9 October 1989 the people of Leipzig were no longer afraid.

37834.q: What was opened in Berlin on 9 November 1989?
37834.e: The Wall had divided Berlin for almost 30 years. That night people from East and West celebrated together.
37834.m: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989.

37835.q: Since which year has Germany been a single country again?
37835.e: On 3 October 1990 East Germany and the Federal Republic became one country again. That day is now German Unity Day.

37836.e: In non-violent resistance people stand up against injustice without hurting others. They demonstrate, strike or boycott.
37836.m: Non-violent resistance means standing up against injustice without violence.

a: Deliberately not buying or using something
37837.e: In a boycott many people together go without something, for example certain goods. They want to change something this way.
37837.m: A boycott is a protest by going without.

37838.q: What do you do in a hunger strike?
37838.e: In a hunger strike someone goes without food to draw attention to an injustice. This can be dangerous for their health.
37838.m: In a hunger strike you protest by not eating.

a: People sit down on a road or path
37839.e: In a sit-in blockade people sit down on a road or in front of a gate, for example. In this way they peacefully block the way.
37839.m: In a sit-in blockade people peacefully block the way.

a: Many people show their opinion together
A football match in a stadium
37840.e: At a demonstration many people go out onto the streets together. With placards and chants they show what they want or reject.
37840.m: At a demonstration people show their opinion together.

a: Peacefully refusing to follow unfair rules
37841.e: In civil disobedience people deliberately break a rule they think is unfair. They do it openly and without violence and accept the punishment.
37841.m: Civil disobedience is peaceful protest against unfair rules.

37842.q: Which hand sign often stands for peace?
a: Two fingers in a V shape
37842.e: The index and middle fingers are spread to form a V. Many peaceful demonstrators use this sign.
37842.m: Two spread fingers are a well-known peace sign.

37843.q: Why did many people in Leipzig carry candles at the demonstrations in 1989?
a: As a sign that they were peaceful
37843.e: Candles show that you don’t want violence. The demonstrators also put them in front of secret police buildings.
37843.m: A candle is a sign of peaceful protest.

37844.q: Why is it hard to fight with a burning candle in your hand?
a: You need both hands for the candle
37844.e: You hold the candle in one hand and shield the flame from the wind with the other. So you have no hand free for stones or sticks.
37844.m: Anyone carrying a candle has no hand free for violence.

37845.q: What is a chain of lights as a protest?
a: Many people stand in a line holding lights
37845.e: In a chain of lights people stand side by side holding candles or lamps. That way they show their opinion quietly and peacefully.
37845.m: A chain of lights is a quiet and peaceful protest.

37846.q: What did thousands of people demonstrate for with candles in Bratislava in 1988?
37846.e: At that time Bratislava was part of communist Czechoslovakia. People stood silently with candles in a square; the police drove them away with water cannon.
37846.m: The candle demonstration in Bratislava was a brave protest against the dictatorship.

37847.q: What is the symbol of the human rights organisation Amnesty International?
37847.e: The candle stands for hope, the barbed wire for imprisonment. Amnesty stands up for people imprisoned for their opinions.
37847.m: The candle in barbed wire stands for hope for prisoners.

a: People stand quietly in one place
A guard in front of a castle
A clock with a loud alarm
37848.e: At a vigil people stand quietly in one place, often with candles. They remember an injustice or demand something.
37848.m: A vigil is a quiet protest, often with candles.

37849.q: What does a burning candle often stand for at a protest?
37849.e: A small flame lights up the darkness. That is why the candle is a sign of hope for a better future.
37849.m: A candle is a sign of hope.

37850.q: What did hundreds of thousands protest against with a chain of lights in Munich in 1992?
37850.e: At that time there were attacks on people from other countries in Germany. With the chain of lights many people showed that they were against it.
37850.m: With chains of lights people show that they are against hatred.

37851.q: Who became King of Spain after Franco’s death in 1975?
37851.e: Juan Carlos I became king two days after Franco’s death. He then helped to make Spain a democracy.
37851.m: Under King Juan Carlos I Spain became a democracy.

37852.q: What is the path from dictatorship to democracy called in Spain?
37852.e: “Transición” is Spanish and means “transition”. It refers to the years after 1975 in which Spain became democratic.
37852.m: The Transición was Spain’s peaceful path to democracy.

37853.q: In which year were the first free elections held in Spain after the dictatorship?
37853.e: On 15 June 1977 Spaniards were able to vote freely for the first time in over 40 years. Many parties were allowed again.
37853.m: In 1977 Spain voted freely again for the first time.

37854.q: In which year did Spain get its new democratic constitution?
37854.e: The people approved the constitution on 6 December 1978. That day is now a public holiday in Spain.
37854.m: Spain has had a democratic constitution since 1978.

37855.q: What form of government does Spain have today?
37855.e: Spain is a parliamentary monarchy. The king is head of state, but the people elect parliament.
37855.m: Spain today is a democracy with a king.

37856.q: What did armed men attempt in the Spanish parliament on 23 February 1981?
37856.e: Armed men of the Guardia Civil stormed parliament in Madrid and wanted to seize power. The attempt failed the very next day.
37856.m: The 1981 coup attempt in Spain failed.

37857.q: Who spoke out on television against the 1981 coup attempt in Spain?
37857.e: In a television address the head of state said clearly that he was defending democracy. The coup plotters then gave up.
37857.m: In 1981 the Spanish king defended the young democracy.

37858.q: In which year did Spain join the European Community, today’s EU?
37858.e: Spain became a member in 1986 together with Portugal. This was only possible because both countries had become democracies.
37858.m: Spain has belonged to the European Community since 1986.

37859.q: Which East German city was called ‘Karl-Marx-Stadt’ from 1953 to 1990?
37859.e: East Germany renamed Chemnitz in honour of Karl Marx. In 1990 the city got its old name back.
37859.m: In East Germany, Chemnitz was called Karl-Marx-Stadt.

37860.q: What did Karl Marx study at university?
37860.e: Marx first studied law in Bonn and Berlin. Later he worked mainly on philosophy and wrote his doctoral thesis on it.
37860.m: Karl Marx studied law and philosophy.

37861.q: In which German city was Karl Marx born?
37861.e: Trier is an old city on the Moselle. The house where Marx was born is a museum today.
37861.m: Karl Marx was born in Trier.

37862.q: What is the name of Karl Marx’s best-known thick book?
37862.e: In ‘Das Kapital’, Marx explains how the economy works with factories and money. The first volume came out in 1867.
37862.m: Karl Marx’s most important book is called ‘Das Kapital’.

37863.q: In which city did Karl Marx live for many years until his death?
37863.e: Marx had to leave Germany and moved to London in 1849. He died there in 1883.
37863.m: Karl Marx spent his last decades in London.

37864.q: What did Karl Marx have on his face in almost every picture?
37864.e: In pictures and statues, Karl Marx is almost always shown with a long, thick beard. That makes him easy to recognise.
37864.m: You can recognise Karl Marx by his big beard.

37865.q: Which job, among others, did Karl Marx have?
37865.e: Karl Marx was a philosopher and wrote for newspapers as a journalist. He wrote many articles and books.
37865.m: Karl Marx was a philosopher and journalist.

37866.q: With which friend did Karl Marx write many of his works?
37866.e: Friedrich Engels was Marx’s closest friend. The two wrote books together, and Engels also supported Marx with money.
37866.m: Karl Marx worked closely with Friedrich Engels.

37867.q: In which century did Karl Marx live?
37867.e: Karl Marx lived from 1818 to 1883. These years belong to the 19th century.
37867.m: Karl Marx lived in the 19th century.

37868.q: What happened to Friedrich Engels’s ashes after his death?
a: They were put in a pyramid.
They were put in a museum.
37868.e: Engels did not want a grave. His ashes were scattered at sea off the English coast near Eastbourne.
37868.m: Engels’s ashes were scattered at sea.

37869.q: How did Friedrich Engels often support his friend Karl Marx?
37869.e: Marx was often poor. Engels earned money in his family’s firm and regularly sent him some of it.
37869.m: Engels often helped Marx out with money.

37870.q: What did Friedrich Engels’s family own?
37870.e: The Engels family owned textile factories where cloth was made. So Engels himself was the son of a factory owner.
37870.m: Friedrich Engels came from a family of factory owners.

37871.q: In which English city did Engels work in one of his father’s factories?
37871.e: Engels worked for many years in Manchester in the cotton firm his father had a share in. There he saw how poorly the workers lived.
37871.m: Engels worked in Manchester for a long time.

37874.e: Friedrich Engels was born in 1820. That made him two years younger than Karl Marx.

37875.q: Where did Friedrich Engels die in 1895?
37875.e: From 1870 Engels lived in London, very close to Marx. He died there in 1895.
37875.m: Friedrich Engels died in London in 1895.

37876.q: What does the Latin word ‘communis’, from which ‘communism’ comes, mean?
37876.e: ‘Communis’ means ‘shared’ or ‘common’ in Latin. In communism, many things are meant to belong to everyone together.
37876.m: The word communism comes from the Latin word for shared.

37877.q: What is the name of a settlement in Israel where in the past almost everything belonged to everyone together?
37877.e: In a kibbutz, people lived and worked together and shared what they owned. The first kibbutzim were founded at the beginning of the 20th century.
37877.m: In a kibbutz, people shared what they owned.

37878.q: What do you call things that belong to a whole group together?
37878.e: Common property does not belong to one single person but to everyone together. Everyone may use it together.
37878.m: What belongs to everyone together is called common property.

37879.q: In Switzerland, what is a meadow or forest called that belongs to everyone in the village together?
37879.e: An Allmend is land that the people of a village use together, for example as pasture for cattle. Many places in Switzerland still have an Allmend today.
37879.m: An Allmend is land that a whole village uses together.

37880.q: What did communism want to do with private ownership of factories?
37880.e: Marx and Engels wanted no one to own a factory alone any more. Private ownership of factories was to be abolished.
37880.m: Communism wanted to abolish private ownership of factories.

37881.q: What do you call things that belong to one person alone?
37881.e: Private property belongs to a single person or family. Only they may decide what happens to it.
37881.m: What belongs to one person alone is private property.

37882.q: Who decided about the factories and the land in the Soviet Union?
37882.e: In the Soviet Union, factories and farms were handed over to the state. The state then decided about them.
37882.m: In the Soviet Union, the factories belonged to the state.

37883.q: What were large collective farms in the Soviet Union called?
37883.e: In a kolkhoz, many farming families worked together on one large farm. In return they had to give up their own fields.
37883.m: Collective farms in the Soviet Union were called kolkhozes.

37884.q: What was a big aim of communism?
a: Everyone should look after only themselves.
37884.e: In communism, factories and land are meant to belong to everyone together. There should no longer be big differences between people.
37884.m: Communism wanted everything to be shared fairly.

37885.q: What do you call a society without rich and poor, as Marx wished for?
37885.e: Marx divided people into classes, for example owners and workers. In a classless society these differences no longer exist.
37885.m: Marx dreamed of a society without classes.

37886.q: How does the saying continue: ‘From each according to his ability, to each according to his ...’?
37886.e: Marx made this saying famous in 1875. It means: everyone works as well as they can, and everyone gets what they need.
37886.m: In communism, everyone is meant to get what they need.

37887.q: What did Marx call the class of rich factory owners?
37887.e: By bourgeoisie, Marx meant the people who own factories and machines. The word comes from French and actually means ‘middle class’ or ‘townspeople’.
37887.m: Marx called the rich factory owners the bourgeoisie.

37888.q: According to Marx, who was to take power in a revolution?
37888.e: Marx believed that working people would one day rise up against the factory owners. After that, a society without classes was to emerge.
37888.m: According to Marx, the workers were to take power.

37889.q: What was supposed to happen to hunger and poverty under communism?
a: They were meant to affect only cities.
37889.e: Marx and Engels hoped that everyone would have enough to live on if everything was shared fairly. No one was to be poor any more.
37889.m: Communism wanted to end poverty for everyone.

37890.q: Were there really no differences between people in communist countries?
a: No, party leaders often had more.
Yes, everyone had exactly the same.
37890.e: In countries like the Soviet Union, party leaders often lived better than everyone else. So the idea of equality was not fully achieved.
37890.m: Even in communist countries, some people had more privileges.

37891.q: Who decides what is produced in a planned economy?
37891.e: In a planned economy, the state sets out in a plan what the factories produce. The factories have to stick to this plan.
37891.m: In a planned economy, the state plans production.

37892.q: What were the economic plans in the Soviet Union that lasted for several years called?
37892.e: The Soviet Union planned its economy five years in advance each time. The first of these plans began in 1928.
37892.m: The Soviet Union planned its economy in Five-Year Plans.

37893.q: Who sets the prices in a planned economy?
37893.e: In a planned economy, the state decides how much bread or shoes cost. That is why prices rarely change.
37893.m: In a planned economy, the state sets the prices.

37894.q: What could often be seen outside shops in planned economies because goods were missing?
37894.e: Often too little was made of what people needed. That is why people queued for a long time when something finally arrived.
37894.m: In planned economies, people often had to queue for a long time.

37895.q: Which German state had a planned economy until 1990?
37895.e: The GDR, East Germany, was a communist country with a planned economy. In 1990 it was reunited with West Germany.
37895.m: East Germany had a planned economy until 1990.

37896.q: What do you call it when there is far too little of a product?
37896.e: A shortage means that more people need something than is available. In planned economies there were often shortages of goods.
37896.m: When a product is missing, it is called a shortage.

37897.q: What happens in a planned economy if the plan provides for too few shoes?
37897.e: The factories only make what is in the plan. If the state plans too little, the goods are missing in the shops.
37897.m: A wrong plan in a planned economy leads to missing goods.

37898.q: Which country still has a very strict planned economy today (as of 2026)?
37898.e: North Korea is considered the country with the strictest planned economy in the world. There, the state controls almost the whole economy.
37898.m: North Korea still has a strict planned economy today.

37899.q: What kind of economy does Switzerland have?
37899.e: In Switzerland, it is mainly companies and customers who decide what is made and bought. This is called a market economy.

37900.q: In a market economy, what mainly decides the price?
37900.e: Supply means how much of a product there is. Demand means how many people would like to buy the product.
37900.m: In a market economy, supply and demand set the price.

37901.q: What usually happens to the price of strawberries when there are lots of them in summer?
37901.e: When there are lots of strawberries, sellers have to make them cheaper so that everything gets sold. That is why the price falls.
37901.m: When there is lots of a product, it usually gets cheaper.

37902.q: What do you call it when several shops compete for the same customers?
37902.e: In competition, companies try to be better or cheaper than others. In this way they want to win more customers.
37902.m: In a market economy there is competition between companies.

37903.q: In a market economy, who decides what a bakery bakes?
37903.e: In a market economy, companies decide for themselves what they make. They bake what customers like to buy.
37903.m: In a market economy, companies decide for themselves what they offer.

37904.q: What usually happens to the price when suddenly all children want a certain toy?
37904.e: When very many people want something, demand is high. Then sellers can ask for more money for it.
37904.m: When many people want something, the price usually rises.

37905.q: Where do buyers and sellers meet in a market economy?
37905.e: A market is any place where things are bought and sold, for example a weekly market or an online shop. That is where the market economy gets its name.
37905.m: The market economy is named after the market, where people buy and sell.

37906.q: Despite the market economy, what can the state do in Switzerland?
37906.e: Even in a market economy there are laws, for example to protect workers. But the state does not set most prices.
37906.m: Even in a market economy, the state sets rules.

37907.q: Who owns the factories under capitalism?
37907.e: Under capitalism, companies and factories belong to individual people or businesses. They decide what happens there.
37907.m: Under capitalism, factories belong to private owners.

37908.q: What do workers get for their work under capitalism?
37908.e: The workers do not own the factory. For their work they receive money, their wage.
37908.m: Employees receive a wage for their work.

37909.q: Under capitalism, what does a company owner mainly want to earn?
37909.e: Profit is the money left over once all costs have been paid. Companies want to make as much profit as possible.
37909.m: Companies under capitalism want to make a profit.

37910.q: What does the word ‘capital’ mean here?
a: Money and property for a business
37910.e: Capital is money, machines or buildings that are used to run a business. That is where capitalism gets its name.
37910.m: Capital is the money and property that companies work with.

37911.q: Who is the best-known critic of capitalism in his books?
37911.e: In many writings, Marx described what he thought was wrong with capitalism. That is why he wished for a different order.
37911.m: Karl Marx was a well-known critic of capitalism.

37912.q: What did Marx think was unfair about capitalism?
a: The owners get rich, the workers stay poor.
37912.e: Marx thought the workers create the value, but the owners keep the profit. He found that unfair.
37912.m: Marx found it unfair that owners get rich and workers stay poor.

37913.q: What do you call someone who sets up and runs their own company?
37913.e: An entrepreneur owns and runs a company. They also carry the risk if the company loses money.
37913.m: Someone who runs their own company is an entrepreneur.

37914.q: What is an advantage of capitalism that many people mention?
37914.e: Because many companies compete with each other, there is usually a big choice of goods. The shops are well stocked.
37914.m: Under capitalism there is usually a big choice of goods.

37915.q: Where did many workers work in the 19th century?
37915.e: With industrialisation, many factories were built. People worked there at machines, often in harsh conditions.
37915.m: In the 19th century, many people worked in factories.

37916.q: Around 1850, how long did factory workers often have to work each day?
37916.e: At that time there were hardly any laws to protect workers. Working days of 12 to 14 hours were normal.
37916.m: Factory workers used to work more than 12 hours a day.

37917.q: Who sadly also had to work in factories in the 19th century?
37917.e: Many families were so poor that children also had to earn money. They often worked many hours in factories.
37917.m: In the past, children also had to work in factories.

37918.q: What did Marx call the working class?
37918.e: By proletariat, Marx meant the people who own nothing except their ability to work. They have to work for a wage.
37918.m: Marx called the working class the proletariat.

37919.q: On which day do workers celebrate Labour Day?
37919.e: 1 May is International Workers’ Day. In many Swiss cities there are marches on this day.

37920.q: What are the organisations called in which workers stand up for better wages?
37920.e: In a trade union, employees join together. Together they negotiate with companies about wages and working hours.
37920.m: Trade unions stand up for workers.

37921.q: What was the maximum the Swiss Factory Act of 1877 allowed per day?
37921.e: The Federal Factory Act of 1877 limited the working day in factories to a maximum of 11 hours. That was great progress at the time.
37921.m: The Factory Act of 1877 limited work to 11 hours a day.

37922.q: Below what age did the Swiss Factory Act of 1877 ban children from working in factories?
37922.e: Under this law, children under 14 were no longer allowed to work in factories. This was so they could go to school.
37922.m: From 1877, children under 14 in Switzerland were no longer allowed to work in factories.

37923.q: What do you call it when workers stop working together to demand more?
37923.e: In a strike, many people deliberately do not work. In this way they want to get better wages or conditions.
37923.m: In a strike, workers stop working together.

37924.q: Which two tools are the best-known symbol of communism?
37924.e: The hammer and sickle are crossed over each other. This symbol was on the flag of the Soviet Union, for example.
37924.m: The hammer and sickle are the symbol of communism.

37925.q: Which people does the hammer stand for in the ‘hammer and sickle’ symbol?
37925.e: The hammer is a tool from the workshop and the factory. It stands for the workers.
37925.m: The hammer stands for the workers.

37926.q: Which people does the sickle stand for in the ‘hammer and sickle’ symbol?
37926.e: The sickle is an old tool for working in the fields. It stands for the farmers.
37926.m: The sickle stands for the farmers.

37927.q: What do you cut with a sickle?
37927.e: In the past, people used it to cut grain and grass by hand, before there were machines for this.
37927.m: You cut grain and grass with a sickle.

37928.q: What do you use a hammer for at work?
37928.e: With a hammer you knock in nails or shape metal. That is why it was a typical tool in workshops and factories.
37928.m: You knock in nails with a hammer.

37929.q: What colour were the hammer and sickle on the flag of the Soviet Union?
37929.e: The hammer and sickle on the flag were golden. They were on a red background.
37929.m: On the Soviet flag, the hammer and sickle were golden.

37930.q: What does the ‘hammer and sickle’ symbol show together?
a: that workers and farmers stand together
37930.e: The two tools are crossed over each other. This is meant to show the unity of people in town and country.
37930.m: The hammer and sickle stand for the unity of workers and farmers.

37932.q: What was the main colour of the flag of the Soviet Union?
37932.e: The flag of the Soviet Union was completely red. In the top left corner there were a hammer, a sickle and a star.
37932.m: The flag of the Soviet Union was red.

37933.q: What was the army of the Soviet Union called in the Second World War?
37933.e: Until 1946 the army of the Soviet Union was called the ‘Red Army’. The colour red stood for the communist revolution.
37933.m: The army of the Soviet Union was called the Red Army.

37934.q: How many yellow stars are on the flag of China?
37934.e: On China’s red flag there is one big yellow star and four small ones. So there are five altogether.
37934.m: The Chinese flag shows five stars.

37935.q: Which flag is red with a single yellow star in the middle?
37935.e: Vietnam is governed by a communist party. Its red flag has a big yellow star in the middle.
37935.m: Vietnam’s flag is red with a yellow star.

37936.q: What does the colour red stand for in the workers’ movement?
37936.e: The red flag was carried at protests and uprisings. Red stands for struggle and revolution.
37936.m: The red flag is a sign of struggle and revolution.

37937.q: Apart from the colour red, which symbol do you often see on communist flags?
37937.e: Many communist flags have a star, often in yellow or red. It is also called the ‘Red Star’.
37937.m: You often see a star on communist flags.

37938.q: What do many people carry at the 1 May marches in Switzerland?
37938.e: On Labour Day, trade unions and parties march through the streets with red flags. Red is the old colour of the workers’ movement.
37938.m: On 1 May you see many red flags at marches.

37939.q: Which colour is the trademark of communist parties?
37939.e: Red flags, red stars and red posters are typical of communist parties. Red stands for the workers’ movement.
37939.m: The colour of the communists is red.

37940.q: Which party has governed China since 1949 (as of 2026)?
37940.e: Since 1949 the Communist Party has ruled China alone. Other parties are not allowed to compete for power.
37940.m: China has been ruled by the Communist Party since 1949.

37941.q: How many parties were allowed to govern in the Soviet Union?
37941.e: In the Soviet Union, only the Communist Party had power. Other parties were banned.
37941.m: In the Soviet Union, only one single party ruled.

37943.q: Who was the leader of Cuba for a long time?
37943.e: Fidel Castro led the revolution in Cuba in 1959. After that he ruled the country for almost 50 years.
37943.m: Fidel Castro was Cuba’s leader for a long time.

37944.q: What is the name of a small left-wing party in Switzerland that was founded in 1944?
37944.e: The Swiss Party of Labour, PdA for short, was founded in Switzerland in 1944. It is close to the ideas of communism.
37944.m: The Party of Labour is a left-wing party in Switzerland.

37945.q: In which year was the Communist Party of Switzerland founded?
37945.e: The Communist Party of Switzerland was founded in 1921. It always remained a small party.
37945.m: The Communist Party of Switzerland was founded in 1921.

37946.q: What is the famous song of the workers’ movement and the communists called?
37946.e: ‘The Internationale’ is sung by communists and socialists all over the world. From 1922 to 1944 it was also the anthem of the Soviet Union.
37946.m: The Internationale is the song of the workers’ movement.

37947.q: In a country where only one party is allowed, what can people hardly do in elections?
37947.e: When only one party is allowed, there is no real choice in elections. In Switzerland, on the other hand, you can choose between many parties.
37947.m: In a one-party state there is no real choice in elections.

37948.q: What was the name of the large communist country that Russia used to be part of?
37948.e: Russia was the largest part of the Soviet Union. Other republics belonged to it too, for example Ukraine.
37948.m: Russia used to be part of the Soviet Union.

37949.q: What was the capital of the Soviet Union?
37949.e: Moscow was the capital of the Soviet Union. Today Moscow is the capital of Russia.
37949.m: The capital of the Soviet Union was Moscow.

37950.q: In which year did the Soviet Union collapse?
37950.e: At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union broke up. After that, its republics became independent countries.

37951.q: Who was the first leader of the Soviet Union?
37951.e: Vladimir Lenin led the revolution in Russia in 1917. He became the first leader of the new state.
37951.m: Lenin was the first leader of the Soviet Union.

37952.q: In which Swiss city did Lenin live before the Revolution of 1917?
37952.e: In 1916 and 1917 Lenin lived in Zurich on the Spiegelgasse. In April 1917 he travelled to Russia by train.
37952.m: Before the Revolution, Lenin lived in Zurich.

37953.q: How many republics belonged to the Soviet Union at the end?
37953.e: In the end, the Soviet Union was made up of 15 Soviet republics. The largest of them was Russia.
37953.m: The Soviet Union was made up of 15 republics.

37954.q: What was the abbreviation for the Soviet Union in English?
37954.e: USSR stands for ‘Union of Soviet Socialist Republics’. That was the full name of the Soviet Union.
37954.m: The Soviet Union was abbreviated to USSR.

37955.q: Who was the first person in space, a cosmonaut from the Soviet Union?
37955.e: On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space. He orbited the Earth once.
37955.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space.

37956.q: Who was the last leader of the Soviet Union?
37956.e: Mikhail Gorbachev led the Soviet Union from 1985. He was its last head of state until it collapsed in 1991.
37956.m: Mikhail Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union.

37957.q: What was the money in the Soviet Union called?
37957.e: In the Soviet Union people paid with roubles. Russia still uses the rouble today.
37957.m: In the Soviet Union people paid with roubles.

37958.q: Why is the Cold War called ‘cold’?
a: It only took place in winter
It only happened at the North Pole
It only lasted a few days
37958.e: The USA and the Soviet Union were enemies but never fought a war directly against each other. That is why people speak of a ‘cold’ war rather than a ‘hot’ one.
37958.m: In the Cold War, the two superpowers never fought directly against each other.

37959.q: After which big war did the Cold War begin?
37959.e: The Second World War ended in 1945. Shortly afterwards, the former allies, the USA and the Soviet Union, became opponents.
37959.m: The Cold War began shortly after the Second World War.

37960.q: Roughly how long did the Cold War last?
37960.e: The Cold War lasted from about 1947 to 1991. That is over 40 years.
37960.m: The Cold War lasted more than 40 years.

37961.q: What position did Switzerland take in the Cold War?
a: It was in the Warsaw Pact
It was part of the Soviet Union
37961.e: Switzerland did not join either of the two military alliances. It stayed neutral, even though it was closely linked to the West economically.
37961.m: Switzerland stayed neutral in the Cold War.

37962.q: Which crisis brought the world very close to a nuclear war in 1962?
37962.e: The Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles on the island of Cuba, close to the USA. After 13 dangerous days the missiles were withdrawn.
37962.m: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 was one of the most dangerous moments of the Cold War.

37963.q: From the 1960s, what had to be built into many new houses in Switzerland?
37963.e: Out of fear of a nuclear war, a law from 1963 required shelters in new buildings. That is why Switzerland has a particularly large number of shelters.
37963.m: Because of the Cold War, many Swiss houses have a shelter.

37964.q: What do you call people who secretly gathered information about the other side in the Cold War?
37964.e: Both sides sent spies to find out the opponent’s secrets. Well-known secret services were the CIA in the USA and the KGB in the Soviet Union.
37964.m: In the Cold War, spies secretly gathered information about the other side.

37965.q: In which century did the Cold War take place?
37965.e: The Cold War took place in the second half of the 1900s. These years belong to the 20th century.
37965.m: The Cold War belongs to the 20th century.

37966.q: What do you call wars in which the superpowers did not fight themselves but let other countries fight for them?
37966.e: The USA and the Soviet Union each supported one side in other countries with weapons and money. One example is the war in Afghanistan in the 1980s.
37966.m: In proxy wars, other countries fought for the superpowers.

37967.q: What were the ‘Fichen’ that upset many people in Switzerland in 1989?
a: Secret police index cards about people
37967.e: Out of fear of communists, the federal police secretly collected information on about 900,000 people and organisations. The scandal is called the secret files scandal (Fichenaffäre).
37967.m: The secret files scandal revealed that the state had secretly watched many people.

37968.q: Which country was the leading power of the West in the Cold War?
37968.e: The USA was the most powerful country on the Western side. The countries of Western Europe stood by its side.
37968.m: The USA led the West in the Cold War.

37969.q: Which country was the leading power of the East in the Cold War?
37969.e: The Soviet Union was the most powerful communist country. It decided what happened in the countries of Eastern Europe.
37969.m: The Soviet Union led the East in the Cold War.

37970.q: What were the countries in Eastern Europe led by the Soviet Union called?
37970.e: The communist countries of Eastern Europe, together with the Soviet Union, formed the Eastern Bloc.
37970.m: The communist countries of Eastern Europe were called the Eastern Bloc.

37971.q: In which camp could people freely choose between several parties?
37971.e: In the West there were free elections with several parties. In the East it was usually only the communist party that decided.
37971.m: Free elections with several parties existed in the West.

37974.q: Which of these countries belonged to the Eastern Bloc in the Cold War?
37974.e: After the Second World War, Poland was communist and closely linked to the Soviet Union. Spain, Italy and Norway belonged to the West.
37974.m: Poland belonged to the Eastern Bloc in the Cold War.

37975.q: Which of these countries belonged to the West in the Cold War?
37975.e: France was a Western, democratic country. Hungary, Bulgaria and Romania were communist.
37975.m: France belonged to the West in the Cold War.

37976.q: What do you call countries that did not want to belong to either camp in the Cold War?
37976.e: Countries such as India or Egypt wanted to join neither the East nor the West. In 1961 they founded the Non-Aligned Movement.
37976.m: Non-aligned countries wanted to belong to neither the East nor the West.

37977.q: What do you call a very powerful country like the USA or the former Soviet Union?
37977.e: A superpower has a large military, lots of money and great influence all over the world. In the Cold War there were two of them.
37977.m: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union were two superpowers.

37978.q: Which city is the capital of the USA?
37978.e: The President, Congress and the Supreme Court of the USA work in Washington. New York is bigger, but it is not the capital.
37978.m: Washington is the capital of the USA.

37979.q: In which building does the President of the USA live and work?
37979.e: The White House in Washington is the official residence of the President of the USA. It is called that because of its white colour.
37979.m: The President of the USA lives and works in the White House.

37980.q: During the Cold War, which was the largest country on Earth by area?
37980.e: The Soviet Union stretched from Europe to the Pacific. It was bigger than any other country.
37980.m: The Soviet Union was the largest country on Earth.

37981.q: Which language was the most important in the Soviet Union?
37981.e: Many peoples with their own languages lived in the Soviet Union. But Russian was the shared language that everyone learned at school.
37981.m: Russian was the most important language in the Soviet Union.

37982.q: What is the flag of the USA called because of the way it looks?
37982.e: The flag of the USA has 13 red and white stripes and 50 white stars on a blue background. That is why it is called the ‘Stars and Stripes’.
37982.m: The flag of the USA is called the Stars and Stripes.

37983.q: What is the money of the USA called?
37983.e: In the USA people pay with the US dollar. It is one of the most important currencies in the world.
37983.m: The money of the USA is called the dollar.

37984.q: Which of the two superpowers was governed by communists?
37984.e: In the Soviet Union only the Communist Party governed. The USA was a democracy with several parties.
37984.m: The Soviet Union was the communist superpower.

37985.q: Which British politician made the expression ‘Iron Curtain’ famous in 1946?
37985.e: In a speech in the USA in 1946, Winston Churchill said that an iron curtain divided Europe. After that the expression became known all over the world.
37985.m: Winston Churchill made the expression ‘Iron Curtain’ famous.

37986.q: Which continent did the Iron Curtain divide?
37986.e: The Iron Curtain ran from north to south right across Europe. It separated Western Europe from Eastern Europe.

37987.q: According to Churchill, on which sea did the Iron Curtain begin in the north?
37987.e: Churchill said the curtain stretched from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste. Stettin, now called Szczecin, is in Poland today.
37987.m: In the north, the Iron Curtain began on the Baltic Sea.

37988.q: According to Churchill, on which sea did the Iron Curtain end in the south?
37988.e: Churchill named the port city of Trieste on the Adriatic as the southern end. The Adriatic is part of the Mediterranean.
37988.m: In the south, the Iron Curtain ended on the Adriatic.

37989.q: Which country was the first to start taking down its border fence with the West in 1989?
37989.e: In May 1989 Hungary began to take down the fence on its border with Austria. Soon many people from East Germany fled to the West via Hungary.
37989.m: In 1989 Hungary was the first country to open a hole in the Iron Curtain.

37990.q: Which of Switzerland’s neighbours bordered directly on the Iron Curtain?
37990.e: Austria bordered on Czechoslovakia and Hungary, which both belonged to the Eastern Bloc. Austria itself was neutral.
37990.m: Austria lay right on the Iron Curtain.

37991.q: What was the Iron Curtain mainly meant to prevent?
37991.e: The governments in the East did not want their citizens to flee to the West. That is why the border was strictly guarded.
37991.m: The Iron Curtain was meant to prevent escape to the West.

37992.q: What is the strip of nature that runs along the former Iron Curtain today called?
37992.e: In the former border strip, plants and animals were able to spread undisturbed for decades. Today it is protected as the Green Belt.
37992.m: Where the Iron Curtain once stood, there is now the Green Belt.

37993.q: In which year was NATO founded?
37993.e: NATO was founded on 4 April 1949. It was meant to protect the Western countries together.

37994.q: What kind of organisation is NATO?
37994.e: In NATO, countries have joined together to defend each other. That is why it is called a military alliance.

37995.q: In which city does NATO have its headquarters?
37995.e: NATO’s headquarters is in Brussels, the capital of Belgium.
37995.m: NATO has its headquarters in Brussels.

37996.q: How many member countries does NATO have (as of 2026)?
37996.e: Many countries have joined since it was founded. In 2026 NATO has 32 members.

37997.q: What is the most important principle of NATO?
a: An attack on one counts as an attack on all
Every country has its own army
37997.e: If one member is attacked, this counts as an attack on all members. Then the countries help each other.
37997.m: In NATO, an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.

37998.q: Which symbol can be seen on the NATO flag?
37998.e: The flag is dark blue with a white compass rose, like on a compass. It stands for the members’ shared path.
37998.m: There is a compass rose on the NATO flag.

37999.e: Sweden was neutral for a long time and joined NATO in March 2024. Finland had already joined a year earlier.
37999.m: Sweden has been a member of NATO since 2024.

38000.q: Which ocean is NATO named after?
38000.e: NATO stands for ‘North Atlantic Treaty Organization’. Its members lie on both sides of the Atlantic.
38000.m: NATO is named after the Atlantic.

38001.q: In which year was the Warsaw Pact founded?
38001.e: The Warsaw Pact was founded in May 1955. Shortly before that, West Germany had joined NATO.
38001.m: The Warsaw Pact was founded in 1955.

38002.q: In which country is the city that the Warsaw Pact is named after?
38002.e: The treaty was signed in Warsaw. Warsaw is the capital of Poland.
38002.m: The Warsaw Pact is named after the Polish capital, Warsaw.

38003.q: Which of these countries was a member of the Warsaw Pact?
38003.e: East Germany belonged to the Warsaw Pact from the start. Austria and Finland were neutral, and Yugoslavia went its own way.
38003.m: East Germany belonged to the Warsaw Pact.

38004.q: How many countries belonged to the Warsaw Pact at the start?
38004.e: At the start they were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania and East Germany. That makes 8 countries.
38004.m: At the start, 8 countries belonged to the Warsaw Pact.

38005.q: Which country led the Warsaw Pact?
38005.e: The Soviet Union was the strongest power in the Warsaw Pact and decided what the alliance did. The treaty was signed in Warsaw, but it was led from Moscow.
38005.m: The Soviet Union led the Warsaw Pact.

38006.q: Which Western alliance was the opponent of the Warsaw Pact?
38006.e: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the East. Facing it was the alliance of the West.
38006.m: The opponent of the Warsaw Pact was NATO.

38007.q: In which year was the Warsaw Pact dissolved?
38007.e: After the end of the communist governments in Eastern Europe, the alliance was no longer needed. It was dissolved in July 1991.

38008.e: The ball had a diameter of 58 centimetres. That is about as big as a large beach ball.
38008.m: Sputnik 1 was about as big as a large beach ball.

38009.q: In which year did Yuri Gagarin fly into space?
38009.e: Gagarin took off on 12 April 1961. Today this day is celebrated as the International Day of Human Space Flight.
38009.m: Yuri Gagarin flew into space in 1961.

38010.q: Which country did Yuri Gagarin come from?
38010.e: Gagarin was a pilot in the Soviet Air Force. He came from a small village in Russia.
38010.m: Yuri Gagarin came from the Soviet Union.

38011.q: How many times did Yuri Gagarin orbit the Earth?
38011.e: Gagarin flew around the Earth exactly once. Then he landed back in the Soviet Union.
38011.m: Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth once.

38012.q: Roughly how long did Yuri Gagarin’s flight last?
38012.e: From take-off to landing, the flight lasted about 108 minutes. That is just under two hours.
38012.m: Yuri Gagarin’s flight lasted just under two hours.

38013.q: What are space travellers from the Soviet Union and Russia called?
38013.e: In Russia they say cosmonaut, in the USA astronaut. Space travellers from China are called taikonauts.
38013.m: Space travellers from Russia are called cosmonauts.

38014.q: What did Yuri Gagarin shout in Russian at take-off?
38014.e: At take-off Gagarin shouted ‘Poyekhali!’. In English this means ‘Let’s go!’ and is very well known in Russia today.
38014.m: At take-off, Yuri Gagarin shouted ‘Let’s go!’.

38015.q: How old was Yuri Gagarin when he flew into space?
38015.e: Gagarin was born in 1934 and flew into space in 1961. So he was 27 years old.
38015.m: Yuri Gagarin was 27 years old on his space flight.

38016.q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
38016.e: Buzz Aldrin followed the commander onto the Moon’s surface shortly afterwards. The two stayed outside for about two and a half hours.
38016.m: Buzz Aldrin was the second person on the Moon.

38017.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in the spacecraft and orbited the Moon?
38017.e: Michael Collins waited in the command module ‘Columbia’ while the other two were on the Moon. He never walked on the Moon.
38017.m: Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone and waited for the others.

38018.q: How does the famous sentence continue: ‘That’s one small step for man, one ... for mankind’?
38018.e: The first person on the Moon said this sentence as he stepped onto the Moon’s surface. It is one of the best-known sentences in history.
38018.m: The first step on the Moon was a giant leap for mankind.

38019.q: Which Swiss university had an experiment on the Moon during Apollo 11?
38019.e: Researchers from Bern built a sail of aluminium foil that caught particles from the Sun. On the Moon it was even set up before the US flag.
38019.m: A solar wind experiment from the University of Bern was part of the first Moon landing.

38020.e: The Saturn V was over 100 metres tall and one of the most powerful rockets ever built. It sent the astronauts on their way to the Moon.
38020.m: Apollo 11 was launched on the huge Saturn V rocket.

a: Both sides build more and more weapons
38021.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union each wanted to be stronger than the other. So both sides built more and more, and ever stronger, weapons.
38021.m: In an arms race, opponents compete to build more and more weapons.

38022.q: Which especially dangerous weapons did the USA and the Soviet Union build in the arms race?
38022.e: Atomic bombs can destroy whole cities. Both superpowers built a great many of them.
38022.m: In the arms race, both sides built many atomic bombs.

38023.q: Which country was the first to have an atomic bomb?
38023.e: The USA tested the first atomic bomb in 1945. In the same year it used atomic bombs against Japan.
38023.m: The USA was the first country to have an atomic bomb.

38024.q: In which year did the Soviet Union test its first atomic bomb?
38024.e: In August 1949 the Soviet Union set off its first atomic bomb. Now both superpowers had this weapon.
38024.m: The Soviet Union had an atomic bomb from 1949.

38025.q: What do you call it when countries agree to reduce their weapons?
38025.e: In disarmament, weapons are destroyed or no longer built. It is the opposite of arming.
38025.m: Disarmament means countries have fewer weapons.

38026.q: Why did neither superpower use its atomic bombs against the other?
a: The bombs were not finished yet
38026.e: Each side could have struck back immediately. This was called the ‘balance of terror’.
38026.m: Fear of mutual destruction prevented a nuclear war.

38027.q: Where were schoolchildren in the USA supposed to duck during a nuclear alarm drill?
38027.e: In the ‘Duck and Cover’ drill, children learned to duck under their desk and protect their head.
38027.m: Schoolchildren in the USA practised ducking under their desks during an alarm.

38028.q: Roughly how many nuclear weapons did the USA and the Soviet Union have together in the 1980s?
38028.e: Around 1986 there were about 70,000 nuclear weapons in the world. Almost all of them belonged to the two superpowers.
38028.m: In the 1980s there were tens of thousands of nuclear weapons.

38029.q: What is meant by the ‘hotline’ in the Cold War?
a: A cable car across the border
38029.e: The hotline was a direct link between the governments of the two superpowers. It meant they could send each other messages quickly.
38029.m: The hotline was a direct communication line between the superpowers.

38030.q: Which two cities did the hotline connect?
38030.e: The line connected the government of the USA with the government of the Soviet Union. It ran through several European countries.
38030.m: The hotline connected Washington and Moscow.

38031.q: In which year was the hotline set up?
38031.e: The link went into operation on 30 August 1963. That was a few months after a dangerous crisis.
38031.m: The hotline was set up in 1963.

38032.q: After which dangerous event was the hotline set up?
a: After the fall of the Berlin Wall
38032.e: In the crisis over nuclear missiles in Cuba, it took a long time for messages to arrive. That was never to happen again.
38032.m: The hotline was a lesson learned from the Cuban Missile Crisis.

38033.e: The two superpowers wanted to prevent a nuclear war breaking out because of a mistake. With the direct line they could quickly clear up what was going on.
38033.m: The hotline was meant to prevent misunderstandings and an accidental war.

38034.q: Was the hotline really a telephone at the beginning?
38034.e: At first, written texts were sent over the line with a teleprinter. A teleprinter is a kind of typewriter that sends texts over a line.
38034.m: At first the hotline was a teleprinter, not a telephone.

38035.q: What is the hotline often popularly called?
38035.e: Many people and many films talk about the ‘red telephone’. Red stands for danger and importance.
38035.m: The hotline is often called the red telephone.

38036.q: Which animals were in the English sentence used to test the hotline?
38036.e: The first test sentence was ‘The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog’s back’. This sentence contains every letter of the English alphabet.
38036.m: The hotline was tested with a sentence about a fox and a dog.

38037.q: What are the peaceful protests in East Germany in 1989 called?
38037.e: Many people in East Germany took to the streets without violence and demanded freedom. In the end the government had to give in.
38037.m: The Peaceful Revolution of 1989 changed East Germany without violence.

38038.q: Which two superpowers faced each other in the Cold War?
a: The USA and the Soviet Union
38038.e: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other. They did not fight each other directly, but they built up huge amounts of weapons.
38038.m: In the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other.

38039.q: What did the USA and the Soviet Union agree on in 1987?
a: To get rid of certain nuclear missiles
To set up a joint army
38039.e: In the INF Treaty, both sides promised to destroy all their land-based intermediate-range missiles. That was an important step towards disarmament.
38039.m: In 1987 the superpowers agreed to get rid of certain nuclear missiles.

38040.q: Which US President was in office when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989?
38040.e: George Bush, the father of the later President George W. Bush, was President of the USA from 1989 to 1993.
38040.m: George Bush was President of the USA when the Wall fell.

38041.q: Who climbed onto a tank in Moscow in August 1991 and helped stop a coup?
38041.e: Opponents of the reforms wanted to seize power. From a tank, Boris Yeltsin called on people to resist, and the coup failed.
38041.m: In 1991 Boris Yeltsin stood on a tank against the coup.

38042.q: Which Soviet republic was the first to declare itself independent in 1990?
38042.e: On 11 March 1990 Lithuania declared its independence from the Soviet Union. Other republics followed afterwards.
38042.m: In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

38043.q: What is the long human chain of 1989 through Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania called?
38043.e: On 23 August 1989, about two million people held hands. In this way they peacefully demanded freedom for their countries.
38043.m: In the Baltic Way, millions of people formed a human chain for freedom.

38044.q: Which country became the largest successor state of the Soviet Union in 1991?
38044.e: At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union broke up into 15 independent states. The largest of them is Russia, with its capital Moscow.
38044.m: Russia is the largest successor state of the Soviet Union.

38045.q: Which former Eastern Bloc country joined NATO in 1999?
38045.e: In March 1999 Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic became members of NATO. They had previously been in the Warsaw Pact.

38046.q: In which city stood the famous wall that divided a city from 1961 to 1989?
38046.e: The Berlin Wall divided the city of Berlin into an eastern and a western part. It stood for about 28 years.
38046.m: The Berlin Wall divided the city of Berlin.

38047.q: In its best-known form, what was the Berlin Wall mainly made of?
38047.e: In the end the Wall was built from large concrete sections. At the beginning it was partly just barbed wire and stones.
38047.m: In the end the Berlin Wall was made of concrete sections.

38048.q: Roughly how high was the Berlin Wall?
38048.e: The concrete wall was about 3.6 metres high. That is about twice as tall as an adult.
38048.m: The Berlin Wall was about 3.6 metres high.

38049.q: What was the guarded strip behind the Berlin Wall called, where people were killed trying to escape?
38049.e: Behind the Wall lay a wide, guarded strip with fences and watchtowers. Because people trying to escape were shot there, it was called the death strip.
38049.m: The strip behind the Wall was called the death strip.

38050.q: From where did border soldiers watch the Berlin Wall?
38050.e: There were many watchtowers along the Wall. From there, border soldiers made sure that no one escaped.
38050.m: Border soldiers guarded the Wall from watchtowers.

38051.q: Which state had the Berlin Wall built?
38051.e: The government of East Germany had the Wall built. The Soviet Union agreed to it.
38051.m: East Germany built the Berlin Wall.

38052.q: Roughly how long was the border around West Berlin?
38052.e: The Wall and the border installations around West Berlin were about 155 kilometres long. Part of it ran right through the middle of the city.
38052.m: The border around West Berlin was about 155 kilometres long.

38053.q: What did the East German government officially call the Berlin Wall?
38053.e: East Germany spoke of the ‘Anti-Fascist Protective Rampart’. In truth, the Wall was mainly meant to stop its own people from escaping.
38053.m: East Germany called the Wall a protective rampart.

38054.q: On which date did the building of the Berlin Wall begin?
38054.e: On Sunday, 13 August 1961, soldiers and police officers sealed off the border. After that, the Wall was built.
38054.m: The building of the Wall began on 13 August 1961.

38055.q: On the first day of building the Wall, what was mainly used to seal off the border?
38055.e: First, barbed wire and barriers were put up. Only in the days that followed was a solid wall built.
38055.m: At the beginning, the border was made of barbed wire.

38056.q: At what time of day did the sealing of the border begin on 13 August 1961?
38056.e: The sealing off began at night, when most people were asleep. In the morning the city was suddenly divided.
38056.m: The border was sealed off overnight.

38058.q: What happened to many families in Berlin after the Wall was built?
a: They were allowed to move to the West together
They all had to move to Bonn
They could visit each other freely every Sunday
38058.e: The Wall separated relatives and friends who lived on different sides. For a long time they could no longer visit each other.
38058.m: The Wall separated many families from each other.

38059.q: Which politician said in June 1961: ‘No one has the intention of building a wall’?
38059.e: Walter Ulbricht was the most powerful politician in East Germany at the time. Only two months after he said this, the building of the Wall began.
38059.m: Walter Ulbricht promised not to build a wall, and then did.

38060.q: What did the young border soldier Conrad Schumann do on 15 August 1961?
38060.e: Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire to West Berlin. A photo of his jump became world-famous.
38060.m: Conrad Schumann escaped with a famous jump over the barbed wire.

38061.q: Which state did East Berlin belong to?
38061.e: East Berlin was the eastern part of Berlin. It belonged to the communist state in the east of Germany.
38061.m: East Berlin belonged to East Germany.

38062.q: Which tall tower with a silver ball was built in East Berlin?
38062.e: The Berlin TV Tower stands in what used to be East Berlin. It was finished in 1969 and is over 360 metres tall.
38062.m: The Berlin TV Tower comes from East Berlin.

38063.q: Which country was in charge of the east of Berlin after the Second World War?
38063.e: After the war, Berlin was divided into four parts. The eastern part was run by the Soviet Union.
38063.m: East Berlin used to be the Soviet part of the city.

38064.q: How can you recognise the little traffic-light man (Ampelmännchen) from East Berlin?
a: He has a dog with him
38064.e: The East Berlin traffic-light man has a hat on his head. Today he is very popular all over Berlin.
38064.m: The traffic-light man with a hat comes from East Germany.

38065.q: After the Wall was built, could people from East Berlin simply travel to West Berlin?
38065.e: After the Wall was built, most people from East Berlin were no longer allowed to go to the West. Only a few, for example pensioners, later got permission.
38065.m: People in East Berlin could not travel freely to the West.

38066.q: Which large square lies in the centre of former East Berlin?
38066.e: Alexanderplatz was an important square in East Berlin. A huge demonstration took place there on 4 November 1989.

38067.q: Which popular children’s character was on East German television every evening?
38067.e: The Sandman was on East German television from 1959. With a short story, he sent the children off to bed.
38067.m: The Sandman is a character from East German television.

38068.q: What was West Berlin often called because it lay in the middle of East Germany?
38068.e: West Berlin was completely surrounded by East Germany. That is why the city was often called an island.
38068.m: West Berlin was like an island in East Germany.

38069.q: Which three countries were in charge of West Berlin after the Second World War?
38069.e: After the war, Berlin was divided into four sectors. The three western sectors belonged to the USA, Great Britain and France.
38069.m: West Berlin was made up of three sectors of the Western powers.

38070.q: What did Berliners call the aeroplanes that supplied West Berlin in 1948 and 1949?
38070.e: During the blockade, planes brought food and coal to West Berlin. Because some pilots dropped sweets, they were called raisin bombers.
38070.m: The raisin bombers supplied West Berlin from the air.

38071.q: Which US President said ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ (‘I am a Berliner’) in West Berlin in 1963?
38071.e: John F. Kennedy visited West Berlin in June 1963. With this sentence he showed that the USA stood by West Berlin.
38071.m: In 1963 John F. Kennedy showed his loyalty to West Berlin with a famous sentence.

38072.q: Which US President demanded in front of the Brandenburg Gate in 1987 that the Wall be torn down?
38072.e: Ronald Reagan called out: ‘Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall!’ With this he challenged the Soviet leader to tear down the Wall.
38072.m: In 1987 Ronald Reagan demanded that the Wall be torn down.

38073.q: Which state was West Berlin closely linked to?
38073.e: West Berlin was closely linked to the Federal Republic of Germany. For example, it had the same currency, the Deutschmark.
38073.m: West Berlin was closely linked to West Germany.

38074.q: After the Wall was built, where were people from East Berlin usually allowed to travel?
a: Only to other Eastern Bloc countries
To every country in the world
38074.e: People from East Berlin were usually only allowed to travel to other Eastern Bloc countries such as Hungary or Czechoslovakia. People from West Berlin, on the other hand, could travel freely, including to Switzerland.
38074.m: West Berliners could travel much more freely than East Berliners.

38075.q: What does the abbreviation GDR stand for?
38075.e: GDR means German Democratic Republic (in German: DDR). That was the name of the state in the east of Germany from 1949 to 1990.
38075.m: GDR is short for German Democratic Republic.

38076.q: What was the capital of East Germany?
38076.e: East Germany made East Berlin its capital. The government and the party were based there.
38076.m: East Berlin was the capital of East Germany.

38077.q: Which tools could be seen in the emblem on the flag of East Germany?
38077.e: On East Germany’s black, red and gold flag there was an emblem with a hammer and a compass in a ring of ears of corn. That made it easy to recognise.
38077.m: The East German flag showed a hammer and compass.

38078.q: What was the name of the long-time leader of East Germany who had to resign in 1989?
38078.e: Erich Honecker led East Germany from 1971 to 1989. In October 1989 he had to resign after huge protests.
38078.m: Erich Honecker was the leader of East Germany for many years.

38079.q: In which part of Germany was the GDR?
38079.e: The GDR lay in the east of today’s Germany. That is why it was also called East Germany.
38079.m: The GDR lay in the east of Germany.

38080.q: Which sentence did people chant at the demonstrations in East Germany in 1989?
a: We are staying in the GDR
38080.e: At the Monday demonstrations, for example in Leipzig, thousands chanted ‘We are the people’. They wanted freedom and a say.
38080.m: ‘We are the people’ was the chant of the demonstrations in East Germany.

38081.q: What was the money in East Germany called?
38081.e: In East Germany people paid with the mark of the GDR. It was worth much less than the Deutschmark in the West.
38081.m: In East Germany people paid with the East German mark.

38082.q: What does the abbreviation FRG stand for?
38082.e: FRG means Federal Republic of Germany (in German: BRD). That was the name of the western German state, and it is still Germany’s name today.
38082.m: FRG is short for Federal Republic of Germany.

38083.q: Which city was the capital of West Germany before reunification?
38083.e: The small city of Bonn on the Rhine was the capital of West Germany. But it was only seen as a temporary capital.
38083.m: Bonn was the capital of the old West Germany.

38084.q: In which year was the Federal Republic of Germany founded?
38084.e: The Federal Republic was founded on 23 May 1949. On that day its Basic Law came into force.
38084.m: The Federal Republic of Germany was founded in 1949.

38085.q: What colours is the flag of the Federal Republic of Germany?
38085.e: The flag of the Federal Republic has black, red and gold stripes. It has no emblem in the middle.
38085.m: The German flag is black, red and gold.

38086.q: What was the money in West Germany called before the euro?
38086.e: In West Germany people paid with the Deutsche Mark, Deutschmark for short. Since 2002 people in Germany have paid with the euro.
38086.m: The Deutschmark was the money of West Germany.

38087.q: What is the head of government in the Federal Republic of Germany called?
38087.e: The Federal Chancellor leads the German government. In Switzerland, the Federal Council with seven members does this.
38087.m: In Germany, the Federal Chancellor leads the government.

38088.q: Which neighbouring country does the Federal Republic of Germany border to the south?
38088.e: Switzerland lies south of Germany. The border runs, for example, along the Rhine near Basel and Schaffhausen.
38088.m: Germany is a northern neighbour of Switzerland.

38089.q: Compared with East Germany, in which direction did the old West Germany lie?
38089.e: West Germany lay west of East Germany. That is why it was called West Germany.
38089.m: The FRG was the western part of Germany.

38090.e: Checkpoint Charlie was a well-known border crossing between East and West Berlin. It was in use from 1961 to 1990.
38090.m: Checkpoint Charlie was a border crossing in Berlin.

38091.q: On which street was the Checkpoint Charlie border crossing?
38091.e: Checkpoint Charlie was on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin. Today a small hut there reminds people of the border crossing.

38092.q: Which soldiers guarded Checkpoint Charlie on the Western side?
38092.e: Checkpoint Charlie was in the American sector of Berlin. That is why American soldiers were stationed there.
38092.m: American soldiers were stationed at Checkpoint Charlie.

38093.q: What faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie in October 1961?
38093.e: In October 1961, American and Soviet tanks faced each other. Luckily both sides drove away again after about 18 hours.
38093.m: In 1961, tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie.

38094.q: What does the word ‘Charlie’ in the name Checkpoint Charlie stand for?
38094.e: In the phonetic alphabet, Charlie stands for the letter C. It was the third checkpoint, after Alpha and Bravo.
38094.m: In the phonetic alphabet, Charlie means the letter C.

38095.q: Who was mainly allowed to use Checkpoint Charlie?
38095.e: At Checkpoint Charlie it was mainly foreigners, diplomats and Allied soldiers who were allowed to cross the border. There were other crossings for West Germans.
38095.m: Checkpoint Charlie was mainly a crossing for foreigners.

38096.q: What did the famous sign at Checkpoint Charlie say?
a: You are leaving the American sector
38096.e: The sign warned: ‘You are leaving the American sector’. The sentence was written on it in English, Russian, French and German.
38096.m: The sign at Checkpoint Charlie warned that you were leaving the American sector.

38097.q: What reminds people of the past at Checkpoint Charlie today?
38097.e: At the former border crossing there is now a copy of the checkpoint hut with sandbags. Many tourists take photos there.
38097.m: Today there is a replica checkpoint hut at Checkpoint Charlie.

38098.q: What stands on top of the Brandenburg Gate?
38098.e: On top of the gate stands the Quadriga. It is a goddess on a chariot pulled by four horses.
38098.m: On the Brandenburg Gate stands the Quadriga with four horses.

38099.q: In which city is the Brandenburg Gate?
38099.e: The Brandenburg Gate stands in the middle of Berlin. It is one of Germany’s best-known landmarks.
38099.m: The Brandenburg Gate is a landmark of Berlin.

38100.q: Which French emperor took the Quadriga to Paris in 1806?
38100.e: Napoleon conquered Berlin in 1806 and had the figures taken to Paris. In 1814 they came back to Berlin.
38100.m: Napoleon took the Quadriga to Paris in 1806.

38101.q: At the time of the Wall, could you walk through the Brandenburg Gate?
38101.e: The Brandenburg Gate was right next to the Wall in the restricted zone. No one was allowed to simply walk through.
38101.m: At the time of the Wall, the Brandenburg Gate was closed off.

38102.q: When was the Brandenburg Gate opened to pedestrians again after the fall of the Wall?
38102.e: On 22 December 1989 a passage was opened at the Brandenburg Gate. Thousands of people celebrated.
38102.m: The Brandenburg Gate was opened shortly before Christmas 1989.

38103.q: What is the Brandenburg Gate a symbol of today?
38103.e: It used to stand for division because it was right by the Wall. Today it is a symbol of German unity.
38103.m: The Brandenburg Gate is a symbol of a united Germany.

38104.q: How many passageways does the Brandenburg Gate have?
38104.e: Between the columns of the gate there are five passageways. The middle one used to be only for the king.
38104.m: The Brandenburg Gate has five passageways.

38105.q: Which century does the Brandenburg Gate date from?
38105.e: The gate was built from 1788 to 1791. That is in the 18th century, so much earlier than the Wall.
38105.m: The Brandenburg Gate is over 200 years old.

38107.q: What was the Trabant affectionately called?
38107.e: The Trabant was usually just called ‘Trabi’. The name is still well known today.
38107.m: The Trabant was popularly called the Trabi.

38108.q: What special material was the outer body of the Trabant made of?
38108.e: The outer body of the Trabant was made of a hard plastic called Duroplast. Underneath there was a steel frame.
38108.m: The Trabi had a plastic body.

38109.q: Roughly what was the top speed of a Trabi?
38109.e: The Trabant had a small two-stroke engine. It could only manage just over 100 kilometres per hour. It was built in Zwickau.
38109.m: A Trabi could go at most about 100 km/h.

38110.q: How long did people in East Germany often have to wait for a new Trabant?
38110.e: There were too few cars in East Germany. That is why people often had to wait many years for their Trabi.
38110.m: People often waited many years for a new Trabi.

38111.q: After the fall of the Wall, what did many people from East Germany drive to the West in?
38111.e: After the border opened, long queues of Trabis drove to the West. The rattling cars became a symbol of the fall of the Wall.
38111.m: The Trabi became a symbol of the fall of the Wall.

38112.q: How many doors did the normal Trabant saloon have?
38112.e: The Trabant saloon only had two doors. Anyone who wanted to sit in the back had to fold the front seat forwards.
38112.m: The Trabi saloon had two doors.

38113.q: Until which year was the Trabant built?
38113.e: The last Trabant was built in April 1991. Altogether about three million were made.

38114.q: On the night the Wall fell, what did many people climb onto at the Brandenburg Gate?
38114.e: In front of the Brandenburg Gate the Wall was wide and flat on top. Many people stood and danced there during the night.
38114.m: When the Wall fell, many people stood on top of the Wall.

38115.q: What did many people do on the night the Wall fell?
38115.e: People from East and West hugged, cheered and drank together. For many, it was the best night of their lives.
38115.m: On the night the Wall fell, people from East and West celebrated.

38117.q: Which word did Günter Schabowski say when asked from when the new travel rules applied?
38117.e: Schabowski said: ‘As far as I know, this takes effect immediately, without delay.’ After that, thousands streamed to the border crossings.
38117.m: Schabowski said the travel rules applied immediately.

38118.q: At what time of day were the first border crossings opened on 9 November 1989?
38118.e: The press conference was in the evening. Late in the evening, under pressure from the crowds, the border soldiers opened the first crossings.
38118.m: The border opened late in the evening of 9 November.

38119.q: What did visitors from East Germany receive in the West as a welcome?
38119.e: Every visitor from East Germany received 100 Deutschmarks of welcome money in the West. Many used it to buy bananas, chocolate or presents.
38119.m: Visitors from East Germany received welcome money in the West.

38120.q: What happened at the border crossings in Berlin on the night of 9 November 1989?
a: The border soldiers opened the gates
The border soldiers built new walls
38120.e: Thousands of people pushed towards the border crossings. Under this pressure, the border soldiers opened the gates late in the evening.
38120.m: On the night the Wall fell, the border crossings opened.

38121.q: What were the people who chipped pieces off the Wall after it fell called in Berlin?
38121.e: These people hacked at the Wall like a woodpecker hacks at wood. That is why they were called ‘Mauerspechte’, wall woodpeckers.
38121.m: Wall woodpeckers chipped pieces off the Berlin Wall.

38122.q: Which tools did the wall woodpeckers usually work with?
38122.e: The wall woodpeckers knocked small pieces out of the concrete with a hammer and chisel. This made holes in the Wall.
38122.m: Wall woodpeckers used a hammer and chisel.

38123.q: What could be heard at many places along the Wall in the days after it fell?
38123.e: Everywhere wall woodpeckers were knocking pieces out of the concrete. That is why there was constant knocking and hammering at the Wall.
38123.m: After the Wall fell, knocking and hammering could be heard all along it.

38124.q: What did many wall woodpeckers do with the pieces they chipped off?
a: They threw them into the river
