38411.q: Which landscape does the large mural in the National Council chamber show?
a: The area around Lake Uri with the Rütli
38411.e: The painting “The Cradle of the Confederation” by Charles Giron shows the landscape around Lake Uri. The Rütli meadow is there.
38411.m: The mural in the National Council chamber shows the cradle of the Confederation.

38412.q: Where do the journalists sit in the National Council chamber?
a: In the basement in front of screens
38412.e: The press galleries are in the corners of the chamber. From there, the media follow the debates.
38412.m: The press watches the National Council from galleries in the corners.

38413.q: What does a list of names for a vote in parliament show?
38413.e: For every vote, a record is kept of how each member voted. This list of names is published.
38413.m: The list of names shows how each member voted.

38414.q: The National Council has voted electronically since 1994, the Council of States only since 2014. How many years later did the Council of States start?
38414.e: The sum is 2014 minus 1994. That makes 20 years.
38414.m: The Council of States introduced electronic voting much later than the National Council.

38415.q: How do members of the National Council mostly vote today?
38415.e: Each member has buttons at their seat for yes, no and abstain. The result appears straight away on a big display board.
38415.m: In the National Council, members vote electronically with buttons.

38416.q: In the National Council, 98 members vote yes, 85 vote no and 7 abstain. The president does not vote. How many members did not take part?
38416.e: Without the president, 199 members can vote. 98 + 85 + 7 = 190 voted, so 199 minus 190 = 9 are missing.
38416.m: Anyone who presses neither yes, no nor abstain does not take part in the vote.

38417.q: May a member press the button for an absent colleague?
a: No, voting for someone else is forbidden
Yes, but only in the Council of States
38417.e: Every member must cast their own vote. Voting on behalf of others is not allowed.
38417.m: In parliament, nobody may vote for another person.

38418.q: Where are the lists of names for the votes published?
38418.e: The lists of names are linked as PDFs above the results in the electronic Official Bulletin. The verbatim records of the debates are there too.
38418.m: The Official Bulletin contains parliament's debates and votes.

38419.q: Why are the votes of the members published?
a: So voters know how they voted
So the Federal Council can punish them
So the cantons can change them
38419.e: Publishing creates transparency. This lets voters check how their representatives voted.
38419.m: Published votes make parliament's work easy to follow.

38420.q: How are elections in the Federal Assembly, such as the Federal Council election, carried out?
a: By standing up in the chamber
38420.e: For elections, ballot papers are handed out and collected again. That way, it stays secret who voted for whom.
38420.m: Elections in parliament are secret and use ballot papers.

a: The Secretary General of the Federal Assembly
The President of the National Council
38421.e: The Parliamentary Services are headed by the Secretary General of the Federal Assembly. The Federal Chancellery, on the other hand, is the Federal Council's staff.
38421.m: The Parliamentary Services are led by the Secretary General of the Federal Assembly.

38422.q: Who do the Parliamentary Services work for?
a: For the National Council and the Council of States
38422.e: The Parliamentary Services are the staff of the Federal Assembly. They support the National Council, the Council of States and their committees. The Federal Council has its own staff, the Federal Chancellery.

38423.q: Where do the Parliamentary Services mainly work?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
At the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
In the UN building in Geneva
At the National Bank in Zurich
38423.e: The Parliamentary Services work where parliament meets: in the Federal Palace in Bern and in buildings nearby.
38423.m: The Parliamentary Services work in the Federal Palace in Bern.

38424.q: Which body used to support parliament as well as the government?
38424.e: In the past, the Federal Chancellery served both the Federal Council and parliament. Today parliament has its own staff, the Parliamentary Services, set out in Article 155 of the Federal Constitution.
38424.m: Parliament has its own staff, the Parliamentary Services.

38425.q: Which task belongs to the Parliamentary Services?
38425.e: The Parliamentary Services plan sessions and committee meetings and do the secretarial work. Bringing laws into force is the job of the Federal Council.
38425.m: The Parliamentary Services organise the work of the councils and committees.

38426.q: What are the Parliamentary Services called in French?
38426.e: In French they are called “Services du Parlement”, in Italian “Servizi del Parlamento”. The Chancellerie fédérale is the Federal Chancellery.
38426.m: In French, the Parliamentary Services are called Services du Parlement.

38427.q: What do the Parliamentary Services write about committee meetings?
38427.e: The secretarial work includes reports, minutes and translations. The committees' minutes are not public.
38427.m: The Parliamentary Services record in minutes what is discussed in the committees.

38428.q: Whom do the Parliamentary Services look after during visits to the Federal Palace?
38428.e: The Parliamentary Services support foreign parliamentary delegations and plan trips for members of parliament. They also inform the public about parliament.
38428.m: The Parliamentary Services also look after guests from other parliaments.

38429.q: Which metal covers the outside of the Federal Palace dome?
38429.e: The dome is covered with copper sheet. Over time, copper forms a green layer in the air.
38429.m: The outside of the Federal Palace dome is made of copper.

38430.q: Why is the Federal Palace dome green today?
a: Because of the patina on the copper
38430.e: Copper reacts with air and rain and forms a turquoise-green patina. This layer protects the metal.
38430.m: The green colour of the dome forms by itself through the patina.

38431.q: What colour was the copper dome of the Federal Palace when it was new?
38431.e: New copper has a reddish shine. Only over the years did the green patina form.
38431.m: At first the dome was copper red and only slowly turned green.

38432.q: What stands at the very top of the dome's lantern, around 60 metres high?
38432.e: On the lantern of the dome, around 60 metres up, there is a gilded Swiss cross. It can be seen from far away.
38432.m: A golden Swiss cross shines at the very top of the Federal Palace.

38433.q: What colour is the Federal Palace dome today?
38433.e: The dome is covered with copper. In the air, copper gets a green layer called patina.
38433.m: The Federal Palace dome is green.

38434.q: Which cantonal coat of arms was originally missing from the Federal Palace dome because the canton did not exist yet?
38434.e: When the Federal Palace was built, there were 22 cantons. The canton of Jura was only created in 1979, and its coat of arms was added later.

38435.q: What do the coloured glass pictures in the Federal Palace dome show?
38435.e: In the glass dome, the cantons' coats of arms glow around the Swiss coat of arms. They show that the cantons together make up Switzerland.
38435.m: The cantonal coats of arms can be seen in the Federal Palace dome.

a: A party when the shell of a building is finished
The election of the Federal Council
38436.e: At a topping-out ceremony, the builders celebrate that the shell of the building is finished. A party like this was also held for the dome of the Federal Palace.
38436.m: A topping-out ceremony is held when the shell of a building is finished.

38437.q: In which city is the Federal Palace with the big dome?
38437.e: The Federal Palace is in Bern. The National Council and Council of States meet here, and the Federal Council is also based here.
38437.m: The Federal Palace with the dome is in Bern.

38438.q: What is the document called in which the Federal Council presents a draft law to parliament and explains it?
38438.e: In the dispatch, the Federal Council explains why a new law is needed and attaches the draft. Then the National Council and the Council of States discuss it.
38438.m: With a dispatch, the Federal Council sends a draft law to parliament.

38439.q: Which procedure usually takes place before the Federal Council adopts the dispatch on a law?
38439.e: In the consultation, cantons, parties, associations and other interested groups can comment on a preliminary draft. The Federal Council evaluates the responses and adjusts the draft.
38439.m: Before the dispatch, the Federal Council gathers opinions in the consultation.

38440.q: Whom does the federal government invite to the consultation before a dispatch is written?
38440.e: The consultation mainly invites the cantons, the political parties and associations. That way, many points of view go into the draft.
38440.m: In the consultation, cantons, parties and associations have their say.

38441.q: Who usually prepares the draft for a dispatch?
38441.e: The experts in the responsible department and its federal offices write the draft. Then the Federal Council decides on it.
38441.m: The federal administration writes the drafts for dispatches.

38442.q: Who finally decides to send a dispatch to parliament?
a: The Federal Council as a whole
The President of the National Council
38442.e: The Federal Council decides as a body, meaning all seven members together. Only then does the dispatch go to the Federal Assembly.
38442.m: A dispatch is decided by the whole Federal Council together.

38443.q: Apart from the explanations, what is attached to a dispatch on a new law?
a: The draft text of the law
The list of everyone entitled to vote
38443.e: The dispatch explains the aim and content of the proposal and contains the draft that parliament is to discuss.
38443.m: Every dispatch on a law comes with a fully written draft.

38444.q: Who is the Federal Council's dispatch on a law addressed to?
38444.e: The dispatch is addressed to the federal parliament, that is, the National Council and the Council of States. They discuss and pass the law.
38444.m: The Federal Council's dispatch is meant for parliament.

38445.q: What do courts often use the dispatch on a law for later?
a: To understand the meaning of the law
38445.e: The dispatch shows what a law was meant to say. That is why courts refer to it when an article is unclear.
38445.m: The dispatch later helps to interpret a law correctly.

38446.q: Which two councils must approve a federal law?
a: The National Council and the Council of States
The National Council and the Federal Council
The Council of States and the Federal Supreme Court
The Federal Council and the cantonal government
38446.e: The Federal Assembly consists of the National Council and the Council of States. A federal law is only passed if both councils agree.
38446.m: A federal law needs the approval of the National Council and the Council of States.

38447.q: What is the council that discusses a proposal first called?
38447.e: The council that deals with a matter first is called the first council. The other council is then the second council.
38447.m: The first council is the first to discuss a proposal.

38448.q: Who decides whether the National Council or the Council of States discusses a proposal first?
a: The presidents of the two councils
A draw in the Federal Palace
38448.e: The presidents of the National Council and the Council of States divide up the business. That way, both councils should have about the same amount of work as first council.
38448.m: The council presidents decide which council discusses a proposal first.

38449.q: What happens if the second council decides an article differently from the first council?
a: The difference goes back to the first council
The law has failed straight away
38449.e: Disagreements between the councils are called differences. They are sent back and forth in the procedure for resolving differences until the councils agree.
38449.m: When there are differences, a proposal goes back and forth between the councils.

38450.q: What is the group called that looks for a compromise when the National Council and the Council of States cannot agree for a long time?
38450.e: If differences remain between the councils after several rounds, a conciliation conference is formed. It is made up of members of both councils and looks for a compromise.
38450.m: The conciliation conference looks for a compromise between the councils.

38451.q: Each council sends 13 members to the conciliation conference. How many members does it have in total?
38451.e: The National Council and the Council of States each send 13 members. 13 plus 13 makes 26.
38451.m: A conciliation conference has 26 members from both councils.

38452.q: What happens if one council rejects the conciliation conference's proposal?
a: The National Council gets its way
38452.e: The conciliation conference's proposal is the last attempt to reach agreement. If one council rejects it, the whole proposal is dropped.
38452.m: If one council rejects the conciliation proposal, the whole law fails.

38453.q: When is the final vote on a federal law held?
a: On the last day of the session
On the first day of the session
38453.e: Once both councils have agreed, they vote once more on the whole text in the final vote at the end of the session.
38453.m: The final vote takes place at the end of a session.

38454.q: Why does neither of the two councils have the last word on a federal law?
a: Because both councils have equal rights
Because the Federal Supreme Court decides
38454.e: Switzerland has a two-chamber system with two equally strong councils. That is why the National Council and the Council of States must agree.
38454.m: The National Council and the Council of States carry exactly the same weight on laws.

38455.q: What are the permanent committees called that discuss proposals on particular policy areas, such as transport or education, in advance?
38455.e: Each legislative committee is responsible for one subject area. There are also supervisory committees that check the work of the government and the administration.
38455.m: Legislative committees specialise in particular policy areas.

38456.q: How many members does a permanent committee of the National Council have?
38456.e: The permanent committees of the National Council each have 25 members. With fewer people, a draft can be discussed in more detail than in the whole council.
38456.m: A National Council committee has 25 members.

38457.q: Why are the committees of the Council of States smaller than those of the National Council?
a: Because the Council of States has fewer members
Because the Council of States works less
Because the Council of States only meets in summer
Because the Federal Council orders it
38457.e: The Council of States has 46 members, the National Council 200. That is why the Council of States' committees have 13 members and the National Council's 25.
38457.m: Council of States committees are smaller because the Council of States is smaller.

38458.q: What does the abbreviation EAC stand for in the Federal Palace?
38458.e: The EAC (WAK in German) discusses proposals on taxes, customs duties and the economy, for example. Each council has its own EAC.
38458.m: The EAC deals with the economy and taxation.

38459.q: Which committee discusses a law on health insurance in advance?
a: The Social Security and Health Committee
38459.e: The Social Security and Health Committee, SSHC for short, is responsible for topics such as the AHV (old-age insurance), health insurance and health.
38459.m: Health proposals go to the Social Security and Health Committee.

38460.q: Are the meetings of parliamentary committees public?
38460.e: Committees should be able to discuss things openly. That is why their meetings are confidential, while the debates in the councils are public.

38461.q: How are committee seats shared out among the parties?
a: According to the size of the parliamentary groups
38461.e: The parliamentary groups get committee seats in proportion to their size in the council. That way, each committee is a small version of the council.
38461.m: Large parliamentary groups have more seats on the committees.

38462.q: Who presents the proposals of the preparatory committee to the council?
38462.e: A spokesperson for the committee explains to the council what the committee decided and why.
38462.m: Committee spokespeople report to the council on the committee's work.

38463.q: What can committees do to prepare for a proposal?
a: Bring laws into force on their own
38463.e: Committees can invite experts, cantons or associations to hearings. That way, they gain knowledge before making proposals.
38463.m: In hearings, committees gather knowledge from experts.

38464.q: What does a council decide in the debate on whether to consider a bill?
a: Whether it wants to discuss the proposal
On the date of the session
38464.e: First, the council decides in principle whether it wants to deal with the proposal at all. Only after that do the details come up.
38464.m: In the debate on considering a bill, the council decides whether to discuss a proposal at all.

38465.q: What does it mean when a council decides “not to consider” a bill?
a: It does not want to discuss the proposal
It postpones it for a week
38465.e: By refusing to consider it, a council declines to discuss the proposal in detail. It is saying no to the draft in principle.
38465.m: Refusing to consider a bill is a no in principle to a proposal.

38466.q: What happens if the first council decides not to consider a bill but the second council decides to consider it?
a: The proposal goes back to the first council
38466.e: If the second council wants to consider it, the first council must decide again whether to consider it. Here too, the two councils must agree.
38466.m: If they disagree about considering a bill, the first council discusses it a second time.

38467.q: What happens if the first council decides for a second time not to consider a bill?
38467.e: There is no conciliation conference on whether to consider a bill. If a council says no for the second time, the proposal is off the table.
38467.m: A second refusal to consider a bill ends a proposal for good.

38468.q: What does a council ask for when it refers a proposal back to the Federal Council?
38468.e: When referring back, the council does agree to consider the bill, but sends the draft back with instructions to revise it.
38468.m: By referring a bill back, parliament asks for a better draft.

38469.q: For which item of business must parliament always agree to consider it?
38469.e: For the federal budget, considering it is compulsory. Without a budget, the federal government could not spend any money the next year.
38469.m: Parliament must always discuss the federal budget.

38470.q: What comes first in the council?
a: The debate on whether to consider the bill
38470.e: A council first decides whether to consider a bill. Only if it does are there a detailed discussion and a vote on the whole proposal.
38470.m: Without agreeing to consider a bill, there is no detailed discussion.

38471.q: Who can propose in the council that a bill should not be considered?
38471.e: The committee or a minority of the committee can propose not considering a bill, and so can individual members. Then the council votes.
38471.m: The whole council votes on a proposal not to consider a bill.

38472.q: How is a law discussed in the detailed discussion?
38472.e: In the detailed discussion, the council goes through the draft article by article and can change each one separately.
38472.m: In the detailed discussion, each article is discussed separately.

38473.q: What is the vote on the whole proposal straight after the detailed discussion in a council called?
38473.e: After the detailed discussion, the council votes in the overall vote on whether it accepts the amended proposal as a whole.
38473.m: The overall vote follows the detailed discussion.

38474.q: What is a minority proposal in the detailed discussion?
a: A proposal from committee members who were outvoted
A proposal from the Federal Supreme Court
38474.e: Members who were outvoted in the committee can bring their view to the council as a minority proposal. The council then decides between the majority and the minority.
38474.m: A committee minority can also present its proposal in the council.

38475.q: What is an individual proposal in the detailed discussion?
a: A proposal from a single member
A proposal from the whole Federal Council
A proposal from all the cantons
38475.e: A member can make their own proposal for a change, even if they do not sit on the committee. The council votes on it.
38475.m: With an individual proposal, any member can suggest a change.

38476.q: Who represents the government's view during the detailed discussion?
a: The responsible member of the Federal Council
A member of a cantonal government
38476.e: During the discussion, the responsible member of the Federal Council is in the chamber. They explain what the Federal Council thinks of the proposals.
38476.m: In the councils, the responsible Federal Council member speaks for the government.

38477.q: What happens if a vote in the council is tied?
a: The president of the council decides
38477.e: The president normally does not vote. In a tie, the president gives the casting vote.
38477.m: In a tie, the president of the council gives the casting vote.

38478.q: What does a council still discuss in the procedure for resolving differences?
a: The election of the Federal Council
38478.e: Articles on which both councils decided the same are settled. In the procedure for resolving differences, only the differences remain.
38478.m: In resolving differences, only the differences count.

38479.q: May a council delete an article of the draft in the detailed discussion?
a: Only with permission from the Federal Supreme Court
38479.e: Parliament is the legislator. It can change articles, add new ones or delete them completely.
38479.m: Parliament may change a draft law freely.

38480.e: Parliament passes laws, while the Federal Council usually issues ordinances. They set out how a law is put into practice.
38480.m: Federal ordinances usually come from the Federal Council.

38481.q: Can you call a referendum against an ordinance of the Federal Council?
38481.e: The optional referendum exists against federal laws, not against ordinances. But an ordinance must keep to the law.
38481.m: There is no referendum against ordinances.

38482.q: Which level comes below the federal law in the ranking of law?
38482.e: At the very top is the Federal Constitution, below it the federal laws and below them the ordinances. A lower level must not contradict a higher one.
38482.m: An ordinance must keep to the law and the constitution.

38483.q: What must an ordinance of the Federal Council be based on?
38483.e: The Federal Council may only issue ordinances if the constitution or a law gives it the power to do so.
38483.m: For every ordinance, the Federal Council needs a basis in the constitution or a law.

38484.q: What does an ordinance usually set out?
a: The election of the Federal Council
38484.e: A law sets out the important principles. The ordinance covers the details, for example forms, deadlines or technical values.
38484.m: Laws set out the principles and ordinances the details.

38485.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what must be set out in a law and not just in an ordinance?
a: The opening hours of a federal office
38485.e: According to the Federal Constitution, important rules, such as who has to pay taxes and how much, belong in a federal law. The people can have a say on them through the referendum.
38485.m: Important rules such as taxes must be set out in a law.

38486.q: What is an emergency ordinance of the Federal Council?
a: A temporary rule for serious crises
A rule only for fire brigades
A permanent change to the constitution
38486.e: In serious crises, the Federal Council may issue temporary ordinances based directly on the constitution. This happened in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic, for example.
38486.m: The constitution only allows emergency ordinances in serious crises and only for a limited time.

38487.q: What is a rule of the Federal Council that sets out a law in more detail called?
38487.e: A law sets out the principles. In an ordinance, the Federal Council sets out exactly how the law is put into practice.
38487.m: An ordinance sets out the details of a law.

38488.q: Why can an ordinance usually be changed more quickly than a law?
a: Parliament and a referendum are not needed
The cantons do not have to agree
It only applies for one year
38488.e: To change an ordinance, the Federal Council needs neither the National Council nor the Council of States, and there is no referendum. That is why it is much quicker.
38488.m: Ordinances can be adjusted more quickly than laws.

38489.q: Who can submit a parliamentary initiative?
38489.e: With a parliamentary initiative, members of parliament themselves propose a new law. It should not be confused with the popular initiative.
38489.m: The parliamentary initiative comes from parliament itself.

38490.q: Who works out the draft law for a parliamentary initiative?
38490.e: If the initiative succeeds, a committee of parliament writes the draft itself. The Federal Council does not help write it here.
38490.m: With a parliamentary initiative, parliament writes the law itself.

38491.q: What is a parliamentary initiative submitted by a committee itself called?
38491.e: If a committee submits the initiative, it is called a committee initiative. The committee can then start work on the draft directly.
38491.m: A committee initiative comes from a committee.

38492.q: How is a parliamentary initiative different from a popular initiative?
a: It comes from parliament instead of the people
It always comes from the Federal Council
It only applies in one municipality
38492.e: A popular initiative is submitted by voters with signatures. A parliamentary initiative is submitted by members, parliamentary groups or committees.
38492.m: The parliamentary initiative comes from parliament, the popular initiative from the people.

38493.q: What happens to the draft law once the committee has finished working it out?
a: Both councils discuss it and vote on it
The Federal Council brings it into force at once
The Federal Supreme Court decides on it
It becomes valid without a vote
38493.e: A draft from a parliamentary initiative is discussed in the National Council and the Council of States like any law. Both councils must agree.
38493.m: Both councils discuss the draft of a parliamentary initiative.

38494.q: Why is the parliamentary initiative seen as the strongest tool in parliament?
a: The Federal Council must carry it out
38494.e: With other motions, the Federal Council has to act. With a parliamentary initiative, parliament writes the draft itself and does not depend on the government.
38494.m: With a parliamentary initiative, parliament can draft a law without the Federal Council.

38495.q: Does the draft from a parliamentary initiative also go out for consultation?
a: Only in the canton of Bern
38495.e: The committee also sends its preliminary draft out for consultation. That way, cantons, parties and associations can have their say.
38495.m: Drafts from parliament also go out for consultation.

38496.q: What may the Federal Council do about the draft of a parliamentary initiative?
a: Bring the draft into force without discussion
38496.e: The Federal Council does not write the draft, but it may give its opinion on it. This opinion goes to the councils.
38496.m: On a parliamentary initiative, the Federal Council only gives its opinion.

38497.q: What does a postulate ask the Federal Council to do?
a: Look into something and report on it
Bring a law into force at once
38497.e: A postulate instructs the Federal Council to check whether a law or measure is needed and to write a report on it.
38497.m: With a postulate, parliament asks for a report on a question.

38498.q: How many councils must approve a postulate for it to be accepted?
38498.e: A postulate is accepted if the council in which it was submitted approves it. The other council does not have to vote on it.
38498.m: For a postulate, the approval of a single council is enough.

38499.q: Must parliament consider a federal popular initiative that has collected enough signatures?
a: Only if the Federal Council agrees
38499.e: For popular initiatives, considering them is required. Parliament must discuss them and give a voting recommendation.
38499.m: Parliament must always discuss a popular initiative.

38500.q: A law says: bikes need lights at night. What is more likely to be in the ordinance?
a: How bright and what colour the lights must be
Who may become a Federal Councillor
38500.e: The law sets the rule. The ordinance sets the details, for example a white light at the front and a red one at the back.
38500.m: Laws set out the principles and ordinances the details.

38501.q: Who can submit a postulate in parliament?
38501.e: Postulates are motions from parliament. Members, parliamentary groups or committees can submit them.
38501.m: A postulate is a motion from parliament.

38502.q: What is the report called that the Federal Council writes because of an accepted postulate?
38502.e: The Federal Council fulfils a postulate with a postulate report. It says what the Federal Council has looked into and what it proposes.
38502.m: A postulate is fulfilled with a postulate report.

38503.q: What does the Federal Council propose on a newly submitted postulate?
a: A review by the Federal Supreme Court
38503.e: The Federal Council says whether it wants to accept the postulate or rejects it. But the council must then decide.
38503.m: The Federal Council gives a recommendation on every postulate.

38504.q: What does the Latin word “postulare”, from which “postulate” comes, mean?
38504.e: “Postulare” means to demand or to request in Latin. With a postulate, parliament demands something from the Federal Council.
38504.m: A postulate is a demand to the Federal Council.

38505.q: Which council has a regular question time?
38505.e: Question time is a tool of the National Council. There, members can ask the Federal Council short questions.
38505.m: Question time exists in the National Council.

38506.q: What happens during the National Council's question time?
a: Members ask the Federal Council questions
38506.e: In question time, members of the National Council ask the Federal Council short questions. A member of the Federal Council answers them in the chamber.
38506.m: In question time, the Federal Council must answer to the National Council.

38507.q: Why must questions and answers be short in question time?
38507.e: Question time lasts no more than 90 minutes. In that time, as many questions as possible should get a turn.
38507.m: In question time, questions and answers are short.

38508.q: How long does question time in the National Council last?
38508.e: Question time is limited to 90 minutes. That is why questions and answers must be short.
38508.m: Question time lasts an hour and a half.

38509.q: Who answers the National Council members' questions in question time?
a: A member of the Federal Council
The President of the National Council
38509.e: The questions are addressed to the Federal Council. A member of the Federal Council reads out the answer that the Federal Council has approved.
38509.m: In question time, the Federal Council answers.

38510.q: What may a National Council member do after the answer in question time?
38510.e: Whoever asked may ask a short follow-up question straight away. The Federal Council member answers it at once.
38510.m: In question time, a short follow-up question is allowed.

38511.q: How are questions for question time submitted?
a: In writing a few days before
38511.e: The questions are submitted in writing a few days in advance. That way, the Federal Council can prepare the answers.
38511.m: Questions for question time are submitted in writing beforehand.

38512.q: The National Council has four ordinary sessions a year, each with two question times. How many question times is that per year?
38512.e: You work out 4 times 2. That makes 8 question times a year.
38512.m: The National Council holds eight question times every year.

38513.q: Who usually decides when a new federal law comes into force?
38513.e: If the law says nothing else, the Federal Council sets the date it comes into force. This leaves time for preparation.
38513.m: The Federal Council usually decides when a law comes into force.

38514.q: What do the transitional provisions of a new law set out?
a: The change from the old law to the new law
38514.e: Transitional provisions set out what applies to cases that began under the old law. That way, the change to the new law is clearly regulated.
38514.m: Transitional provisions make the change from old to new law easier.

38515.q: What must happen to a new law before it applies?
a: It must be approved by the Federal Supreme Court
It must be read out in every school
38515.e: Everyone must be able to know which rules apply. That is why a new law is officially published before it comes into force.
38515.m: A law is published before it applies.

38516.q: On which date do especially many new laws and ordinances come into force in Switzerland?
38516.e: Many acts come into force at the start of the year. This makes planning easier, for example for taxes and charges.
38516.m: The start of the year is a common date for new rules.

38517.q: What is special about a federal law that has been declared urgent?
a: It can come into force immediately
It needs no vote in parliament
It only applies to one canton
38517.e: An urgent federal law can apply straight after it is passed. A referendum is still possible, but only afterwards.
38517.m: An urgent law applies immediately and must be time-limited.

38518.q: How long do you have to collect signatures for a referendum against a new federal law?
38518.e: A referendum needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days. Only after that can the law come into force, if no referendum succeeds or the people vote yes.
38518.m: You have 100 days for a referendum.

38519.q: What does it mean when a law “comes into force”?
a: It must be applied from then on
It is discussed for the first time
It is put in the archive
It is explained to the people for the first time
38519.e: From the day it comes into force, a law is valid. Authorities, courts and everyone must then keep to it.
38519.m: A law only applies from the day it comes into force.

38520.q: May a new, stricter criminal law apply to acts committed before it existed?
a: Yes, if the Federal Council wants it
38520.e: Criminal law has a ban on retroactive laws: people may only be punished for what was already forbidden at the time of the act. This protects against arbitrary treatment.
38520.m: New criminal laws may not punish more harshly after the fact.

38521.q: Can a law come into force in several parts at different times?
38521.e: Some parts need more preparation than others. That is why the Federal Council can bring a law into force in stages.
38521.m: A law can also come into force step by step.

38522.q: What does the abbreviation “SR” stand for with federal laws?
38522.e: The Classified Compilation (SR) contains all federal laws and ordinances in force. Each law has a number there; the Code of Obligations, for example, is 220.
38522.m: SR is the Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation.

38523.q: How is the Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation organised?
38523.e: The acts are organised by topic, for example state, private law or criminal law. That way, you find the rules on one topic together.
38523.m: The SR organises the law by topic.

38524.q: Where is the easiest place to read the federal laws in force today?
a: Only in the Federal Palace in Bern
38524.e: The Classified Compilation is freely available to everyone on the internet. There you can find the Civil Code under number 210, for example.
38524.m: You can read the federal laws online in the SR.

38525.q: Which act comes right at the front of the national law section of the Classified Compilation?
38525.e: The Federal Constitution is Switzerland's most important law. It has the number 101 and comes right at the front of national law.
38525.m: The Federal Constitution has the SR number 101.

38526.q: Apart from Swiss law, what else can you find in the Classified Compilation?
38526.e: The SR also contains international treaties, that is, agreements with other countries. Their numbers begin with a 0.
38526.m: In the SR, international treaties begin with a zero.

38527.q: Why do the laws in the Classified Compilation have numbers?
a: So you can find them quickly, sorted by topic
Because they are sorted by price
Because each number stands for a year
38527.e: The numbers sort the laws by subject area. The first digit shows the topic, for example 3 for criminal law.
38527.m: The numbers in the SR sort the law by topic.

38528.q: How often is the electronic Classified Compilation updated?
38528.e: The electronic version is updated continuously whenever an act changes. That way, it always shows the current state.
38528.m: The electronic SR is always up to date.

38529.q: Apart from federal laws and ordinances, what else does the Classified Compilation contain?
38529.e: The SR also contains the constitutions of the cantons as well as international treaties. Court judgements are not part of it.
38529.m: The cantonal constitutions can also be found in the SR.

38530.q: What is the official federal publication called in which the Federal Council's dispatches appear?
38530.e: Dispatches, draft laws and decisions of parliament appear in the Federal Gazette. It is an important official publication of the Confederation.
38530.m: Dispatches and decisions of parliament appear in the Federal Gazette.

38531.q: What can you find in the Federal Gazette?
38531.e: In the Federal Gazette, the Confederation publishes the Federal Council's dispatches, draft laws and decisions of parliament.
38531.m: The Federal Gazette contains federal dispatches and decisions.

38532.q: Why does the Confederation publish its laws and decisions for everyone?
a: So that everyone knows which rules apply
So that only lawyers read them
38532.e: Laws apply to everyone. That is why every person must be able to read what has been decided.
38532.m: Laws are published so that everyone can know them.

38533.e: The Federal Gazette is published by the Federal Chancellery. It is the Federal Council's staff office.
38533.m: The Federal Chancellery publishes the Federal Gazette.

38534.q: In which languages is the Federal Gazette published?
38534.e: The Federal Gazette is published in the three official languages German, French and Italian. Each version is equally binding.
38534.m: The Federal Gazette is published in three official languages.

38535.q: What is the Federal Gazette called in French?
38535.e: The French edition is called “Feuille fédérale”, the Italian one “Foglio federale”.
38535.m: In French, the Federal Gazette is called “Feuille fédérale”.

38536.q: In which additional language do acts of particular importance appear in a supplement to the Federal Gazette?
38536.e: Acts of particular importance also appear in Romansh. The Federal Council chooses them in agreement with the canton of the Grisons.
38536.m: Especially important acts are also published in Romansh in the Federal Gazette.

38537.q: Where can you read the Federal Gazette today?
a: Only for a fee at a kiosk
38537.e: The Federal Gazette and all federal law are available for free on a federal internet platform.
38537.m: The Federal Gazette is freely available online.

38538.q: Apart from a partial revision, what else can a popular initiative ask for?
a: A total revision of the Federal Constitution
The removal of the Federal Council
The overturning of a court judgement
38538.e: With 100,000 signatures, you can also ask for a complete renewal of the Federal Constitution. The only such initiative that collected enough signatures failed in the popular vote in 1935.
38538.m: A popular initiative can also ask for a completely new Federal Constitution.

38540.q: Why was the number of signatures for popular initiatives raised in 1977?
38540.e: With women's right to vote in 1971 and population growth, the number of voters had grown a lot. That is why the hurdle was adjusted.
38540.m: The number of signatures was raised because the number of voters had grown a lot.

38541.q: A committee has collected 112,000 signatures, of which 9,000 are invalid. How many valid signatures does it have above the limit of 100,000?
38541.e: 112,000 minus 9,000 makes 103,000 valid signatures. 103,000 minus 100,000 makes 3,000 signatures to spare.
38541.m: Only valid signatures count for an initiative to succeed.

38542.q: What can happen if a popular initiative breaks very important rules such as the ban on torture?
a: It needs twice as many signatures
It only applies in one canton
38542.e: No initiative may break very important rules of international law, such as the ban on torture. Otherwise it is declared invalid and does not go to a vote.
38542.m: Popular initiatives may not break the ban on torture.

38543.q: For most popular initiatives, who writes the exact new constitutional text?
38543.e: Almost all initiatives come with a finished text. The initiative committee wrote it before collecting signatures.
38543.m: The initiative committee usually writes the exact text of the initiative.

38544.q: May parliament change the content of a popular initiative's text before the people vote?
a: No, the people vote on the original text
Yes, as much as it likes
Yes, but only the Federal Council
38544.e: Parliament may not change the wording of an initiative. But it can make its own counter-proposal.
38544.m: The people vote on the original text of a popular initiative.

38545.q: How often is a popular initiative with enough signatures declared invalid?
38545.e: Declarations of invalidity are very rare. Almost all initiatives that collect enough signatures go to a vote.
38545.m: Only very few popular initiatives have ever been declared invalid.

38547.q: Which international treaty is subject to the optional referendum?
a: A treaty of unlimited duration that cannot be terminated
Every contract of a private company
38547.e: According to the Federal Constitution, treaties of unlimited duration that cannot be terminated, joining international organisations and treaties with important law-making provisions are among those subject to the optional referendum.
38547.m: Important international treaties can also be put to the people with a referendum.

38548.q: A referendum committee hands in 58,000 signatures, and 6 per cent of them are invalid. Has the referendum succeeded?
38548.e: 6 per cent of 58,000 is 3,480 invalid signatures. 58,000 minus 3,480 makes 54,520 valid ones, which is more than the 50,000 needed.
38548.m: For a referendum, only the valid signatures count.

38549.q: At federal level, can you call a referendum against a law that has applied for years?
38549.e: A referendum can only be called against newly passed laws and decisions within the deadline. Anyone who wants to change an existing law needs an initiative or a motion in parliament.
38549.m: A referendum is only possible against new decisions of parliament.

38550.q: How many times has the cantonal referendum been used successfully at federal level so far (as of 2025)?
38550.e: In 2003, several cantons called a referendum against a federal tax package. It is the only case in which a cantonal referendum succeeded.
38550.m: The cantonal referendum is very rare in Switzerland.

38551.q: Roughly what percentage of the approximately 5.6 million voters (as of 2024) are the 50,000 signatures for a referendum?
38551.e: 50,000 divided by 5,600,000 is about 0.009. That is just under 1 per cent of voters.
38551.m: A referendum needs the signatures of less than one per cent of voters.

38552.q: Can you call an optional referendum against the annual federal budget?
a: No, the budget cannot be challenged by referendum
Yes, but only every four years
Only if the Federal Council agrees
38552.e: Parliament passes the budget with a simple federal decree. At federal level, there is no referendum against such decrees.
38552.m: Parliament alone decides on the federal budget.

38553.q: Why is the referendum also called the “brake” of direct democracy?
a: It can stop decisions of parliament
38553.e: With the referendum, the people can reject a law passed by parliament. The initiative, on the other hand, is seen as the “accelerator” because it gets new things started.
38553.m: The referendum works as a brake, the initiative as an accelerator.

38555.q: With which vote does parliament finally pass a federal law?
a: The final vote in both councils
The debate on whether to consider the bill
38555.e: After the discussion, the National Council and the Council of States each hold a final vote on the whole law at the end of the session. Only then can a referendum be called.
38555.m: A federal law is only passed after the final vote in both councils.

38556.q: A popular initiative is published in the Federal Gazette on 1 March 2024. When does its collection period end?
38556.e: The collection period lasts 18 months, that is one year and six months. Counting from 1 March 2024, it ends on 1 September 2025.
38556.m: Eighteen months of collection time is a year and a half.

38557.q: When does the collection period for a popular initiative begin?
a: When it is published in the Federal Gazette
38557.e: After the preliminary check by the Federal Chancellery, the initiative text is published in the Federal Gazette. The 18 months run from that day.
38557.m: The collection period starts on the day of publication in the Federal Gazette.

38558.q: What collection period applied to popular initiatives before 1977?
38558.e: Before 1977, you could collect for as long as you liked. Only the Federal Act on Political Rights of 1976 limited the period to 18 months.
38558.m: There has only been a fixed collection period for popular initiatives since 1977.

38559.q: On average, how many valid signatures must a committee collect per month to reach 100,000 in 18 months?
38559.e: 100,000 divided by 18 is around 5,556. Rounded, that is about 5,600 valid signatures a month.
38559.m: If you collect evenly, you need several thousand signatures every month.

38560.q: Who decides whether the collection period was kept and the initiative has succeeded?
38560.e: The Federal Chancellery counts the certified signatures handed in and checks the deadline. Then it rules whether the initiative has succeeded.
38560.m: The Federal Chancellery decides whether a popular initiative has succeeded.

38561.q: Why do many committees hand in their initiative before the 18 months are up?
a: After that the initiative becomes more expensive
The signatures expire after a year
38561.e: Once there are enough certified signatures with some to spare, collecting more is hardly worth it. Handing it in early brings the initiative to the people sooner.
38561.m: An initiative can be handed in at any time within the collection period.

38562.q: What happens to a popular initiative that has only 95,000 valid signatures after 18 months?
a: It goes to a vote anyway
38562.e: The deadline cannot be extended. If valid signatures are missing, the initiative has failed and there is no vote.
38562.m: The collection period is strict and is not extended.

38563.q: Roughly how many days are 18 months?
38563.e: A year has 365 days, half a year around 183 days. 365 + 183 makes about 548 days.
38563.m: Eighteen months is roughly a year and a half.

38564.q: A new federal law is officially published on 1 October. In which month does the referendum deadline end?
38564.e: The referendum period lasts 100 days. Counting from 1 October, it ends on 9 January.
38564.m: The referendum period lasts just over three months.

38565.q: How long is the referendum period today?
38565.e: For a referendum, the signatures must be handed in within 100 days of the law being published. The 18 months apply to the popular initiative.

38566.q: After 60 days, a committee has 32,000 valid signatures for a referendum. On average, how many must it collect per day in the remaining 40 days?
38566.e: 50,000 minus 32,000, that is 18,000 signatures, are still missing. 18,000 divided by 40 days makes 450 signatures a day.
38566.m: For a referendum, what counts is whether there are enough valid signatures at the end of the deadline.

38567.q: On average, how many valid signatures per week does a referendum need if you count on around 14 weeks?
38567.e: 50,000 divided by 14 is around 3,571. That is about 3,600 valid signatures a week.
38567.m: A referendum needs fast and well-organised collecting.

38568.q: What must have arrived at the Federal Chancellery by the end of the 100 days?
a: The signatures with certification of voting rights
Just a list of the committee members
38568.e: For a referendum, the signature lists including certification must be handed in within the deadline. Lists that arrive too late do not count.
38568.m: For a referendum, only what is handed in on time and certified counts.

38569.q: If no referendum is called, when is the earliest a new federal law can come into force?
a: On the day of the final vote
38569.e: While the referendum period is running, it is not known whether there will be a vote. Only when the deadline has passed unused can the Federal Council bring the law into force.
38569.m: A law can only come into force after the referendum period has passed unused.

38570.q: Why is a referendum harder to collect than an initiative, counted per day?
a: You may only collect on Sundays
38570.e: For 50,000 signatures there are only 100 days, whereas for 100,000 signatures there are 18 months. So for a referendum you have to get many more signatures per day.
38570.m: With a referendum, the time pressure is much greater than with an initiative.

38571.q: Can the 100-day referendum period be extended during the summer holidays?
a: Yes, by the length of the holidays
38571.e: The 100-day deadline is fixed and runs during the holidays too. That is why many committees start collecting straight after publication.
38571.m: The referendum period runs without a break.

38572.q: For which kind of proposal is there always a popular vote at federal level?
a: For every change to the Federal Constitution
For every ordinance of the Federal Council
38572.e: Every change to the constitution is subject to the mandatory referendum. Nobody has to collect signatures for it.
38572.m: Changes to the Federal Constitution always go to the people.

38573.q: In which year did the people and the cantons accept the Federal Constitution in force today?
38573.e: The total revision of the Federal Constitution went to a vote on 18 April 1999 and was accepted. It came into force on 1 January 2000.
38573.m: Today's Federal Constitution was accepted in 1999.

38574.q: What would be needed if Switzerland wanted to join the EU?
a: A yes from the people and the cantons
Only a yes from the Federal Council
Only a yes from the Federal Supreme Court
Only a yes from the cantonal governments
38574.e: Joining a community such as the EU is subject to the mandatory referendum. The people and the cantons must agree.
38574.m: The people and the cantons would have to vote on joining the EU.

38576.q: What does a change to the Federal Constitution need to be accepted?
a: A majority of the people and a majority of the cantons
Only a majority of the people
Only a majority of the cantons
Only a yes from the Federal Council
38576.e: For a change to the constitution, the majority of voters must say yes and, in addition, the majority of the cantons. This is called the double majority of people and cantons.
38576.m: Changes to the constitution need a majority of the people and of the cantons.

38577.q: A change to the constitution gets 11 whole and 2 half cantonal votes. Is that enough for a majority of the cantons?
a: No, half a vote is missing
38577.e: Two half cantonal votes together make one whole vote. 11 + 1 makes 12 out of 23 cantonal votes, and that is a majority.
38577.m: For the majority of the cantons, half-cantons each count as half a cantonal vote.

38579.q: Since when has there been a mandatory referendum for constitutional changes at federal level?
38579.e: Even the first Federal Constitution of 1848 required the people and the cantons to approve changes to the constitution. It is the oldest of the people's rights in the federal state.
38579.m: The mandatory constitutional referendum has existed since the federal state was founded.

38580.q: What happens to a direct counter-proposal if the committee withdraws its initiative?
a: Only the counter-proposal goes to a vote
The counter-proposal is dropped as well
The counter-proposal comes into force without a vote
The Federal Council decides on it alone
38580.e: The direct counter-proposal is a change to the constitution and is subject to the mandatory referendum. Without the initiative, the people and cantons vote only on it.
38580.m: After the initiative is withdrawn, only the direct counter-proposal is voted on.

38581.q: At which level is an indirect counter-proposal usually?
a: At the level of a law
At the level of the constitution
At the level of a cantonal ordinance
38581.e: With an indirect counter-proposal, parliament changes a law to take up part of the initiative's aim. An optional referendum can be called against this law.
38581.m: An indirect counter-proposal is usually a change to a law.

38582.q: Why does parliament often make a counter-proposal to an initiative?
a: It wants to take up the aim in a more moderate way
It wants to ban the vote
It wants to count the signatures
38582.e: With a counter-proposal, parliament takes up part of an aim when the initiative goes too far for it. That way, voters get an alternative.
38582.m: A counter-proposal offers a more moderate solution than the initiative.

38583.q: Which law was the indirect counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative?
38583.e: Parliament passed the Climate Protection Act as an indirect counter-proposal. After a referendum, the people accepted it on 18 June 2023.
38583.m: The Climate Protection Act was created as a counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative.

38584.q: An initiative and a direct counter-proposal go to a vote together. How many questions do you answer on the ballot paper?
38584.e: You vote on the initiative and on the counter-proposal, and you also answer the deciding question. That makes three questions.
38584.m: With an initiative and a counter-proposal, there are three questions.

38585.q: May you vote yes both to the initiative and to the direct counter-proposal?
a: Yes, the double yes is allowed
No, that makes the ballot paper invalid
Only with permission from the municipality
Only in the canton of Bern
38585.e: You may accept both proposals. With the deciding question, you then say which one you would prefer.
38585.m: A double yes is allowed for an initiative and a counter-proposal.

38586.q: With which form of popular initiative is a direct counter-proposal not possible?
a: With an initiative on the environment
With an initiative with a withdrawal clause
38586.e: A general proposal does not yet contain a finished text, only an instruction to parliament. That is why it cannot be set against a counter-proposal.
38586.m: Parliament cannot set a direct counter-proposal against a general proposal.

38587.q: Why does an indirect counter-proposal not appear on the ballot paper at the same time as the initiative?
a: It is a law with its own referendum
It only applies in one canton
It is decided by the Federal Supreme Court
38587.e: The indirect counter-proposal is a law. The people only vote on it if someone calls an optional referendum.
38587.m: An indirect counter-proposal is only voted on after a referendum.

38588.q: What may you do with the double yes?
a: Vote yes to the initiative and to the counter-proposal
Put the same ballot paper in twice
Vote for another person as well
Vote twice at the ballot box
38588.e: If an initiative and a counter-proposal go to a vote, you may approve both. The deciding question then decides which proposal applies if both are accepted.
38588.m: With a double yes, you approve both the initiative and the counter-proposal.

38589.q: What problem was there before the double yes was introduced?
a: Supporters of a change were split
There were too many voting days
The cantons were not allowed to vote
The ballot papers were too small
38589.e: Anyone who wanted a change had to choose between the initiative and the counter-proposal. So the yes votes were split, and often both proposals failed.
38589.m: The double yes stops supporters of a change from weakening each other.

38590.q: How many questions are on the ballot paper when an initiative with a direct counter-proposal goes to a vote?
38590.e: You are asked about the initiative, about the counter-proposal and, in the deciding question, which proposal you prefer.
38590.m: With an initiative and a counter-proposal, you answer three questions.

38591.q: What is the deciding question for?
a: It decides which proposal applies if both get a yes
It elects the President of the Confederation
38591.e: If the initiative and the counter-proposal are both accepted, only one proposal can come into force. The deciding question shows which one voters prefer.
38591.m: The deciding question decides between two accepted proposals.

38592.q: What is a counter-proposal to a popular initiative?
a: Parliament's own proposal on the same topic
A second initiative by the same people
38592.e: Parliament can set its own proposal against an initiative. This counter-proposal often goes less far than the initiative.
38592.m: A counter-proposal is parliament's proposal on an initiative.

38593.q: What happens if the initiative and the counter-proposal are both rejected?
38593.e: The deciding question only counts if both proposals were accepted. If both are rejected, the constitution stays unchanged.
38593.m: The deciding question only matters with a double yes.

38594.q: May you put a cross for the deciding question even if you voted no twice before?
a: Yes, the deciding question is separate
No, then the ballot paper is invalid
Only with permission from the municipality
Only if you are on the committee
38594.e: Each of the three questions is counted on its own. Even someone who rejects both proposals can say which one they prefer in case of a double yes.
38594.m: Anyone can answer the deciding question, even after two noes.

38595.q: What applies if the initiative is rejected but the direct counter-proposal is accepted by the people and the cantons?
38595.e: Only the counter-proposal was accepted, so it comes into force. The deciding question is not needed in this case.
38595.m: If only the counter-proposal is accepted, the counter-proposal applies.

38596.q: Until when can an initiative committee withdraw its popular initiative?
a: Until the Federal Council sets the voting day
38596.e: Withdrawal is possible until the Federal Council has set the popular vote. After that, the initiative will definitely go to the people.
38596.m: An initiative can be withdrawn until the Federal Council has set the voting date.

38597.q: What majority on the initiative committee is needed to withdraw?
a: An absolute majority of the members
38597.e: Withdrawal is decided by an absolute majority of the members of the initiative committee who are still entitled to vote.
38597.m: To withdraw, more than half of the committee must agree.

38598.q: What must be on every signature list so that withdrawal is possible later?
38598.e: With the withdrawal clause, the people signing know that the committee may withdraw the initiative. It is required on all lists.
38598.m: The withdrawal clause on the signature list allows the committee to withdraw later.

38599.q: Why do committees sometimes withdraw their initiative?
a: A counter-proposal meets part of their aim
The collection period is too long
The voting booklet is too thick
38599.e: When parliament passes a useful counter-proposal, committees often decide not to risk a vote. That way, they secure a partial success.
38599.m: A withdrawal often secures a partial success through a counter-proposal.

38600.q: What does a “conditional withdrawal” of a popular initiative mean?
a: It only applies if the indirect counter-proposal comes into force
It only applies in good weather
It only applies in some cantons
It only applies for one year
38600.e: If a referendum is called against the indirect counter-proposal and the law is rejected, the withdrawn initiative still goes to a vote after all.
38600.m: A conditional withdrawal only applies if the indirect counter-proposal stands.

38601.q: Who may withdraw a popular initiative?
38601.e: Only the initiative committee can withdraw its initiative. This needs an absolute majority of its members.
38601.m: Only the initiative committee can withdraw an initiative.

38602.q: Which initiative was conditionally withdrawn in favour of the transplant law with an opt-out system?
38602.e: Parliament passed the opt-out system as an indirect counter-proposal. After a referendum, the people accepted the law on 15 May 2022, and the withdrawal became final.
38602.m: The organ donation initiative was withdrawn in favour of a law.

38603.q: Can an initiative still be handed in again after it has been withdrawn?
a: Only as a new initiative with new collecting
No, the topic is banned for ever
38603.e: A withdrawal is final. Anyone who wants to bring the aim to the people again must launch a new initiative and collect 100,000 signatures again.
38603.m: After a withdrawal, the same aim needs a new collection of signatures.

38604.q: Who certifies that the people signing a popular initiative are entitled to vote?
38604.e: The municipality keeps the electoral register. It checks each signature and confirms the person's right to vote.
38604.m: The municipality confirms the voting rights of the people who sign.

38605.q: Why may only voters from the same municipality sign one signature list?
a: Each municipality only checks its own electoral register
Because otherwise the lists get too long
Because each municipality has a different initiative
38605.e: Certification is done by the municipality where the person is entitled to vote. That is why each list must name the political municipality.
38605.m: A signature list always applies to only one political municipality.

38606.q: Why do initiative committees often have signatures certified while they are still collecting?
a: Otherwise people who moved away or died are not certified
Because otherwise the municipality charges a fine
Because the Federal Council orders it
38606.e: If a person has moved away or died in the meantime, the municipality can no longer confirm their right to vote. That is why committees certify as they go.
38606.m: Early certification stops valid signatures from being lost.

38607.q: What details must a person give on the signature list so that the municipality can find them?
a: Surname, first name, date of birth and address
38607.e: With surname, first name, date of birth and home address, the municipality can find the person in the electoral register. They must also sign in their own hand.
38607.m: Certification needs name, date of birth, address and signature.

38608.q: How many times may a voter sign the same popular initiative?
38608.e: The law allows each voter to sign the same request only once. Double signatures would distort the result.
38608.m: Each voter may sign a popular initiative only once.

38609.q: Who certifies the voting rights of Swiss people living abroad for an initiative?
a: The municipality whose electoral register they are on
38609.e: Swiss people abroad are on the electoral register of a Swiss municipality, usually where they last lived or their place of origin. This municipality certifies their right to vote.
38609.m: For Swiss people abroad, too, a Swiss municipality certifies their right to vote.

38610.q: What is a criminal offence when signing a popular initiative?
38610.e: Anyone who forges someone else's signature or signs with a false name commits an offence. The municipality can spot such signatures when checking.
38610.m: Signatures for the people's rights may only be given in your own hand and your own name.

38611.q: What can a voter do who cannot write but wants to support an initiative?
a: Another voter writes their name in
They put a fingerprint on the list
They must go to the Federal Chancellery in person
38611.e: The law allows a voter of their choice to write in their name. That person then signs with their own signature.
38611.m: Anyone who cannot write may have a voter write their name in for them.

38612.q: How many valid signatures must an initiative committee collect for a federal popular initiative?
38612.e: A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures from voters, collected within 18 months.

38613.q: Which condition must all members of an initiative committee meet?
a: They must be entitled to vote
38613.e: Only Swiss citizens who are entitled to vote may start a popular initiative.
38613.m: Only voters may sit on an initiative committee.

38614.q: Where are the names of the initiative committee members listed?
38614.e: Every signature list must show the names and addresses of the committee members. That way, the people signing know who is behind the initiative.
38614.m: The signature list names all members of the initiative committee.

38615.q: Which body checks the title of a popular initiative before collecting begins?
38615.e: In the preliminary check, the Federal Chancellery makes sure the title is not misleading, promotional or easily confused. It also checks the signature list.
38615.m: The Federal Chancellery checks an initiative before collecting starts.

38616.q: What does the Federal Chancellery not check in the preliminary check?
a: Whether the initiative's content is good
Whether the signature list is complete
Whether the committee is properly made up
38616.e: The preliminary check only covers form, title, translations and the committee. Whether an aim makes sense is decided later by parliament and the people.
38616.m: The Federal Chancellery does not judge the content of an initiative.

38617.q: Who is often behind the initiative committee of a federal popular initiative?
38617.e: Most initiatives are launched by parties, associations, trade unions or citizens' movements. They provide the committee members and organise the collecting.
38617.m: Popular initiatives are often backed by parties, associations or groups of committed citizens.

38618.q: Why may an initiative committee no longer change the text once collecting has started?
a: Because the paper is already printed
Because the Federal Council keeps it secret
38618.e: Every signature is for the published wording. A later change would distort the will of the people who signed.
38618.m: The text of an initiative is fixed once collecting starts.

38619.q: Who writes the initiative's arguments in the federal voting booklet?
a: The President of the National Council
38619.e: In the voting booklet, the committee gets space for its own arguments. Next to them is the position of the Federal Council and parliament.
38619.m: The initiative committee also has its say in the voting booklet.

38620.q: On how many dates a year are federal votes normally held in Switzerland?
38620.e: Every year, the Federal Council sets four possible voting Sundays. Several proposals can go to a vote on one date.
38620.m: There are up to four federal voting Sundays a year.

38621.q: Who decides which proposals go to the people on a voting Sunday?
38621.e: The Federal Council decides at least four months before the date which proposals will be voted on.
38621.m: The Federal Council decides what is voted on on a voting Sunday.

38622.q: By when at the latest must voters receive their voting papers?
38622.e: According to the Federal Act on Political Rights, voters receive the papers no earlier than four and no later than three weeks before voting day.
38622.m: The voting papers arrive no later than three weeks before the date.

38623.q: How do the vast majority of voters in Switzerland vote today?
a: At the ballot box on Sunday
38623.e: Postal voting is possible throughout Switzerland and very popular. In many cantons, around nine out of ten voters vote by post.
38623.m: Most voters in Switzerland vote by post.

38624.q: When do the ballot boxes close on voting Sunday in most municipalities?
38624.e: In most municipalities, the ballot boxes are open on Sunday morning and close at 12 noon at the latest. Then the counting begins.
38624.m: On voting Sunday, the ballot boxes usually close at midday.

38625.q: What is a projection on voting Sunday?
a: An estimate of the result from partial results
38625.e: Research institutes use the first municipalities to be counted to work out what the overall result is likely to be. The official result follows later.
38625.m: A projection estimates the voting result before everything is counted.

38626.q: What is the Federal Council's booklet called that is sent out with the voting papers?
38626.e: The Federal Council's explanations, often called the “voting booklet”, explain the proposals with the arguments of both sides.
38626.m: The voting explanations give information about the proposals.

38627.q: Who counts the votes on voting Sunday?
38627.e: Volunteers and staff in each municipality's polling office count the votes. The results are then passed on to the canton and the Confederation.
38627.m: The votes are counted in the municipalities.

38628.q: By when must a postal voting envelope reach the municipality to count?
a: By the time the ballot boxes close
By one week after the vote
By the Monday after the vote
By the end of the month
38628.e: Postal votes only count if they reach the municipality by the time the ballot boxes close on voting Sunday at the latest. That is why you should send the envelope a few days before.
38628.m: A postal voting envelope must reach the municipality before the ballot boxes close.

a: The share of voters who voted
38629.e: Voter turnout shows as a percentage how many of the people entitled to vote took part in a vote.
38629.m: Voter turnout measures how many people entitled to vote took part.

38630.q: Is a federal vote still valid if only 30 per cent of voters take part?
a: Yes, there is no minimum turnout
No, at least 50 per cent are needed
No, at least 75 per cent are needed
Only if the Federal Council agrees
38630.e: Switzerland has no minimum turnout for federal votes. The people who voted decide, however many there are.
38630.m: A federal vote is valid whatever the turnout.

38631.q: Turnout was very high in the 1992 EEA vote. What does that mean?
a: A great many voters took part
A great many cantons voted no
The vote took a very long time
38631.e: Turnout shows how many people entitled to vote took part. In 1992, it was almost 79 per cent, much more than usual.
38631.m: The 1992 EEA vote got an unusually large number of voters involved.

38632.q: Which canton has compulsory voting with a small fine for people who do not vote?
38632.e: In the canton of Schaffhausen, voters must vote or they pay a small fine. That is why Schaffhausen usually has one of the highest turnouts.
38632.m: Schaffhausen is the only canton with compulsory voting.

38633.q: Roughly what has the average turnout in federal votes been over recent decades?
38633.e: Since the 1970s, average turnout has mostly been between 40 and 50 per cent. For disputed proposals, it can be much higher.
38633.m: On average, a little under half of Swiss voters take part in a vote.

38634.q: What does “selective participation” in votes mean?
a: Many people only vote on topics that interest them
You may only answer every second question
38634.e: Studies show that many voters vote now and then, but not always. That is why, over several votes, more people take part than a single turnout figure shows.
38634.m: Many voters take part in only some of the votes.

38635.q: In 1922 there was a vote with over 86 per cent turnout. But who was not allowed to vote at all back then?
38635.e: Women have only had the vote at federal level since 1971. So the record turnout of 1922 refers only to men.
38635.m: Before 1971, only men could vote at federal level.

38636.q: How does turnout change when a proposal is highly disputed and much discussed?
a: It always stays exactly the same
38636.e: Highly disputed proposals get many voters involved who do not usually take part. Then turnout can be well above average.
38636.m: Disputed proposals bring more voters to the ballot box.

38637.q: In a municipality, turnout is 60 per cent and there are 2,500 voters. How many people voted?
38637.e: 60 per cent of 2,500 is 0.6 times 2,500, which is 1,500 people.
38637.m: From the turnout and the number of voters, you can work out how many people voted.

38639.q: How did the vote on the 1947 AHV Act turn out?
38639.e: Around four out of five voters said yes. It was one of the clearest results of that time.
38639.m: In 1947, the AHV (old-age insurance) was clearly accepted.

38640.q: Why is the AHV (old-age and survivors' insurance) so important for Switzerland?
a: It gives almost everyone a basic income in old age
38640.e: Before the AHV, many old people were poor. Since 1948, they have received a pension and so have something to live on.
38640.m: The AHV protects old people from poverty.

38641.q: Who was not yet allowed to take part in the 1947 AHV vote?
38641.e: Women only got the vote at federal level in 1971. So only men decided on the AHV (old-age insurance).
38641.m: Only men voted in the 1947 AHV vote.

38642.q: Who pays the AHV contribution on a salary?
38642.e: Part of the salary is deducted for the AHV (old-age insurance). The employer adds the same amount.
38642.m: Employees and employers share the AHV contribution.

38643.q: What happened to the first AHV law in the popular vote of 1931?
38643.e: The constitutional mandate for old-age insurance had existed since 1925. The first law for it failed in 1931 with less than 40 per cent yes.
38643.m: The first attempt at an AHV (old-age insurance) failed in 1931.

38644.q: In 1947, around 860,000 people said yes and around 215,000 said no to the AHV. Roughly how many times more yes than no votes was that?
38644.e: 215,000 times 4 makes 860,000. So there were about four times as many yes votes as no votes.
38644.m: In 1947, there were four times more yes than no votes for the AHV.

38645.q: How many years passed between the AHV constitutional article of 1925 and the acceptance of the AHV Act?
38645.e: The AHV Act was accepted in 1947. 1947 minus 1925 makes 22 years.
38645.m: It took more than twenty years from the constitutional mandate to the AHV Act.

38646.q: Which governing party recommended a no to joining the UN in 2002?
38646.e: The SVP and some smaller right-wing parties fought against joining. The FDP, CVP and SP were in favour.
38646.m: On joining the UN, the SVP was on the no side.

38647.q: Where did the Schwarzenbach Initiative of 1970 tend to get support?
38647.e: There was a yes majority mainly in rural cantons such as Uri, Schwyz or Fribourg. The big city cantons rejected it.
38647.m: The Schwarzenbach Initiative found support mainly in rural cantons.

38648.q: What did the Alpine Initiative mainly want to protect?
a: The Alps from too much lorry traffic
Ski resorts from too little snow
38648.e: More and more lorries were driving through the Alps. The initiative wanted to protect nature and people in the Alpine valleys from noise and exhaust fumes.
38648.m: The Alpine Initiative protects the Alps from transit traffic.

38649.q: What did Switzerland vote on in 1970 with the Schwarzenbach Initiative?
a: A limit on the number of foreigners
38649.e: The initiative wanted to cut the share of foreigners sharply. It is one of the best-known votes on immigration.
38649.m: The Schwarzenbach Initiative wanted fewer foreigners in Switzerland.

38650.q: Where does the Schwarzenbach Initiative get its name from?
a: From the politician who launched it
38650.e: Zurich National Councillor James Schwarzenbach launched the initiative “against foreign infiltration”. That is why it bears his name.
38650.m: The Schwarzenbach Initiative is named after the man who started it.

38651.q: What was the position of the big parties on the Schwarzenbach Initiative?
38651.e: Schwarzenbach belonged to a small party. All the big parties, the Federal Council and business fought against his initiative.
38651.m: The big parties rejected the Schwarzenbach Initiative.

38652.q: What would acceptance of the Schwarzenbach Initiative have meant for many foreign workers?
a: They would have had to leave Switzerland
They would automatically have become Swiss
Nothing would have changed for them
38652.e: The initiative wanted to cut the share of foreigners in most cantons to no more than 10 per cent. Around 300,000 people would have had to leave the country.
38652.m: If it had been accepted, many foreigners would have had to leave Switzerland.

38653.q: Why was Geneva to get an exception under the Schwarzenbach Initiative?
a: Because of the many international organisations
Because Geneva is the smallest canton
Because no foreigners lived in Geneva
Because Geneva did not belong to Switzerland then
38653.e: Many international organisations have their headquarters in Geneva. That is why a higher limit was to apply there.
38653.m: Geneva had an exception because of the international organisations.

38654.q: How did the vote on the Schwarzenbach Initiative turn out?
a: Rejected with around 54 per cent no
Accepted with around 51 per cent yes
Rejected with around 80 per cent no
Accepted with around 60 per cent yes
38654.e: Around 46 per cent voted yes and around 54 per cent no. So the initiative failed fairly narrowly.
38654.m: The Schwarzenbach Initiative was narrowly rejected in 1970.

38655.q: Who was allowed to vote on the Schwarzenbach Initiative in 1970?
38655.e: Women only got the vote at federal level from 1971. So in 1970 only men voted, and a great many of them did.
38655.m: In 1970, only men could vote in federal votes.

38656.q: What did the opponents of the Schwarzenbach Initiative warn about?
a: Rents in Bern being too high
38656.e: The opponents feared that many businesses would have to close because there would not be enough workers.
38656.m: The opponents saw the Schwarzenbach Initiative as a danger to the economy.

38657.q: How did the vote on abolishing the Swiss Armed Forces turn out?
a: Accepted, but never put into practice
38657.e: In 1989, a majority of the people and the cantons said no. The army stayed, but was later made smaller.
38657.m: The initiative to abolish the army was rejected in 1989.

38659.q: According to the 1989 initiative, what should Switzerland develop besides abolishing the army?
38659.e: The full title was “for a Switzerland without an army and for a comprehensive peace policy”. Instead of soldiers, Switzerland was to focus on promoting peace.
