39750.m: The Magna Carta comes from England.

39751.q: Which group forced the English king to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215?
39751.e: The powerful nobles, the barons, rebelled against King John. They wanted to limit his power.
39751.m: The barons forced the king to agree to the Magna Carta.

39752.q: In which language was the Magna Carta written?
39752.e: In the Middle Ages, important documents in Europe were usually written in Latin.
39752.m: The Magna Carta was written in Latin.

39753.q: Which principle does the Magna Carta contain?
a: No free man may be imprisoned without a judgement
The king is elected by the people
The church is separate from the state
39753.e: Free men could only be punished after a lawful judgement or according to the law. This idea still shapes the rule of law today.
39753.m: The Magna Carta protected free men from arbitrary imprisonment.

39754.q: Who declared the Magna Carta invalid shortly after 1215?
39754.e: The Pope took King John's side and declared the charter void in August 1215. Later, however, it was issued again.
39754.m: The Pope declared the first Magna Carta invalid.

39755.q: Where can you see an original copy of the 1215 Magna Carta today?
a: In the British Library in London
In the Federal Palace in Bern
39755.e: Two of the four surviving copies are in the British Library in London. The others are in the cathedrals of Lincoln and Salisbury.
39755.m: Copies of the Magna Carta are kept in England today.

39756.q: In which country was the Bill of Rights of 1689 passed?
39756.e: The English Parliament passed the Bill of Rights in 1689 and so strengthened its rights against the king.
39756.m: The Bill of Rights of 1689 comes from England.

39757.q: Which event came directly before the Bill of Rights of 1689?
39757.e: In 1688 the king was overthrown without much bloodshed. This is called the Glorious Revolution.
39757.m: The Bill of Rights followed the Glorious Revolution.

39758.q: What is the Bill of Rights of 1689?
a: A law that strengthened the rights of parliament
39758.e: In it, the English Parliament set out what the king was no longer allowed to do without its consent.
39758.m: The Bill of Rights strengthened parliament against the king.

39759.q: Who gained more power through the Bill of Rights?
39759.e: For example, the king could no longer raise taxes without the consent of parliament. This made parliament stronger.
39759.m: The Bill of Rights gave parliament more power.

39760.q: Under the Bill of Rights, what could the king only do with the consent of parliament?
39760.e: Without parliament, the king could not collect money from the people. This gave parliament a strong means of pressure.
39760.m: After the Bill of Rights, the king needed parliament for taxes.

39761.q: Which right did the Bill of Rights guarantee members of parliament?
39761.e: What was said in parliament could not be prosecuted in any court. This meant members could debate freely.
39761.m: The Bill of Rights gave members of parliament freedom of speech.

39762.q: According to the Bill of Rights, what was the king not allowed to keep in peacetime without parliament?
39762.e: An army in peacetime needed the consent of parliament. The king was not to be able to use an army against his own people.
39762.m: Without parliament, the king could not keep a standing army in peacetime.

39763.q: Which form of state developed in England after the Bill of Rights?
39763.e: The king remained head of state, but parliament gained more and more power. This system still exists in the United Kingdom today.
39763.m: After the Bill of Rights, a parliamentary monarchy developed in England.

39764.q: Who was the main author of the US Declaration of Independence?
39764.e: Jefferson wrote the draft, which a committee including Benjamin Franklin and John Adams revised. He later became the third President of the USA.
39764.m: Thomas Jefferson wrote the US Declaration of Independence.

39765.q: In which city was the US Declaration of Independence adopted?
39765.e: The Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in what is now Independence Hall.
39765.m: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in Philadelphia.

39766.q: From which country did the American colonies declare independence in 1776?
39766.e: The colonies resisted taxes and laws of the British King George III.
39766.m: The USA broke away from Britain in 1776.

39767.q: How many colonies declared their independence together in 1776?
39767.e: The 13 stripes on the US flag are still a reminder of these founding colonies today.
39767.m: Thirteen colonies declared their independence in 1776.

39768.q: Which rights does the US Declaration of Independence name as unalienable?
a: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
39768.e: According to the Declaration, all men are created equal and have these rights from birth.
39768.m: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

39769.q: Which assembly adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776?
39769.e: The Continental Congress was made up of representatives of all the colonies. The Senate only came into being with the constitution of 1787.
39769.m: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.

39770.q: On which day does the USA celebrate its independence?
39770.e: On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. That is why 4 July is the national holiday of the USA.
39770.m: The USA celebrates its independence on 4 July.

39771.q: Who signed the US Declaration of Independence?
39771.e: 56 representatives from all 13 colonies signed the Declaration. The British king was the opponent they wanted to break away from.
39771.m: Representatives of all 13 colonies signed the Declaration of Independence.

39772.q: In which year was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen proclaimed in France?
39772.e: It was written in the first year of the French Revolution, on 26 August 1789.
39772.m: France proclaimed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789.

39773.q: Which assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789?
39773.e: The representatives of the Third Estate had declared themselves the National Assembly and wanted to give France a constitution.
39773.m: The French National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

39775.q: What does the first article of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen say?
a: People are born free and equal in rights
39775.e: The first article says that all people are born free and equal in rights. This was a big break with the privileges of the nobility and the king.
39775.m: According to the 1789 Declaration, all people are free and equal in rights.

39776.q: Which event on 14 July 1789 came before the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen?
39776.e: People in Paris stormed the Bastille prison, a symbol of royal power. Today 14 July is France's national holiday.
39776.m: The storming of the Bastille was on 14 July 1789.

39777.q: Which woman wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen” in 1791?
39777.e: Olympe de Gouges criticised the fact that the 1789 Declaration forgot women. She demanded equal rights for women.
39777.m: In 1791 Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights for women.

39778.q: What is the famous motto of the French Revolution?
a: Un pour tous, tous pour un
39778.e: The words mean liberty, equality, fraternity. Today they are France's official motto.
39778.m: Liberty, equality, fraternity is the motto of France.

39779.q: Which principle does the 1789 Declaration require for every constitution?
39779.e: According to the Declaration, a society without guaranteed rights and without separation of powers has no constitution. So power should be divided among several bodies.
39779.m: The 1789 Declaration requires the separation of powers.

39780.q: What does the English word “suffrage”, from which “suffragette” comes, mean?
39780.e: “Suffrage” means the right to vote. The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote.
39780.m: The word “suffrage” means the right to vote.

39781.q: Who founded the suffragettes' women's organisation in Manchester in 1903?
39781.e: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union together with her daughters.
39781.m: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the suffragettes' organisation.

39782.q: What was the motto of Emmeline Pankhurst's suffragette organisation?
39782.e: The suffragettes wanted to attract attention with actions instead of just asking.
39782.m: The motto of the suffragettes was “Deeds, not words”.

39783.q: How did many suffragettes protest when they were in prison?
39783.e: Many suffragettes refused to eat in prison. The authorities then often fed them by force.
39783.m: Many suffragettes went on hunger strike in prison.

39784.q: How did the suffragettes draw attention to their demand for women's right to vote?
a: With secret letters to their friends
39784.e: The suffragettes demonstrated, disrupted events and even smashed windows. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison ran onto the track at the horse race in Epsom and died of her injuries.
39784.m: The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote with eye-catching actions.

39785.q: Which colours did the suffragettes wear as a sign of recognition?
39785.e: Purple stood for dignity, white for purity and green for hope.
39785.m: The suffragettes wore purple, white and green.

39786.q: In which year did women in Britain get the same right to vote as men?
39786.e: In 1918, at first only women aged 30 and over who met certain conditions could vote. From 1928 the same voting age of 21 applied to women and men.
39786.m: Since 1928 women in Britain have voted on equal terms with men.

39787.q: What were the women's rights campaigners in Britain called who fought for the vote only by peaceful means?
39787.e: The suffragists around Millicent Fawcett relied on petitions and talks instead of attention-grabbing actions.
39787.m: The moderate women's rights campaigners were called suffragists.

39788.q: Which country was the first self-governing country to introduce women's right to vote at national level, in 1893?
39788.e: At that time New Zealand was a British colony with its own government. Women voted for the first time on 28 November 1893.
39788.m: In 1893 New Zealand was the first country to introduce women's right to vote.

39789.q: What were women in New Zealand allowed to do from 1893?
a: Go to school for the first time
Drive a car for the first time
Become a Federal Councillor for the first time
39789.e: Since 1893 women in New Zealand have been able to vote in elections for parliament. This made New Zealand a model for the world.
39789.m: Women in New Zealand have voted since 1893.

39790.q: How did many people in New Zealand show in 1893 that they wanted women's right to vote?
a: With a petition full of signatures
With a popular initiative like in Switzerland
39790.e: Thousands signed a large petition to parliament. The sheets glued together were many metres long.
39790.m: A large petition helped the women in New Zealand.

a: A campaigner for women's right to vote in New Zealand
39791.e: Kate Sheppard collected signatures and won over politicians. Today she even appears on a New Zealand banknote.
39791.m: Kate Sheppard campaigned for women's right to vote in New Zealand.

39792.q: To which country did New Zealand belong as a colony in 1893?
39792.e: New Zealand was a British colony with its own government. That is why it could pass its own electoral law.
39792.m: In 1893 New Zealand was a British colony.

39793.q: What were women in New Zealand not yet allowed to do in 1893?
39793.e: In 1893 women only got the right to vote. They were only allowed to stand as candidates themselves a few years later.
39793.m: Being allowed to vote and being elected are two different rights.

39794.q: Were Māori women also allowed to vote in New Zealand in 1893?
a: Yes, they also got the right to vote
39794.e: The 1893 law applied to women of European origin and to Māori women. The Māori voted in their own constituencies.
39794.m: In New Zealand, Māori women could also vote in 1893.

39795.q: How many years after New Zealand (1893) did Switzerland introduce women's suffrage at federal level in 1971?
39795.e: Calculation: 1971 minus 1893 = 78. Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe.
39795.m: Switzerland introduced women's suffrage 78 years after New Zealand.

39796.q: In which city does the Australian parliament meet?
39796.e: Canberra is the capital of Australia. The Parliament House is there, even though Sydney and Melbourne are bigger.
39796.m: The Australian parliament meets in the capital, Canberra.

a: You have to go and vote
You are not allowed to vote
You may only vote once in your life
You have to stand as a candidate
39797.e: With compulsory voting, everyone entitled to vote has to vote. In Australia, anyone who does not vote without a reason pays a fine.
39797.m: Compulsory voting means you have to go and vote.

39798.q: What happens in Australia if you do not vote without a good reason?
39798.e: Anyone who does not vote has to pay a fine if they cannot give a valid reason.
39798.m: Anyone in Australia who does not vote without a reason pays a fine.

39799.q: Because of compulsory voting, how high is turnout in Australia usually?
39799.e: Usually over 90 per cent of those registered cast their vote. In comparison, turnout in Switzerland is often below 50 per cent.
39799.m: Thanks to compulsory voting, usually over 90 per cent vote in Australia.

39800.q: On which day of the week are national elections in Australia always held?
39800.e: Saturday is a day off work for many people. That makes voting easier.
39800.m: In Australia people always vote on a Saturday.

39801.q: From what age do you have to register on the electoral roll in Australia?
39801.e: Registering is compulsory from 18. At 16 or 17 you can register in advance voluntarily, but you can only vote from 18.
39801.m: In Australia you have to register as a voter from the age of 18.

39802.q: What do voters do on the ballot paper in the election for the Australian House of Representatives?
a: They put a ball into an urn
39802.e: You rank all the candidates in order of preference with numbers. That way your further choices also count if your favourite is knocked out.
39802.m: In Australia you number the candidates in order of preference.

39803.q: What do volunteers in Australia often sell outside polling stations on election day?
39803.e: The so-called “democracy sausage” is a sausage in bread. Schools and clubs use the money raised to support their projects.
39803.m: In Australia, a barbecued sausage outside the polling station is part of election day.

39804.q: Why do people in Australia, as in Switzerland, fill in their ballot paper in secret?
a: So that nobody sees who they vote for
So that the vote is quicker
So that they do not lose the paper
39804.e: The secret ballot with official ballot papers was introduced in Australia in 1856. It protects each person's free decision.
39804.m: The secret ballot protects people's free decision.

39805.q: Why did India's first parliamentary election in 1951/52 take several months?
a: The country was huge and a great many people voted
The votes were recounted every day
The election was banned every week
Only one person could vote per day
39805.e: India is very large and even then had hundreds of millions of inhabitants. That is why voting took place in many stages from October 1951 to February 1952.
39805.m: Because of the size of the country, India's first election took months.

39806.q: From which country did India become independent in 1947, before electing its first parliament in 1951/52?
39806.e: India was a British colony for a long time and became independent in 1947. A few years later the people elected their parliament for the first time.
39806.m: India became independent from Britain in 1947.

39808.q: What was special about India's first parliamentary election in 1951/52?
a: It was the largest election in the world at the time
There was only a single candidate
39808.e: About 173 million people were entitled to vote. No democratic election had ever been so large before.
39808.m: India's first election was the largest democratic election in the world at the time.

39809.q: Who was allowed to vote in India's first parliamentary election?
39809.e: From the start, India gave all adults the same right to vote, whether woman or man, rich or poor. At that time it applied from the age of 21.
39809.m: All adults could vote in India's first election.

39810.q: How were people who could not read helped in India's first election?
a: With readers in the voting booth
With voting by show of hands
39810.e: Each candidate had their own ballot box with their name and a symbol. That way people could vote correctly even without being able to read.
39810.m: Symbols helped people who could not read in India's first election.

39811.q: What was the task of the Election Commission in India's first election?
39811.e: The Election Commission under Sukumar Sen planned the election with hundreds of thousands of polling stations. It made sure that everyone entitled to vote could do so.
39811.m: An election commission organises the elections.

39812.q: How many chambers does the Indian parliament have?
39812.e: The Indian parliament has two chambers. The Lok Sabha, the “House of the People”, is elected by the people. The Rajya Sabha represents the states.
39812.m: Like the Swiss parliament, the Indian parliament has two chambers.

39813.q: What form of state has India had since its constitution of 1950?
39813.e: With the constitution of 26 January 1950, India became a republic. Since then the people have elected their parliament, and there is no king.
39813.m: India has been a republic since 1950.

39814.q: What does the third Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Switzerland has also ratified, allow?
a: Children can complain to the UN
Children no longer have to go to school
39814.e: With the third Optional Protocol, children whose rights have been violated can send a communication to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. Before that, however, they have to use up all legal options in their own country.
39814.m: Thanks to an optional protocol, children can complain to the UN.

39815.q: According to Article 12, what should a child's opinion be taken into account according to?
39815.e: The child's opinion is taken into account appropriately and in line with their age and maturity. The older and more mature a child is, the more weight their opinion has.
39815.m: The more mature a child is, the more their opinion counts.

39816.q: What does the right to have a say under Article 12 NOT mean?
a: The child may give their opinion
39816.e: Having a say means that the child is heard and their opinion goes into the decision. But responsibility for the decision often lies with adults or authorities.
39816.m: Having a say means being heard, but not always deciding alone.

39817.q: According to Article 12, where does a child expressly have the right to be heard?
39817.e: Paragraph 2 of Article 12 requires that a child be heard in court and administrative proceedings that affect them, either directly or through a representative.
39817.m: Children may also give their view in court and before authorities.

39818.q: Under Article 12, does a child always have to give their opinion?
a: No, they may, but they do not have to
Yes, they are legally obliged to
Only if their parents demand it
39818.e: Article 12 gives the child a right, not a duty. So a child can also decide that they do not want to comment on a question.
39818.m: Having a say is a right, not a duty.

39819.q: Who can represent a child's interests in court proceedings in Switzerland?
39819.e: A court can appoint a representative for the child, often a lawyer or a specialist. They bring the child's point of view into the proceedings.
39819.m: A child's representative brings the child's view to court.

39820.q: Which word from Latin describes children and young people having a say?
39820.e: Participation comes from the Latin “participare”, to take part. It means that children are involved in decisions that affect them.

39821.q: Which of the four basic principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child is in Article 12?
39821.e: The Convention has four basic principles: non-discrimination, the best interests of the child, the right to life and development, and participation. Participation is set out in Article 12.
39821.m: Participation is a basic principle of children's rights.

39822.q: Which UN body checks whether states are putting children's rights into practice?
a: The Committee on the Rights of the Child
39822.e: States regularly send reports to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. It examines them and makes recommendations, including to Switzerland.
39822.m: A UN committee checks how children's rights are put into practice.

39824.q: What is a typical aim of a children's parliament?
39824.e: In a children's parliament, children learn to put forward concerns, discuss them and vote. In this way they practise democracy on a small scale.
39824.m: In a children's parliament, children learn how democracy works.

39825.q: What is the body for older young people that is similar to a children's parliament called?
39825.e: Many municipalities and cantons have youth parliaments for young people. They work in a similar way to children's parliaments but often deal with more political topics.
39825.m: Young people can take part in a youth parliament.

39826.q: How are decisions usually made in a children's parliament?
39826.e: As in a real parliament, the children's parliament votes on proposals. Whatever the majority wants is accepted.
39826.m: In a children's parliament, the majority decides.

39827.q: Which concern fits best in a municipality's children's parliament?
39827.e: Children's parliaments deal with topics from the children's everyday life where they live, for example playgrounds, routes to school or leisure activities.
39827.m: Children's parliaments deal with topics from children's everyday lives.

39828.q: What do some children's parliaments in Switzerland get from their municipality so they can carry out their own projects?
39828.e: Some municipalities give their children's parliament a small sum of money. The children then decide themselves which projects to support with it.
39828.m: With their own budget, children can carry out projects themselves.

39829.q: How does a decision of a children's parliament usually reach the adults in politics?
a: As a proposal to the municipal authority
39829.e: The children's parliament can send proposals or wishes to the municipal council or town parliament. These authorities then consider whether to put the idea into practice.
39829.m: Children's parliaments submit their concerns to the municipality.

39830.q: Why is it called a children's parliament?
a: It meets in the Federal Palace
It is elected by the people
39830.e: A parliament is an assembly that discusses and votes. The children's parliament copies this way of working, but it has no power to make laws.
39830.m: A children's parliament works on the model of a parliament.

39831.q: Who usually represents a class on the pupils' council?
39831.e: Each class elects one or two representatives. They bring the class's concerns to the pupils' council and report back afterwards.
39831.m: Class representatives bring their class's wishes to the pupils' council.

39832.q: What is the regular meeting within a single class called, at which concerns are collected?
39832.e: In the class council, pupils discuss problems and ideas in their class. They can then pass important concerns on to the pupils' council.
39832.m: In the class council, a class discusses its concerns.

39833.q: Which topic can a pupils' council typically have a say on?
39833.e: A pupils' council puts forward ideas about school life, such as the playground, project days or rules in the school building. It does not decide on marks or hiring.
39833.m: The pupils' council has a say in everyday school life.

39834.q: What do pupils learn in particular on the pupils' council?
39834.e: On the pupils' council, children and young people practise giving reasons for an opinion, listening and finding compromises. These are important democratic skills.
39834.m: On the pupils' council you practise representing concerns.

39835.q: What records what was discussed and decided on the pupils' council?
39835.e: The minutes record the most important discussions and decisions. That way everyone knows later what was agreed.

39836.q: Who usually supports a pupils' council?
39836.e: Usually a teacher or a school social worker supports the pupils' council. They help with organising it but do not decide in place of the children.
39836.m: An adult supporter helps the pupils' council.

39837.q: Why is a pupils' council an example of representative democracy?
39837.e: In a representative democracy, people elect representatives who decide for them. On the pupils' council, the representatives stand for their whole class.
39837.m: On the pupils' council, elected pupils represent their classmates.

39838.q: What should class representatives do after a meeting of the pupils' council?
39838.e: Representatives are the link between the class and the pupils' council. They tell their class about the decisions and take new concerns with them.
39838.m: Representatives tell their class about the pupils' council.

39839.q: Where does the plenary meeting of the Federal Youth Session take place?
a: In the National Council chamber in Bern
At the UN headquarters in Geneva
At the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
39839.e: The young people discuss in working groups and meet at the end in the National Council chamber of the Federal Palace. There they vote on their demands.
39839.m: The Youth Session meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.

39840.q: What can parliamentary committees do with a petition from the Youth Session?
a: Take up the concern with a parliamentary proposal
Put it straight into force as a law
Hand it to the Federal Supreme Court
39840.e: The committees examine the petition. They can follow up the concern, for example with a motion or a postulate, or propose that no action be taken on it.
39840.m: Committees can take up concerns from the Youth Session.

39841.q: Where are the Youth Session's demands first worked out?
39841.e: The participants work in themed working groups, supported by experts and members of parliament. Only after that do the demands go to the plenary meeting.
39841.m: The demands are worked out in working groups.

39842.q: Who mainly organises the Federal Youth Session?
39842.e: An organising committee of young volunteers aged roughly 16 to 25 plans the event. So the Youth Session is created by young people for young people.
39842.m: Young volunteers organise the Youth Session.

39843.q: What criticism is sometimes made of the Federal Youth Session?
a: That it has little direct influence
That it is too expensive for taxpayers
39843.e: Critics complain that petitions rarely achieve anything directly. Supporters, on the other hand, stress that young people experience politics in practice there.
39843.m: The influence of the Youth Session is debated.

39844.q: In what form are the accepted demands of the Youth Session handed to the federal parliament?
39844.e: The demands go to parliament as petitions. The responsible committees have to deal with them but are not obliged to put them into practice.
39844.m: Demands of the Youth Session are submitted as petitions.

39845.q: Apart from the debates, what else is part of the Youth Session programme?
a: An election campaign for the National Council
39845.e: The supporting programme includes meetings with members of parliament, a games evening and a party. This helps the participants get to know each other.
39845.m: At the Youth Session, young people meet real politicians.

39846.q: How are the topics of the Federal Youth Session chosen?
39846.e: Young people can vote online in advance on which topics will be dealt with. In this way young people help decide the content themselves.
39846.m: The topics of the Youth Session are chosen online.

39847.q: Which group has worked since 2001 to make sure the Youth Session's demands are followed up?
39847.e: About ten young people are involved in the Youth Session Forum. They follow the petitions and keep in contact with members of parliament.
39847.m: The Youth Session Forum follows up the demands.

39848.q: Who started a school strike for the climate in Stockholm in 2018?
39848.e: In August 2018 Greta Thunberg, who was 15 at the time, sat down in front of the Swedish parliament. Her protest inspired young people all over the world, including in Switzerland.
39848.m: Greta Thunberg started the climate strikes in 2018.

39849.q: What does the name of the movement “Fridays for Future” refer to?
39849.e: The young people went on strike on Fridays for more climate protection.
39849.m: Fridays for Future means Fridays for the future.

39850.q: On which day of the week did the school strikes for the climate usually take place?
39850.e: The Fridays for Future movement is named after Friday. On that day pupils stayed away from lessons to demonstrate.
39850.m: The climate strikes usually took place on a Friday.

39851.q: When did the big climate strikes by pupils begin in Switzerland?
39851.e: In December 2018 many young people demonstrated for the climate for the first time in Zurich and other cities. From early 2019 there were regular strikes.
39851.m: The Swiss climate strike movement began at the end of 2018.

39852.q: In which city did the largest climate demonstration in Switzerland, with about 100,000 people, take place in September 2019?
39852.e: On 28 September 2019, according to the organisers, about 100,000 people marched through Bern. It was one of the largest demonstrations in Swiss history.
39852.m: The largest climate demonstration in Switzerland took place in Bern in 2019.

39853.q: By when does Climate Strike Switzerland demand net zero greenhouse gas emissions within the country?
39853.e: The Climate Strike demands net zero by 2030. That is much earlier than the federal government's target of 2050.
39853.m: The Climate Strike demands net zero by 2030.

39854.q: What does the Climate Strike want when it calls for a “climate emergency” to be declared?
a: All cars should be banned immediately
39854.e: With a climate emergency, politicians are meant to recognise that the climate crisis is urgent. Decisions should first be checked for their effects on the climate.
39854.m: A climate emergency is meant to make climate protection a priority.

39855.q: How is the Climate Strike Switzerland movement organised?
a: As a grassroots democracy in local groups
39855.e: The Climate Strike has no party ties and no fixed leadership. Decisions are made in open meetings, and there are regional groups in almost all cantons.
39855.m: The Climate Strike is a grassroots democratic movement.

39856.q: What does easyvote offer young people?
39856.e: Easyvote explains proposals in votes and elections in a way that is easy to understand. It stays politically neutral and gives no voting recommendation.
39856.m: Easyvote explains votes simply and neutrally.

a: The Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments
39857.e: Easyvote is run by the Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments, DSJ for short. It encourages young people to take part in politics.
39857.m: Easyvote belongs to the Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments.

39858.q: What does easyvote NOT give about a vote?
39858.e: Easyvote presents the arguments of both sides but does not say how to vote. The decision stays with the voters.
39858.m: Easyvote does not say how to vote.

39859.q: Why is easyvote mainly meant for young adults?
a: So that more young people go and vote
Because only young people may vote
Because older people do not vote
39859.e: In Switzerland, young adults take part in votes less often than older people. Clear information is meant to make it easier for them to get started.
39859.m: Easyvote wants to get more young people to the ballot box.

39860.q: Which format does easyvote use to explain proposals especially briefly and clearly?
39860.e: Easyvote publishes short explainer clips and infographics about the proposals. They work well on social media and in lessons.
39860.m: Short explainer clips make votes easy to understand.

39861.q: What does the term turnout mean?
a: The share of eligible voters who vote
The number of proposals being voted on
39861.e: Turnout shows what percentage of eligible voters actually voted. Among young people it is often lower than among older people.
39861.m: Turnout shows how many eligible voters take part.

39862.q: In which special form does easyvote also explain votes so that everyone understands them?
39862.e: Easyvote offers texts in Easy Read language. They use short sentences and simple words so that people with reading difficulties can have a say too.
39862.m: Easy Read language makes voting information understandable for everyone.

39863.q: What is easyvote's app called that reminds you about votes?
39863.e: With the votenow app you get information about upcoming votes and elections. That way you never miss a voting date.
39863.m: The votenow app reminds you about votes.

39864.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution allows people to gather peacefully for a demonstration?
39864.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of assembly as a fundamental right. Everyone may take part in or organise peaceful gatherings.
39864.m: Freedom of assembly protects peaceful demonstrations.

39866.q: In Switzerland, where do you usually have to apply for a permit for a demonstration on the street?
39866.e: Anyone using public spaces such as streets and squares for a rally usually needs a permit from the municipality or town. The police or a town office is often responsible.
39866.m: A demonstration on public land is usually approved by the municipality.

39867.q: Why does a demonstration on public streets usually need a permit?
a: Because public space is used in a special way
Because the federal government checks every opinion
39867.e: A demonstration uses streets and squares more than usual. The authority has to balance traffic, safety and other interests, but it does not check the demonstrators' opinions.
39867.m: The permit regulates the use of streets and squares.

39868.q: Which detail typically belongs in an application for a demonstration?
39868.e: The application includes the date, time, route or place, expected number of participants and a responsible person. This lets the authority plan.
39868.m: A demonstration application gives the time, place and route.

39869.q: What can happen if a demonstration is held without the necessary permit?
a: The police can break it up
39869.e: At unauthorised rallies the police can step in and break up the demonstration. Depending on the canton, those responsible may be fined.
39869.m: An unauthorised demonstration can be broken up.

39870.q: What is a rally called that comes about without preparation as a direct reaction to a current event?
39870.e: A spontaneous rally comes about at short notice, for example after a surprising event. Special rules often apply because there is no time for an application.
39870.m: A spontaneous rally comes about at short notice after an event.

39871.q: What condition must a gathering meet to be protected by freedom of assembly?
a: It must come from a party
It must take place on a Sunday
39871.e: Peaceful gatherings are protected. Anyone who uses violence or damages property cannot rely on this fundamental right.

39872.q: Which other fundamental right is closely linked to demonstrating, because you make your view known?
39872.e: Anyone who demonstrates expresses an opinion in public. That is why, besides freedom of assembly, freedom of expression under Article 16 of the Federal Constitution also protects this activity.
39872.m: Demonstrating is a way of expressing an opinion.

39873.q: May a child in Switzerland submit a petition?
39873.e: Article 33 of the Federal Constitution gives everyone the right of petition, regardless of age or nationality.
39873.m: Anyone may submit a petition, including children.

39874.q: What is a petition that is signed on the internet called?
39874.e: Many petitions are collected on internet platforms today. It is important that the petition is submitted to the right authority at the end.
39874.m: An online petition collects signatures on the internet.

39875.q: Which details go with each signature on a petition sheet?
39875.e: Signers write down their name and address and sign. This shows that real people support the concern.
39875.m: A petition sheet has name, address and signature.

39876.q: Which federal authorities can you send a petition to at federal level?
a: The Federal Assembly or the Federal Council
39876.e: At federal level, petitions usually go to the Federal Assembly, which is parliament, or to the Federal Council. In parliament the responsible committees examine the concerns.
39876.m: At federal level, petitions go to parliament or the Federal Council.

39877.q: Why can a petition achieve something even though it is not binding?
39877.e: A petition shows the authorities and the public that a topic matters to many people. Politicians then often take up such concerns.

39878.q: What should definitely be in a petition?
a: As many foreign words as possible
39878.e: A good petition says briefly and clearly what is being asked for and why. It also includes who it is addressed to, who sends it and the signatures.
39878.m: A petition needs a clear request and reasons.

39879.q: Who do you send a petition to if you want a new zebra crossing outside the school?
39879.e: The municipal authority is usually responsible for roads and routes to school in a municipality. A petition should always go to the authority that can solve the problem.
39879.m: A petition goes to the authority that is responsible.

39880.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what must NOT happen to a person because of a petition?
a: They must not suffer any disadvantage
They must not receive an answer
They must not keep a copy
39880.e: Article 33 states expressly that nobody may suffer any disadvantage from a petition. So you can raise concerns without fear of punishment.
39880.m: Nobody may be punished because of a petition.

39881.q: Where does the word petition come from?
a: From the Latin word for asking
From the Greek word for city
From the French word for paper
From the English word for pet
39881.e: Petition comes from the Latin “petere”, which means to ask or to request. So a petition is a written request to an authority.
39881.m: A petition is a written request.

39882.q: What does an ombudsman's office basically do?
a: It mediates neutrally when there are problems
39882.e: An ombudsman's office is an independent point of contact. It listens, gives advice and mediates between the people affected and authorities or institutions.
39882.m: An ombudsman's office mediates independently when there are problems.

39883.q: How much does advice from the Swiss Children's Rights Ombuds Office cost for children?
a: A month of the parents' wages
39883.e: Advice is free for children and young people. That way everyone can get help, even without money.
39883.m: The Children's Rights Ombuds Office advises children for free.

39884.q: Who is the Swiss Children's Rights Ombuds Office mainly for?
39884.e: The Ombuds Office mainly advises children and young people who feel that their rights are not being respected. It explains everything in a child-friendly way.
39884.m: The Children's Rights Ombuds Office mainly helps children and young people.

39885.q: In which situations does the Swiss Children's Rights Ombuds Office typically help?
39885.e: The office gives children legal advice and mediates in complex proceedings, for example in divorces, placements away from home or decisions of the child protection authority.
39885.m: The Ombuds Office helps children in difficult proceedings.

39886.q: What does it mean that the Ombuds Office is easy to access?
39886.e: Easy to access means there are hardly any hurdles. Children can get in touch without complicated forms or a lawyer.
39886.m: Easy-access services are easy to reach.

39887.q: Which country does the word ombudsman originally come from?
39887.e: The word ombudsman comes from Swedish and means something like agent or representative. This office has existed in Sweden since the 19th century.
39887.m: The word ombudsman comes from Swedish.

39888.q: Which children's right does the Ombuds Office especially support when it helps children be heard by authorities?
39888.e: Children should be heard in proceedings that affect them. The Ombuds Office helps them put their point of view across clearly.
39888.m: Children have a right to be heard.

39889.q: What does it mean that an ombudsman's office is independent?
a: It is not bound to any side
39889.e: Independent means that the ombudsman's office does not work for an authority or a party. Only then can it mediate fairly.
39889.m: An independent office does not take sides.

39890.q: What can a municipality do to become more child-friendly?
39890.e: Child-friendly municipalities provide, for example, safe routes to school, good playgrounds and a say for children. Such measures are in the action plan.
39890.m: Safe routes to school make a municipality more child-friendly.

39891.q: Who can apply for the “Child-Friendly Municipality” label?
39891.e: The label is aimed at municipalities. With it they show that they make a special effort for children and young people.
39891.m: Municipalities can apply for the label.

39892.q: What can a municipality do when its “Child-Friendly Municipality” label expires?
39892.e: The label is limited in time. If the municipality wants to keep it, it has to show in a recertification that it is still working on its measures.
39892.m: An expired label can be renewed.

39893.q: How does a municipality begin the process towards the “Child-Friendly Municipality” label?
a: With an assessment of the current situation
39893.e: First it is analysed how child-friendly the municipality already is, for example in education, health, child protection and planning. Then measures are planned.
39893.m: It starts with an assessment of the current situation.

39894.q: What is the document called in which a municipality sets goals and measures for being more child-friendly?
39894.e: The action plan says what the municipality wants to improve for children in the next few years. It is a requirement for the label.
39894.m: In the action plan, the municipality sets out its measures.

39895.q: On the way to becoming a “Child-Friendly Municipality”, who is expressly asked for their opinion?
a: The municipality's children and young people
39895.e: The views and needs of children and young people are gathered, for example in workshops. In this way the municipality puts the right to have a say into practice.
39895.m: Children have a say in the child-friendly municipality.

39896.q: Roughly how many municipalities in Switzerland held the “Child-Friendly Municipality” label in 2025?
39896.e: According to UNICEF, about 80 municipalities were certified (as of 2025). Switzerland has over 2,000 municipalities in total.
39896.m: About 80 Swiss municipalities are recognised as child-friendly.

39897.q: Who decides in the end whether a municipality receives the “Child-Friendly Municipality” label?
39897.e: After an external review, an expert committee decides whether to award the label. This keeps the assessment independent.
39897.m: An expert committee awards the label.

39898.q: What is voluntary work done in a club or an organisation called?
39898.e: Voluntary work in clubs and organisations is called formal. Helping neighbours or friends outside an organisation is called informal.
39898.m: Voluntary work in a club is called formal.

39899.q: What is honoured on International Volunteer Day?
39899.e: The UN created a special day for volunteering. On this day people thank everyone who works voluntarily for others.
39899.m: An international day honours voluntary work.

39900.q: What does doing something “in an honorary capacity” mean?
39900.e: Anyone with an honorary post voluntarily takes on a task, usually in a club, and gets no wages for it. At most, expenses are sometimes paid.

39901.q: According to the Civil Code, which body is the highest body of an association?
39901.e: According to Article 64 of the Civil Code, the general meeting is the highest body. There the members decide together, for example on the statutes and elections.
39901.m: In an association, the members have the final say at the general meeting.

39902.q: What is needed for an association to be founded in Switzerland?
a: A permit from the federal government
39902.e: An association comes into being as soon as written statutes show that it wants to exist as a body. An entry in the commercial register is usually not needed.

39903.q: Who checks the annual accounts in an association?
39903.e: Auditors check whether the money was handled correctly. They report on this at the general meeting.

39904.q: Which document in Switzerland confirms voluntary work, for example for a job application?
39904.e: The social time record lists voluntary work and the skills gained. It can be added to a job application.
39904.m: The social time record confirms voluntary work.

39905.q: For which age group does the federal Youth+Sport programme support sports activities, which are often led by volunteers?
39905.e: Youth+Sport supports sports courses and camps for children and young people aged 5 to 20. Many leaders do this voluntarily in clubs.
39905.m: Youth+Sport supports sport for children and young people.

39906.q: What is the typical task of a youth committee in a municipality?
a: It advises the authority on youth matters
39906.e: A youth committee discusses topics that affect children and young people and makes proposals to the municipal council. It can suggest youth clubs or events, for example.
39906.m: The youth committee advises the municipality on youth matters.

39907.q: What is the committee called that advises the Federal Council on matters concerning children and young people?
a: Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs
39907.e: The Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs, EKKJ for short, observes the situation of young people in Switzerland and makes recommendations to the Federal Council.
39907.m: The EKKJ advises the federal government on child and youth affairs.

39908.q: What is the work with young people in youth clubs outside school called, which youth committees often support?
39908.e: Open youth work offers voluntary meeting places and projects for young people in their free time. Many municipalities fund it and are advised on it by a youth committee.
39908.m: Open youth work offers young people voluntary leisure activities.

39909.q: Who elects the members of the Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs?
a: The people at the ballot box
39909.e: The EKKJ is an extra-parliamentary commission. Its members are elected by the Federal Council.
39909.m: The Federal Council elects the members of the EKKJ.

a: An expert body that advises the government
A committee made up only of members of parliament
39910.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions are made up of experts and representatives of society. They advise the Federal Council and the administration with their knowledge.
39910.m: Extra-parliamentary commissions advise the government with expert knowledge.

39911.q: Which federal law of 2011 regulates support for out-of-school work with children and young people?
a: The Child and Youth Promotion Act
39911.e: The Child and Youth Promotion Act, KJFG for short, was passed in 2011 and came into force in 2013. Among other things, it supports youth organisations and participation projects.
39911.m: The Child and Youth Promotion Act supports youth work.

39912.q: What is seen as an important feature of a good youth committee in a municipality?
39912.e: A youth committee is more credible if young people also take part. That way their experience goes directly into the proposals.
39912.m: Young people should have a say in the youth committee.

39913.q: What can a municipal youth committee propose to the municipal authority?
39913.e: Youth committees make suggestions about activities for young people, for example youth clubs, skate parks or events. The responsible authority then has to decide.
39913.m: Youth committees suggest activities for young people.

39914.q: Which federal department is responsible for finance?
a: The Department of Home Affairs FDHA
39914.e: The Federal Department of Finance (FDF) is responsible for federal finances. Its Finance Administration prepares the budget and the accounts.
39914.m: The Federal Department of Finance is responsible for federal finances.

39915.q: Who approves the federal government's annual budget?
a: The people at the ballot box
39915.e: The Federal Council presents a draft, but the budget is approved by the National Council and the Council of States. There is no popular vote on the budget.
39915.m: The federal budget is approved by parliament.

39916.q: In which session does parliament debate the budget for the following year?
39916.e: The budget is dealt with in the winter session in December so that it applies from 1 January.
39916.m: The federal budget for the next year is approved in the winter session.

39917.q: Which area does the federal government spend the most money on?
39917.e: About a third of federal spending goes to social welfare, mainly as contributions to social insurance. After that come areas such as finance, transport, and education and research.
39917.m: Most federal spending goes to social welfare.

39918.q: What is the report called that shows the federal government's actual income and spending after the end of a year?
39918.e: The budget is the plan made in advance. The federal accounts then show how much was really taken in and spent.
39918.m: The federal accounts show how much money the federal government really spent.

39919.q: Roughly how much money does the federal government spend per year (as of 2024)?
39919.e: For some years federal spending has been over 80 billion francs a year. The cantons and municipalities also have their own budgets.
39919.m: The federal government spends about 85 billion francs every year.

39920.q: Where does by far the largest part of the federal government's income come from?
39920.e: About nine tenths of federal income is taxes and levies, such as VAT and direct federal tax. There is also smaller income such as fees or income from shareholdings.
39920.m: The federal government is funded mainly by taxes.

39921.q: Which tax do you pay when shopping in a shop, which brings the federal government a lot of money?
39921.e: VAT is included in the price of most goods and services. It is one of the federal government's most important sources of income.
39921.m: VAT is included in the price and is an important source of federal income.

39922.e: VAT is included in the price of many goods and services. Companies pass it on to the federal government.
39922.m: VAT is included in the price of goods and services.

39923.q: Which authority charges VAT on goods brought into Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security
The Federal Office of Public Health
39923.e: When goods are imported, VAT is charged at the border so that imported goods are taxed the same as goods from within the country.
39923.m: Customs charges VAT on imported goods.

39924.q: What is the standard VAT rate in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
39924.e: The standard rate is 8.1 per cent. A lower rate applies to food, and a special rate to hotel stays.
39924.m: The standard VAT rate is 8.1 per cent.

39925.q: Where can you see after shopping how much VAT you have paid?
39925.e: The receipt shows how much VAT is included in the price. So the tax is already in the price.
39925.m: The VAT is shown on the receipt.

39926.q: How much VAT do you pay on bread compared with a bike?
a: Less, food has a lower rate
More, food has a higher rate
39926.e: A reduced rate of 2.6 per cent applies to food. On a bike you pay the standard rate of 8.1 per cent.
39926.m: Food has a lower VAT rate.

39927.q: What was VAT raised for from 2024?
39927.e: With the AHV 21 reform, the people and the cantons accepted a VAT increase in 2022. The extra money goes into old-age provision.
39927.m: Part of VAT helps to fund the AHV.

39928.q: Do very small companies also have to account for VAT?
a: No, only above a certain annual turnover
Yes, all of them without exception
39928.e: Anyone with a turnover of less than 100,000 francs a year is exempt from the tax obligation. But small businesses can choose to register voluntarily.
39928.m: Very small companies do not have to account for VAT.

39929.q: Which authority collects VAT within the country?
a: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs
39929.e: The Federal Tax Administration (FTA) is responsible for VAT within the country. It also checks companies' VAT returns.
39929.m: The Federal Tax Administration deals with VAT.

39930.q: Who actually bears the cost of VAT in the end?
39930.e: Companies pass the tax on to the federal government but add it to the price. So it is paid by everyone who buys something.
39930.m: VAT is paid by whoever buys something.

39931.q: What does the federal government charge direct federal tax on for private individuals?
39931.e: Private individuals pay direct federal tax on their income, companies on their profit.
39931.m: Direct federal tax is calculated on income.

39932.q: Apart from private individuals, who also pays direct federal tax?
39932.e: Private individuals pay direct federal tax on their income, companies on their profit.
39932.m: Companies also pay direct federal tax.

39933.q: Who collects direct federal tax from people on behalf of the federal government?
39933.e: The cantons calculate and collect direct federal tax. They may keep part of it and give the rest to the federal government.
39933.m: The cantons collect direct federal tax for the federal government.

39934.q: During which event did the federal government first charge a direct tax, the war tax?
39934.e: To cover the high costs of guarding the borders in the First World War, the federal government charged a war tax from 1916. Before that, only the cantons and municipalities had direct taxes.
39934.m: The federal government's first direct tax came about in the First World War.

39935.q: Who pays the most direct federal tax?
a: People with a very high income
39935.e: The higher your income, the more tax you have to pay. People who earn very little often pay no direct federal tax at all.
39935.m: People who earn more pay more direct federal tax.

39936.q: What do companies pay direct federal tax on?
a: On the number of their windows
39936.e: Companies pay direct federal tax on their profit, which is what is left after costs have been taken away.
39936.m: Companies pay direct federal tax on their profit.

39937.q: Direct federal tax is limited in time. Who has to agree for it to be extended?
a: The people and the cantons in a vote
39937.e: Direct federal tax is in the Federal Constitution for a limited time. An extension needs a constitutional change, which means a yes from the people and the cantons.
39937.m: The people and the cantons vote on extending direct federal tax.

39938.q: What does it mean that direct federal tax is progressive?
a: Higher incomes pay a higher percentage
Everyone pays the same number of francs
Lower incomes pay a higher percentage
39938.e: With a progressive tax, the tax rate rises with income. People who earn little pay little or no direct federal tax.
39938.m: With a progressive tax, the tax rate rises with income.

39939.q: Who voted in 2001 on introducing the debt brake?
39939.e: The debt brake is in the Federal Constitution. That is why the people and the cantons had to agree, and in 2001 they did so by a large majority.
39939.m: The people and the cantons decided on the debt brake.

39940.q: Why was the debt brake introduced?
a: The federal government had too much money left over
The cantons did not want any more taxes
39940.e: In the 1990s federal debt rose sharply. The debt brake was meant to stop this trend.
39940.m: The debt brake is meant to stop federal debt growing and growing.

39941.q: What does the debt brake require of the federal government?
a: Not to spend more than it takes in over an economic cycle
To pay off all debts within a year
Never to spend money on roads again
39941.e: Over several years, spending must not be higher than income. That way debt does not keep growing.
39941.m: The debt brake is meant to stop the federal government permanently spending more than it takes in.

39942.q: What does the debt brake allow in an economic crisis with falling income?
39942.e: The debt brake takes the economic situation into account. In bad times the federal government may spend a little more than it takes in.
39942.m: In a recession, the debt brake allows a small deficit.

39943.q: What does the debt brake require when the economy is doing very well?
39943.e: In good years the federal government has to spend less than it takes in. The surpluses balance out the deficits of the bad years.
39943.m: In good years the debt brake means the federal government must make a surplus.

39944.q: What does the federal government have to do if it has spent more than allowed in a year?
39944.e: Spending that is too high is recorded. The federal government has to balance it out again by saving in the following years.
39944.m: The federal government has to save later what it overspent.

39945.q: In a severe crisis, who decides on spending above the limit of the debt brake?
39945.e: In severe crises, parliament can decide on extraordinary spending. This needs an especially large majority in both chambers.
39945.m: Parliament decides on exceptions to the debt brake.

39946.q: During which event from 2020 did the federal government spend billions as extraordinary spending outside the normal spending limit?
39946.e: During the pandemic the federal government spent a great deal of money on help such as short-time work and loans to companies. This spending was booked as extraordinary.
39946.m: In the coronavirus pandemic the federal government used the debt brake's exception rule.

39947.q: How many pillars does the Swiss old-age provision system have?
39947.e: The first pillar is the AHV, the second the pension fund and the third private saving. Together they secure money in old age.
39947.m: Swiss old-age provision rests on three pillars.

39948.q: What happens to the money in your pension fund when you change jobs?
a: It goes to the pension fund of the new job
It is paid out to the employer
39948.e: Thanks to vested benefits rules, you take your pension fund savings with you when you change jobs. Without a new job, it goes into a vested benefits account.
39948.m: When you change jobs, you take your pension fund money with you.

39949.q: What is the second pillar of old-age provision?
a: Occupational pension provision with the pension fund
39949.e: The second pillar is occupational pension provision. Employees and employers pay into a pension fund together.
39949.m: The pension fund is the second pillar.

39950.q: What is the third pillar of old-age provision?
39950.e: The third pillar is voluntary saving for old age. There is the restricted pillar 3a and the flexible pillar 3b.
39950.m: The third pillar is private saving for old age.

39951.q: What is the aim of the first pillar of old-age provision?
39951.e: The first pillar is meant to give everyone the bare necessities for living in old age. On its own it is usually not enough for the standard of living people are used to.
39951.m: The first pillar is meant to cover the minimum needed to live in old age.

39952.q: What is the aim of the second pillar together with the first?
a: To continue the usual standard of living
To pay for the children's studies
39952.e: According to the constitution, the first and second pillars together should make it possible to continue one's usual standard of living in an appropriate way.
39952.m: Together, the first and second pillars are meant to secure the usual standard of living in old age.

39953.q: Who pays into an employee's pension fund?
39953.e: Employees and employers pay into occupational pension provision together. The employer has to pay at least half.
39953.m: Employees and employers pay into the pension fund together.

39954.q: What is the advantage of paying into pillar 3a?
a: You can deduct it from your taxable income
You get it back twice over
You can take it out freely at any time
You no longer have to pay AHV
39954.e: Payments into restricted pension provision 3a are tax-deductible up to a maximum amount each year. In return, the money is tied up until shortly before retirement.

39955.q: Where does the money for the pension from the pension fund come from?
a: From your own money that you have saved
39955.e: In the pension fund, each insured person builds up their own savings during their working life. Their pension is paid from this later.
39955.m: In the pension fund you save your own money for old age.

39956.q: Why does the AHV keep money aside, a so-called reserve?
a: To balance out years with less income
39956.e: Sometimes less money comes in from contributions than is paid out in pensions. Then the reserve helps so that the pensions can still be paid.
39956.m: The AHV's reserves balance out ups and downs.

39957.q: Which benefit do pensioners receive if their pension and income are not enough to live on?
39957.e: Supplementary benefits to the AHV and IV cover minimum needs if pensions and income are not enough. People have a legal right to them.
39957.m: Supplementary benefits help if the AHV pension is not enough to live on.

39958.q: Do all pensioners get the same amount of AHV?
a: No, but the highest full pension is only twice the lowest
Yes, everyone gets exactly the same
No, rich people get ten times more
No, only age decides the amount
39958.e: The pension depends on the years of contributions and on income. But the maximum full pension is only twice as high as the minimum.
39958.m: The maximum AHV pension is twice as high as the minimum.

39959.q: How is the AHV mainly funded?
a: People in work pay the pensions of today's retired people
Each person saves into their own account
The pensions come from lottery winnings
39959.e: The AHV works on a pay-as-you-go system. Today's contributions are used straight away for today's pensions.
39959.m: In the AHV, younger people's contributions pay for older people's pensions.

39960.q: The AHV contribution is 8.7 per cent of wages, and the employer pays half. What share do employees pay themselves?
39960.e: Half of 8.7 per cent is 4.35 per cent. The employer pays the same share.
39960.m: Employees and employers each pay half of the AHV contribution.

39961.q: How many years of contributions without gaps are needed for a full AHV pension?
39961.e: Anyone who pays contributions without a gap from the age of 21 to the reference age of 65 reaches 44 years of contributions. Missing years lead to a reduced pension.
39961.m: A full AHV pension needs 44 years of contributions without gaps.

39962.q: Where are AHV contributions settled and pensions paid out?
39962.e: The AHV is run by cantonal compensation offices and by compensation offices of trade associations. They collect the contributions and pay out the pensions.
39962.m: The compensation offices are responsible for the AHV.

39963.q: What happens to the AHV pension if you put off drawing it for a few years?
a: The pension always stays the same
39963.e: Anyone who puts off drawing their old-age pension for one to five years then receives a higher pension with a supplement for the rest of their life.
39963.m: If you draw your AHV pension later, you get a higher pension.

39964.q: From when do apprentices and other people in work pay AHV contributions on their wages?
a: From the year after their 17th birthday
From the year after their 14th birthday
From the year after their 20th birthday
From the year after their 25th birthday
39964.e: People in work pay AHV contributions from 1 January after their 17th birthday. People who do not work pay from the age of 20.
39964.m: If you work, you pay AHV contributions from the year after your 17th birthday.

39965.q: What does the abbreviation IV stand for?
39965.e: IV is short for invalidity insurance (Invalidenversicherung). It supports people who cannot work, or can only partly work, because of an illness, an accident or a disability.

39966.q: Which principle applies to the IV?
39966.e: The IV first tries to bring the people affected back into the world of work with measures. Only if that does not work is there a pension.
39966.m: With the IV, returning to work comes before a pension.

39967.q: Who pays the IV contributions that are deducted from wages?
39967.e: IV contributions are deducted from wages. Employers add the same amount as the employees pay.
39967.m: Employees and employers pay IV contributions together.

a: People who can no longer fully work because of illness or an accident
39968.e: The IV helps people who can no longer fully work because of an illness, an accident or a disability. Pensioners get money from the AHV, unemployed people from unemployment insurance.
39968.m: The IV helps people who cannot fully work because of illness or an accident.

39969.q: Which other social insurance is the IV often mentioned together with?
39969.e: The AHV and IV belong to the first pillar of old-age provision. People often write AHV/IV, and the contributions are deducted from wages together.
39969.m: The AHV and IV belong together to the first pillar.

39970.q: Who checks in each canton whether someone receives IV benefits?
39970.e: The IV is a federal law, but it is carried out by the cantons. Each canton has an IV office for this.
39970.m: Each canton has an IV office that examines applications.

39971.q: What can the IV pay for a child with a disability, for example?
a: An aid such as a wheelchair
39971.e: The IV pays for aids such as wheelchairs or hearing aids and also for therapies. This helps children with disabilities live as independently as possible.
39971.m: The IV pays for aids such as wheelchairs.

39972.q: What does someone who can only partly work because of an illness often receive from the IV?
39972.e: Anyone who can still partly work earns part of their wages themselves. The IV then pays part of a pension, a so-called partial pension.
39972.m: Anyone who can work partly receives a partial pension.

39973.q: What is the voluntary insurance called that pays, for example, for a private room in hospital?
39973.e: Basic insurance pays for the general ward in hospital. For things like a private room you need voluntary supplementary insurance, which an insurer may also refuse.
39973.m: Only supplementary insurance pays for a private room in hospital.

39974.q: What is the law called that regulates compulsory health insurance?
39974.e: The Federal Act on Health Insurance, KVG for short, regulates basic insurance. It came into force in 1996.
39974.m: Basic insurance is regulated in the KVG.

39975.q: What is the lowest deductible for adults in basic insurance?
39975.e: Every year adults pay at least the first 300 francs of their medical costs themselves. Children have no minimum deductible.
39975.m: The lowest deductible for adults is 300 francs.

39976.q: What happens to the premium if you choose a high deductible?
39976.e: With a high deductible you pay more of your medical costs yourself. In return the monthly premium becomes lower.
39976.m: With a high deductible, the premium falls but the risk rises.

39977.q: What percentage of the costs above the deductible do you usually pay as your own share?
39977.e: After the deductible, the insured person usually pays 10 per cent of the further costs themselves. The health insurer pays the rest.
39977.m: Your own share is usually 10 per cent of the costs.

39978.q: Who in Switzerland must have basic insurance with a health insurer?
39978.e: Basic insurance is compulsory. Everyone living in Switzerland, including children and babies, must be insured.
39978.m: In Switzerland everyone must have basic insurance.

39979.q: What does the basic insurance premium NOT depend on?
39979.e: The premium is a per-person premium that is the same for everyone, however much they earn. But it differs by region, age group, deductible and health insurer.
39979.m: The health insurance premium does not depend on income.

39980.q: May a health insurer refuse someone for basic insurance?
a: No, it must accept all residents
Yes, if the person is ill
Yes, if the person is over 50
39980.e: Basic insurance has an obligation to accept. Every health insurer must accept everyone living in Switzerland, regardless of age or health.
39980.m: Every health insurer must accept everyone for basic insurance.

39981.q: Which federal office approves basic insurance premiums?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
39981.e: Every year the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) checks and approves the health insurers' premiums for basic insurance.
39981.m: Basic insurance premiums are approved by the FOPH.

39982.q: Who receives a premium reduction for health insurance?
39982.e: People who earn little receive a contribution towards their health insurance premium. This is meant to keep premiums affordable for everyone.
39982.m: Premium reductions help people with a small income.

a: The federal government and the cantons
39983.e: The federal government pays the cantons a contribution, and the cantons add money of their own. Together they spend several billion francs on this every year.
39983.m: The federal government and the cantons pay for premium reductions together.

a: Because health insurance premiums are too expensive for some people
Because health insurers have too much money
39984.e: Everyone must have health insurance and pay a premium every month. For people with a small income that is a lot of money, so the federal government and the cantons help.
39984.m: Premium reductions help when the premium is too expensive.

39985.q: For whom is the premium reduction especially large?
a: For children from families with a small income
For members of the Federal Council
39985.e: The cantons must greatly reduce the premiums of children from families with low and middle incomes, by at least 80 per cent.
39985.m: Children's premiums are greatly reduced for low and middle incomes.

39986.q: What is a health insurance premium?
a: The amount you pay regularly to the health insurer
39986.e: You usually pay the premium to the health insurer every month. In return, the insurer covers part of the costs if you become ill.
39986.m: You pay the premium regularly to the health insurer.

39987.q: Where is the premium reduction usually paid?
a: In cash at the municipal counter
39987.e: The cantons pay the money directly to the health insurer. The insurer then charges the insured person a lower premium.
39987.m: The premium reduction goes directly to the health insurer.

39988.q: Who decides exactly who is entitled to a premium reduction?
39988.e: The cantons set the income limits and the procedure. That is why the rules differ from canton to canton.
39988.m: Each canton has its own rules for premium reductions.

39989.q: How did voters decide on the premium relief initiative on 9 June 2024?
39989.e: The initiative wanted to limit premiums to at most 10 per cent of income. It was rejected with about 55 per cent voting no. However, an indirect counter-proposal requires the cantons to spend more money on premium reductions.
39989.m: The premium relief initiative was rejected in 2024.

a: It pays money if you lose your job
It pays pensions in old age
39990.e: Anyone who loses their job receives money from unemployment insurance for a certain time. That way they can look for a new job calmly.
39990.m: Unemployment insurance helps if you lose your job.

39995.q: What does the abbreviation RAV stand for?
39995.e: The RAV (Regionales Arbeitsvermittlungszentrum) advise jobseekers, find jobs for them and check their efforts in looking for work.
39995.m: Unemployed people register with the regional employment centre.

39996.q: Which unemployment insurance benefit helped many companies avoid redundancies during the coronavirus pandemic?
39996.e: With short-time work, employees temporarily work less, and unemployment insurance covers part of the lost wages. That way companies can keep their staff.
39996.m: Short-time work compensation protects jobs in a crisis.

39997.q: A company goes bust and can no longer pay wages. Who helps the employees?
39997.e: If an employer goes bankrupt, unemployment insurance pays the outstanding wages for work already done, for a limited period.
39997.m: If an employer goes bankrupt, unemployment insurance helps.

39998.q: What can happen if a person on social assistance breaks their obligations through their own fault?
a: Their basic allowance can be cut
They have to move to another canton
They lose the right to vote
39998.e: Anyone who, for example, does not take part in integration measures can expect cuts. The basic allowance can be cut by up to 30 per cent.
39998.m: Anyone who breaks their obligations on social assistance can receive less money.

39999.q: Does a person on social assistance still have to have health insurance?
a: No, they are exempt from the obligation
39999.e: In Switzerland everyone must have health insurance. For people on social assistance, the premiums and costs such as the deductible and own share are covered.
39999.m: People on social assistance also have health insurance.

40000.q: Which group in Switzerland especially often depends on social assistance?
a: Pensioners with a full AHV pension
40000.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, children and single parents have a particularly high risk of needing social assistance. One reason is that only one wage is available.
40000.m: Single-parent families especially often need social assistance.

40001.q: What does the principle of subsidiarity mean in social assistance?
a: Help is only given if you cannot help yourself
Everyone gets the same amount of money
Help is only given in winter
40001.e: First your own means, wages and other insurance must be used. Social assistance is the last safety net of social security.
40001.m: Social assistance only steps in when all other help is not enough.

40002.q: What is the basic allowance in social assistance meant for?
40002.e: The basic allowance covers daily spending such as food, clothing, personal care and transport. Rent is calculated separately.
40002.m: The basic allowance covers everyday living costs.

40003.q: How does social assistance deal with housing costs?
a: Any rent is paid in full
Only owned homes are paid for
40003.e: Social assistance pays the rent for a reasonable flat. If the flat is too expensive, a move can be required.
40003.m: Social assistance covers the costs of a reasonable flat.

40004.q: Roughly how many people in Switzerland receive social assistance?
a: About 3 per cent of the population
About 15 per cent of the population
About 30 per cent of the population
40004.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, the social assistance rate has been about 3 per cent for years. The share varies greatly from canton to canton.
40004.m: About three in a hundred people in Switzerland receive social assistance.

40005.q: What can be required if someone comes into a lot of money after receiving social assistance, for example through an inheritance?
a: Nothing, the help is a gift
40005.e: Depending on cantonal law, social assistance that was received lawfully has to be paid back if a person's financial situation improves greatly.
40005.m: Social assistance may have to be paid back in certain cases.

40006.q: What is meant by public service (service public) in Switzerland?
a: Basic provision of important services for all regions
40006.e: Public service includes, for example, the post, public transport, radio and television, and electricity and water. They should be available everywhere in good quality at fair prices.
40006.m: Public service ensures good basic provision throughout the country.

40007.q: Who was responsible for the post before the federal government took it over in 1849?
40007.e: Before the federal state was founded, the cantons organised the postal service. On 1 January 1849 the federal government took over the post.
40007.m: The federal government has been responsible for the post since 1849.

40008.q: Into which two companies was the PTT split in 1998?
40008.e: PTT stood for post, telephone, telegraph. In 1998 the postal services were given to Swiss Post and telecommunications to Swisscom.
40008.m: In 1998 the PTT became Swiss Post and Swisscom.

40009.q: What may only Swiss Post deliver in Switzerland?
40009.e: Only Swiss Post may deliver domestic letters up to 50 grams. With this monopoly it funds part of the basic service.
40009.m: Swiss Post has a monopoly on light letters.

40010.q: Why can Swiss Post not simply close all post offices in the countryside?
a: It must be easy to reach for almost everyone
Because it earns the most there
40010.e: Swiss Post must provide a basic service. 90 per cent of the population should be able to reach a post office or post agency within 20 minutes.
40010.m: Swiss Post must be easy to reach for almost everyone.

40011.q: How did the SBB come about?
a: The federal government bought large private railways
It grew out of the post
40011.e: In 1898 the people agreed that the federal government should buy the large private railways. From 1902 the trains ran as the SBB.
40011.m: The SBB came about because the federal government bought large private railways.

a: Private shareholders on the stock exchange
40012.e: Since 1999 the SBB has been a special statutory public limited company. All the shares belong to the Swiss Confederation.
40012.m: The SBB belongs entirely to the federal government.

40013.q: What did the SBB introduce in 1982 so that trains run regularly at the same minute?
40013.e: With the regular-interval timetable, trains leave, for example, every hour at the same minute. This makes connections easier and train travel easy to plan.
40013.m: Thanks to the regular-interval timetable, trains in Switzerland run regularly at the same time.

40014.q: Roughly how many countries founded the UN with the Charter in 1945?
40014.e: 51 states were founding members of the UN in 1945. Today the UN has 193 members.
40014.m: Around 50 countries founded the UN in 1945.

40015.q: What can the UN Security Council decide under the Charter if a country threatens peace?
a: A new king for the country
40015.e: The Security Council can decide on sanctions, for example trade bans. As a last resort, it may also authorise military measures.
40015.m: The Security Council can impose sanctions if peace is threatened.

40016.q: How many permanent members with a veto does the UN Security Council have under the Charter?
